question: Endometriosis is best diagnosed by

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Assessment and management of endometriosis 2025__JC__000194
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Assessment and management of endometriosis 2025
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Diagnosis of endometriosis
  Content: Key recommendations: Consider endometriosis when a woman has at least one of chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea that disrupts daily activities, deep dyspareunia, cyclical bowel symptoms—especially dyschezia—cyclical urinary symptoms—especially dysuria or haematuria—or infertility (Best practice). Offer abdominal and pelvic examination when symptoms suggest endometriosis; look for restricted organ mobility, tender posterior vaginal nodules and pelvic or abdominal masses (Grade 1C). Do not delay discussion or initiation of empirical treatment for suspected disease, since treatment may improve quality of life (Best practice). Refer suspected or confirmed cases to a Gynaecologist for severe, persistent or recurrent symptoms; examination findings; associated infertility; ineffective, intolerable or contraindicated initial management; or imaging suggestive of a higher stage or deeply infiltrating disease, including endometrioma or invasion of other organs (Best practice). Refer suspected or confirmed deeply infiltrative disease affecting the bowel, bladder or ureter to a specialist endometriosis service (Best practice). Offer transvaginal ultrasound during investigation and consider transabdominal ultrasound when the transvaginal approach is unsuitable (Grade 1A). MRI is not a first-line diagnostic investigation, but is recommended when deeply infiltrative disease of the bowel, bladder or ureter is suspected (Grade 1B). Do not use computed tomography (CT) or positron emission tomography-CT (PET-CT) to diagnose endometriosis (Best practice). Negative imaging must not be used to exclude endometriosis (Grade 1B). Do not use biomarkers, including serum CA-125, for diagnosis (Grade 1A). Consider laparoscopy for suggestive symptoms when empirical treatment fails or is unsuitable, including when imaging is negative (Best practice). Biopsy suspected lesions during laparoscopy for histological confirmation; negative histology does not completely exclude disease (Grade 1B). Refer for laparoscopy to a Gynaecologist with suitable laparoscopic training and skills to optimise assessment of the abdomen and pelvis (Best practice).

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Bašković et al. 2025 The Evaluation, Diagnosis, and Management of Ovarian Cysts, Masses, and Their Complications in Fetus__JC__000200
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Bašković et al. 2025 The Evaluation, Diagnosis, and Management of Ovarian Cysts, Masses, and Their Complications in Fetus
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 2.4. Adolescents
  Content: Adolescent ovaries contain follicles at different stages. Most adolescent cysts are follicular, arising when a developing follicle neither ovulates nor involutes. Large cysts may cause urinary frequency, constipation, or lower abdominal pressure; torsion, rupture, and hemorrhage cause intense acute pain. The differential diagnosis includes obstructive genital anomalies, ovarian tumors, tubal disease, uterine masses, and urinary or gastrointestinal conditions. Ultrasound is the first imaging examination. Follicular cysts generally resolve within eight weeks. Monophasic combined estrogen/progestin oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) with ≥ 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol are commonly recommended to inhibit the ovarian-hypothalamic axis, suppress ovulation, and prevent new functional cysts. Persistence for ≥3 months, size ≥ 6 cm, pelvic pain, or urinary frequency are indications for laparoscopic cystectomy or aspiration, although some simple cysts measuring 6 to 12 cm resolve and can be monitored safely in selected patients. Cystectomy is usually preferred over aspiration because aspiration has a high recurrence rate. For asymptomatic corpus luteum cysts, observation for three months is recommended; monophasic combined estrogen/progestin OCPs containing ≥ 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol are also prescribed, and cystectomy alone is seldom justified. Persistent or non-involuting cysts should undergo cystectomy with preservation of ovarian tissue. One illustrated 13-year-old had about a week of brief recurrent cramping; imaging showed a nonperfused right ovarian solid-cystic mass measuring 9.1 × 8.8 cm, and surgery identified torsion with partial necrosis and a mature teratoma on histology. Another illustrated 14-year-old had intermittent pain, anorexia, and a palpable right ovarian cyst measuring 16.2 × 14.6 cm that compressed nearby structures; after aspiration of 2 L of clear contents, ovarian-sparing laparoscopic cystectomy yielded a simple cyst.

  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: Hypertension
  Description: Blood pressure of 140 mmHg systolic or higher, or 90 mmHg diastolic or higher, during pregnancy.
  Epidemiology: Hypertensive disorders affect around 8% to 10% of all pregnant women.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Chronic hypertension
      Distinguishing features: Hypertension present at the booking visit, before 20 weeks, or when the woman is already taking antihypertensive medication on referral to maternity services.
    - Name: Gestational hypertension
      Distinguishing features: New hypertension after 20 weeks without significant proteinuria.
    - Name: Pre-eclampsia

      Interpretation: Hypertension is 140 mmHg systolic or higher, or 90 mmHg diastolic or higher; severe hypertension is over 160 mmHg systolic or over 110 mmHg diastolic.

    Long term effects:
      - A history of a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy is associated with greater risk of hypertension and cardiovascular disease later in life.

  Heading: 11.2 Epidemiology/aetiology/pathophysiology/risk factors
  Content: About 15% of couples seek infertility care after failing to conceive within 12 consecutive months. Difficulty conceiving a first child affects one in eight couples, and difficulty conceiving another affects one in six. A male-associated factor, usually accompanied by abnormal semen parameters, is identified in 50% of involuntarily childless couples. Every infertile couple should therefore have the male partner assessed by a urologist trained in male reproduction. Potential contributors include congenital or acquired urogenital abnormalities, genetic abnormalities, malignancy, urogenital infection, varicocele, raised scrotal temperature, endocrine or immunological factors, prior scrotal surgery and exposure to gonadotoxic radiotherapy or chemotherapy. Advanced paternal age is an additional risk factor. The female partner’s age and ovarian reserve may affect the choice and timing of assisted reproductive technology (ART) or surgery. Assessment after 6 months without conception when the female partner is older than 35 years remains debated. Table 11.1 reports the distribution of male infertility causes and associated factors across its stated patient groups.

Document sections:
  Heading: Hyperandrogenism Diagnostic Evaluation
  Content: In adult women, hirsutism, alopecia, and acne indicate clinical hyperandrogenism and can signal biochemical hyperandrogenism. Assessment should measure total and free testosterone; the calculated free androgen index can estimate free testosterone. Main conclusion: Early recognition and treatment of ectopic pregnancy are essential to reduce the risk of rupture and severe hemorrhage. Management should reflect hemodynamic stability, implantation site, diagnostic findings, and the patient’s fertility goals, with urgent surgery when rupture is suspected.

Narrative summary: This educational review examines the presentation, diagnosis, and management of ectopic pregnancy rather than reporting a new clinical study. Ectopic pregnancy affects approximately 1% to 2% of pregnancies in the United States and accounts for 2.7% of pregnancy-related deaths. Approximately 97% occur in the fallopian tube. Lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding are common, while dizziness, fainting, shoulder pain, or severe pelvic pain may indicate rupture.

Evaluation combines serum β-hCG measurements with ultrasound, particularly TVUS. A β-hCG level >2000 mIU/mL without a visible intrauterine pregnancy is highly suggestive of ectopic pregnancy; the review also notes a suggested discriminatory cutoff of up to 3500 mIU/mL to avoid misdiagnosing a viable pregnancy. When pregnancy location remains uncertain, serial β-hCG measurements and repeat imaging may be needed.

Hemodynamic instability or suspected rupture requires urgent surgical intervention. For selected asymptomatic patients with low, declining β-hCG, expectant management may be considered; 88% of ectopic pregnancies with an initial β-hCG level of <200 mIU/mL resolved spontaneously. In appropriate candidates, methotrexate is a medical option, with reported success of approximately 70% to 95%; β-hCG monitoring continues until the level is undetectable. Surgical options include salpingostomy and salpingectomy. For cesarean scar ectopic pregnancy, expectant management is not recommended except in select cases of confirmed fetal demise, and systemic methotrexate alone is not recommended.

Main conclusion: Menstrual irregularity during the first 2 years after menarche is often physiological, but associated anemia or dysmenorrhea warrants treatment or investigation. Identifying pathological causes without prematurely labeling adolescents, and coordinating care across specialties, may improve quality of life and help prevent serious health problems.

Narrative summary: This review examined the causes, diagnosis, and treatment of menstrual disorders in adolescence. The authors searched PubMed in April 2024, screened 1724 abstracts, assessed 115 full texts, and included 71 articles in a narrative analysis; they also consulted relevant ESHRE and awmf guidance. In the first 2 years after menarche, irregular cycles commonly reflect anovulation and immaturity of the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis rather than disease. Disabling heavy bleeding, anemia, or pain are exceptions that require attention. The review distinguishes this physiological pattern from conditions including bleeding disorders, amenorrhea, hypogonadism, premature ovarian insufficiency, hyperandrogenemia, endometriosis, and genital malformations. Assessment is guided by symptoms and developmental stage and may include history, examination, abdominal sonography, and selected laboratory or other investigations. Treatment depends on the cause: options discussed include hormonal management of heavy bleeding, correction of anemia, restoration of adequate estrogenization in hypogonadism, and appropriate management of suspected endometriosis or obstructive malformations. The authors caution against diagnosing PCOS prematurely in adolescence and favor individualized monitoring when features indicate increased risk. They emphasize collaboration among primary care, pediatric, gynecological, and hematological clinicians, particularly when adolescents fall between pediatric and adult services. Remaining knowledge gaps include blood-test reference ranges, drug doses, and alternative treatments.

Document sections:
  Heading: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome Clinical Features
  Content: A comprehensive clinical assessment is essential because history and examination inform 2 out of 3 diagnostic criteria and help identify alternative conditions. Relevant information includes menstrual and fertility history, obesity, and hyperandrogenic features. Under the 2023 International Evidence-Based PCOS Guidelines, irregular cycles are characterized as follows: cycles in the first year postmenarche are considered part of normal pubertal transition; within 1 to <3 years postmenarche, intervals <21 or >45 days are irregular; from 3 years postmenarche until perimenopause, intervals <21 or >35 days or <8 cycles per year are irregular; any cycle 1 year postmenarche with an interval >90 days is irregular; and primary amenorrhea by age 15 or >3 years post thelarche (breast development) is included. Hair loss may affect the vertex or crown or be diffuse; more severe hyperandrogenism may cause bitemporal loss and frontal hairline recession. Adolescents with severe acne or acne resistant to oral or topical antibiotics may have a 40% chance of developing PCOS. Persistent or worsening acne in females in their mid-20s to 30s calls for particular attention to hyperandrogenism. Hirsutism consists of coarse, dark terminal hair in a typically male distribution. Increased muscle mass, reduced breast size, voice deepening, and clitoromegaly are uncommon in PCOS; such virilization suggests elevated androgens and warrants investigation, especially for an ovarian or adrenal androgen-producing tumor. Hirsutism should be assessed objectively with the modified Ferrim-Gallwey scoring system. Depending on ethnicity, a modified Ferriman-Gallwey score (mFG) of 4 to 6 should be used for detection, while recognizing that self-treatment can obscure examination findings.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Diagnosis of endometriosis
  Content: Key recommendations: Consider endometriosis when a woman has at least one of chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea that disrupts daily activities, deep dyspareunia, cyclical bowel symptoms—especially dyschezia—cyclical urinary symptoms—especially dysuria or haematuria—or infertility (Best practice). Offer abdominal and pelvic examination when symptoms suggest endometriosis; look for restricted organ mobility, tender posterior vaginal nodules and pelvic or abdominal masses (Grade 1C). Do not delay discussion or initiation of empirical treatment for suspected disease, since treatment may improve quality of life (Best practice). Refer suspected or confirmed cases to a Gynaecologist for severe, persistent or recurrent symptoms; examination findings; associated infertility; ineffective, intolerable or contraindicated initial management; or imaging suggestive of a higher stage or deeply infiltrating disease, including endometrioma or invasion of other organs (Best practice). Refer suspected or confirmed deeply infiltrative disease affecting the bowel, bladder or ureter to a specialist endometriosis service (Best practice). Offer transvaginal ultrasound during investigation and consider transabdominal ultrasound when the transvaginal approach is unsuitable (Grade 1A). MRI is not a first-line diagnostic investigation, but is recommended when deeply infiltrative disease of the bowel, bladder or ureter is suspected (Grade 1B). Do not use computed tomography (CT) or positron emission tomography-CT (PET-CT) to diagnose endometriosis (Best practice). Negative imaging must not be used to exclude endometriosis (Grade 1B). Do not use biomarkers, including serum CA-125, for diagnosis (Grade 1A). Consider laparoscopy for suggestive symptoms when empirical treatment fails or is unsuitable, including when imaging is negative (Best practice). Biopsy suspected lesions during laparoscopy for histological confirmation; negative histology does not completely exclude disease (Grade 1B). Refer for laparoscopy to a Gynaecologist with suitable laparoscopic training and skills to optimise assessment of the abdomen and pelvis (Best practice).

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_06
  Name: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (P-PROM)
  Synonyms:
    - P-PROM
  Description: Membranes rupture before 37+0 weeks of pregnancy while established labour has not begun.
  Clinical presentation: A woman may report symptoms suggestive of membrane rupture; examination may show a pool of amniotic fluid.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Speculum examination
      Purpose: Look for pooling of amniotic fluid.
      When indicated: When symptoms suggest P-PROM and labour has not become established.
      Interpretation: Visible pooling supports care for P-PROM without further diagnostic testing. If no pooling is seen, test vaginal fluid with insulin-like growth factor binding protein-1 or placental alpha-microglobulin-1.
    - Test: insulin-like growth factor binding protein-1 test
      Purpose: Help assess possible P-PROM when amniotic fluid is not seen on speculum examination.
      When indicated: When symptoms suggest P-PROM but pooling of amniotic fluid is absent.
      Interpretation: A positive result must be considered alongside clinical condition, medical and pregnancy history, and gestational age; it is not sufficient on its own to determine care. A negative result with no visible amniotic fluid makes P-PROM unlikely.
    - Test: placental alpha-microglobulin-1 test
      Purpose: Help assess possible P-PROM when amniotic fluid is not seen on speculum examination.
      When indicated: When symptoms suggest P-PROM but pooling of amniotic fluid is absent.
      Interpretation: A positive result must be considered alongside clinical condition, medical and pregnancy history, and gestational age; it is not sufficient on its own to determine care. A negative result with no visible amniotic fluid makes P-PROM unlikely.
    - Test: Clinical assessment
      Purpose: Contribute to diagnosis of intrauterine infection alongside laboratory tests and fetal heart rate assessment.
      When indicated: When assessing a woman with P-PROM for intrauterine infection.
      Interpretation: Discordant clinical and test findings warrant continued observation and consideration of repeat testing.
    - Test: C-reactive protein
      Purpose: Contribute to diagnosis of intrauterine infection.
      When indicated: When assessing a woman with P-PROM for intrauterine infection.
      Interpretation: A single result must not be used alone to confirm or exclude intrauterine infection.
    - Test: White blood cell count
      Purpose: Contribute to diagnosis of intrauterine infection.
      When indicated: When assessing a woman with P-PROM for intrauterine infection.
      Interpretation: It must not be used alone to confirm or exclude intrauterine infection.
    - Test: Measurement of fetal heart rate using cardiotocography
      Purpose: Contribute to diagnosis of intrauterine infection.
      When indicated: When assessing a woman with P-PROM for intrauterine infection.
      Interpretation: It must not be used alone to confirm or exclude intrauterine infection.
    - Test: nitrazine
      Purpose: The guideline advises against using this test to diagnose P-PROM.
  Follow up:
    Recommended tests:
      - After a positive vaginal-fluid test, re-evaluate diagnostic status at a later time as an alternative to offering care consistent with P-PROM.
      - If clinical assessment and tests for intrauterine infection disagree, continue observation and consider repeating the tests.
    Survivorship notes: After a negative vaginal-fluid test with no amniotic fluid observed, advise return for reassessment if further symptoms suggest P-PROM or preterm labour.

    - Refer severe pain that does not respond to first-line analgesia and hormonal suppression to a pain specialist.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: paracetamol
      Evidence level: moderate-quality evidence
      Recommendation grade: Grade 2B
      Summary: Offer as an analgesic option, alone or with NSAIDs; it does not change the pathological course of endometriosis.
      Key outcomes: A systematic review found that paracetamol was not more effective than placebo for pain reduction; the underlying evidence was described as very low quality.
    - Name: NSAIDs
      Evidence level: moderate-quality evidence
      Recommendation grade: Grade 2B
      Summary: Offer for pain, alone or together with paracetamol, while accounting for gastrointestinal effects and possible kidney injury with long-term use.
    - Name: neuromodulator therapies
      Evidence level: moderate-quality evidence
      Recommendation grade: Grade 2B
      Summary: May be used for endometriosis-associated pain, generally within a broader strategy coordinated with a specialist pain management service. Discussed examples are amitriptyline, nortriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin and pregabalin.
      Key outcomes: In RCTs concerning chronic pelvic pain, neuromodulators were not shown to be clearly superior to placebo.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: opioid medication
      Reason: Its use for endometriosis-associated pain is not recommended because of adverse effects and the potential for dependence.
  Special considerations: Evidence for analgesics specifically in endometriosis is limited. Neuromodulators can cause severe, dose-limiting adverse effects.

Document sections:
  Heading: 6.2. Amenorrhea
  Content: Amenorrhea can have hormonal or organic causes and may be primary or secondary. Primary amenorrhea denotes no menarche by age 16; secondary amenorrhea means no menstruation for more than 90 days after previous periods. Pregnancy should be excluded before further investigation, and a previously regular cycle that becomes irregular warrants assessment. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (WHO I) occurs with pubertas tarda and is largely constitutional without pathological significance, although gonadal, hypothalamic, pituitary, or genetic disorders—including Sheehan syndrome and Kallmann syndrome—can cause it. Common adolescent causes of hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction (WHO II) are a high-risk constellation for polycystic ovary syndrome and central dysregulation associated with stress, anorexia, or competitive sport. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (WHO III), or premature ovarian insufficiency, involves loss of ovarian activity before age 40 years and affects approximately 1:10,000 patients under age 20. Potential causes are Turner syndrome, a Fragile X premutation, autoimmune predisposition, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or ovarian surgery. Organic amenorrhea (WHO IV) includes genital malformations such as Meier–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome and hymenal atresia, often first identified because of primary amenorrhea or dysmenorrhea. Reported incidences of the various causes differ so greatly by study and population that no general statement can be made. Absent follicular maturation can prevent adequate estrogenization and endometrial thickening, so bleeding does not occur. In the short term, estrogen deficiency can prevent pubertal onset and secondary sexual development; in the long term, it can impair bone, cognitive, and cardiovascular health. Girls with hypo- or hypergonadotropic hypogonadism consequently need treatment to induce puberty and sustain adequate estrogenization.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Main conclusion: Early recognition and treatment of ectopic pregnancy are essential to reduce the risk of rupture and severe hemorrhage. Management should reflect hemodynamic stability, implantation site, diagnostic findings, and the patient’s fertility goals, with urgent surgery when rupture is suspected.

Narrative summary: This educational review examines the presentation, diagnosis, and management of ectopic pregnancy rather than reporting a new clinical study. Ectopic pregnancy affects approximately 1% to 2% of pregnancies in the United States and accounts for 2.7% of pregnancy-related deaths. Approximately 97% occur in the fallopian tube. Lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding are common, while dizziness, fainting, shoulder pain, or severe pelvic pain may indicate rupture.

Evaluation combines serum β-hCG measurements with ultrasound, particularly TVUS. A β-hCG level >2000 mIU/mL without a visible intrauterine pregnancy is highly suggestive of ectopic pregnancy; the review also notes a suggested discriminatory cutoff of up to 3500 mIU/mL to avoid misdiagnosing a viable pregnancy. When pregnancy location remains uncertain, serial β-hCG measurements and repeat imaging may be needed.

Hemodynamic instability or suspected rupture requires urgent surgical intervention. For selected asymptomatic patients with low, declining β-hCG, expectant management may be considered; 88% of ectopic pregnancies with an initial β-hCG level of <200 mIU/mL resolved spontaneously. In appropriate candidates, methotrexate is a medical option, with reported success of approximately 70% to 95%; β-hCG monitoring continues until the level is undetectable. Surgical options include salpingostomy and salpingectomy. For cesarean scar ectopic pregnancy, expectant management is not recommended except in select cases of confirmed fetal demise, and systemic methotrexate alone is not recommended.

Document sections:
  Heading: 6.10. Endometriosis
  Content: Dysmenorrhea means painful menstruation. Primary dysmenorrhea occurs without a specific pathological condition; secondary dysmenorrhea occurs with a reproductive-system disorder causing menstrual cramps, such as endometriosis or fibroids. Endometriosis affects approximately 2% of adolescent women. It is an estrogen-dependent inflammatory condition involving functional endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity. Refractory pain, noncyclic lower abdominal pain, dysmenorrhea, dysuria, dyschezia, or dyspareunia makes it a likely diagnosis; increased absence from school or sport can also be a clue. Pain often accompanies nausea, vomiting, dyschezia, constipation, or vasovagal reactions. Definitive confirmation requires histology, but medication is first-line treatment. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for pain and hormonal treatment with progestogens or an extended-use contraceptive pill (off-label use) can be used to limit disease progression until childbearing is desired. GnRH analogs warrant great caution in adolescents because of adverse skeletal effects and long-term osteoporosis risk. Persistent symptoms may justify surgery, which should be performed at a highly experienced center to preserve ovarian reserve. Diagnosis appears delayed and treatment often inadequate in both adolescents and adults. Possible reasons include low ultrasonographic detection and reluctance to operate on adolescents. Clinical findings can nevertheless justify treatment without histological confirmation, and girls benefit from such treatment.

  Content: Patients may have no symptoms; when symptoms occur, abnormal uterine bleeding is the most common. Abdominal pain, pelvic pain, and infertility may also occur. One in four reproductive-aged women with abnormal bleeding has an endometrial polyp in the cavity. Evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding should establish its cause and severity, associated symptoms, and comorbidities. A thorough medical and surgical history helps exclude other causes. No bleeding pattern is diagnostic of a polyp, but the bleeding history should be characterized; menorrhagia and intermenstrual spotting are reported most often. Tamoxifen, commonly used for breast cancer, can act as an agonist or antagonist in tissues bearing estrogen receptors. It has anticancer effects in breast tissue but carcinogenic effects in endometrial tissue. Chronic tamoxifen use is associated with endometrial polyps at an incidence of 20% to 35%. Hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms may also be associated with polyp formation, irregular bleeding, and ultrasound evidence of endometrial thickening. Clinical examination should include a general assessment, bimanual examination, and sterile speculum examination. The cervix and vaginal vault should be examined completely to exclude other structural explanations for symptoms. A pedunculated polyp may be visible at the external os.

  Content: About 15% of couples seek infertility care after failing to conceive within 12 consecutive months. Difficulty conceiving a first child affects one in eight couples, and difficulty conceiving another affects one in six. A male-associated factor, usually accompanied by abnormal semen parameters, is identified in 50% of involuntarily childless couples. Every infertile couple should therefore have the male partner assessed by a urologist trained in male reproduction. Potential contributors include congenital or acquired urogenital abnormalities, genetic abnormalities, malignancy, urogenital infection, varicocele, raised scrotal temperature, endocrine or immunological factors, prior scrotal surgery and exposure to gonadotoxic radiotherapy or chemotherapy. Document sections:
  Heading: Overview
  Content: Uterine rupture in pregnancy is uncommon but often catastrophic, with substantial fetal and maternal morbidity. Numerous factors raise risk, although rupture remains uncommon even in high-risk groups. Publications from 1976-2012 described 2,084 ruptures among 2,951,297 pregnant women across 25 reports, giving an overall rate of 1 in 1,146 pregnancies (0.07%). Early manifestations are usually nonspecific, complicating diagnosis and sometimes delaying treatment. The interval from diagnosis to delivery is generally only 10-37 minutes before clinically important fetal injury becomes inevitable; catastrophic bleeding, fetal anoxia, or both cause that injury. Warning findings vary, and the brief opportunity for definitive treatment makes rupture particularly concerning to clinicians.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 4.8.4.3 Management of ureteric fistulae
  Content: Higher-risk operations require surgeons able to protect ureteric blood supply and promptly recognise injury. An intraoperative injury should be repaired immediately using debridement, adequate vascularity, a tension-free anastomosis and internal stenting. After relevant abdominal or pelvic surgery, unexpectedly slow recovery, fluid leakage or pelvicalyceal dilatation should raise suspicion of delayed upper-tract injury. No operative approach has proved superior; consensus favours established tissue-repair principles and experienced teams. Options include internal or external drainage, nephrostomy and stenting, and repair early (< 2 weeks) or later (> 3 months) when needed. Functional and anatomical imaging after repair should detect ureteric stricture or declining renal function. Early postoperative UVF, chiefly following hysterectomy, is the most frequent upper-tract fistula presentation in urological practice. In an RCT of 3,141 women undergoing open or laparoscopic gynaecological surgery, prophylactic ureteric stents did not alter the low injury risk (1%). Selected endoscopic approaches include retrograde or antegrade stenting with nephrostomy, or ureteroscopic realignment, but long-term success is unknown. Distal antegrade ureteric occlusion plus nephrostomy often palliates terminal malignant-fistula leakage. Failure or secondary stricture after endoluminal treatment usually calls for abdominal repair, potentially including end-to-end anastomosis, reimplantation with psoas hitch or Boari flap, or bowel replacement. Nephrectomy is a last resort, particularly with poor function on the affected side and a normal opposite kidney.

Document sections:
  Heading: 5. Special Features in Diagnostics
  Content: Usual assessment comprises a detailed history, physical examination, sonography of internal genitalia, and measurement of height and weight. Examination should reflect the adolescent’s developmental stage and sexual activity. Tanner stages categorize pubertal development and help assess age-appropriate hormonal-axis function and progression. External genital inspection uses gentle separation and lateral or caudal traction of the labia majora; a pediatric speculum is seldom needed. Abdominal sonography is performed with a full bladder. It assesses the uterus and ovaries, including uterine shape as an indicator of estrogenization, endometrial thickness, antral follicles, cysts, and follicular persistence. Genetic assessment, magnetic tomography (MRI), or, rarely, laparoscopy may address specific diagnostic questions. A GnRH test can assess pituitary function; an ACTH test can be useful when congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is suspected. In amenorrhea, a progestogen test can assess endogenous estrogen activity and endometrial function; in uterine amenorrhea, an estrogen–progestogen test can assess endometrial responsiveness. Hormone measurements, bone-age or bone-density assessment, glucose-metabolism assessment, and testing for suspected chronic disease are reserved for particular questions. Pregnancy, sexually transmitted diseases, and trauma should be excluded according to symptoms. Figures 3 and 4 illustrate abdominal sonographic views of an adolescent ovary and uterus.

  Epidemiology: Approximately 15% of couples do not achieve pregnancy within 12 consecutive months and seek medical care. One in eight couples have difficulty conceiving a first child, and one in six have difficulty conceiving a subsequent child.
  Clinical presentation: Abnormal semen parameters commonly accompany a male-associated factor, but semen analysis alone cannot distinguish fertile from infertile men.

      Distinguishing features: Difficulty conceiving a first child.
    - Name: secondary infertility
      Distinguishing features: Difficulty conceiving a subsequent child.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Medical, reproductive and family history
      Purpose: Identify possible causes and relevant health, lifestyle and behavioural factors.
      When indicated: During assessment of men seeking help for fertility problems.
    - Test: Physical examination
      Purpose: Assess male reproductive health, including testicular volume.
      When indicated: During assessment of men seeking help for fertility problems.
    - Test: Semen analysis
      Purpose: Assess semen and sperm characteristics using WHO reference values.
      When indicated: During the initial evaluation; obtain at least two consecutive analyses when the baseline result is abnormal.
      Interpretation: One analysis is sufficient if results meet WHO criteria. Abnormal results on at least two analyses warrant further andrological investigation. The 2021 lower reference limits (5th centile, with 95% CI) are semen volume 1.4 (1.3–1.5) ml; total sperm number 39 (35–40) 106/ejaculate; sperm concentration 16 (15–18) 106/ml; total motility 42 (40–43)%; progressive motility 30 (29–31)%; vitality 54 (50–56)%; and normal morphology 4 (3.9–4.0)%.
    - Test: Serum total testosterone, FSH and LH
      Purpose: Assess hormonal status and detect hypogonadism.
      When indicated: At least in all cases of oligozoospermia and azoospermia.
    - Test: Prader orchidometer or testicular US
      Purpose: Estimate testicular volume.
      When indicated: During assessment of infertile men.
    - Test: Scrotal US
      Purpose: Examine testicular structure, identify tumours and assess possible signs of obstruction.
      When indicated: In men with infertility; particularly useful when clinical assessment of testicular volume is difficult.
      Interpretation: Possible signs of obstruction include a dilated rete testis, an enlarged epididymis with cystic lesions, or an absent vas deferens.
    - Test: Female partner fertility assessment, including ovarian reserve
      Purpose: Inform the timing and choice of treatment for the couple.
      When indicated: In parallel with diagnosis and management of the infertile male.
    - Test: ROS measurement
      Purpose: Assess oxidative stress.
      When indicated: Routine testing is not recommended.
      Interpretation: Testing methods are not standardised and require further validation.

      - Infertile men have increased risks of cardiometabolic disorders, cardiovascular mortality and overall mortality compared with fertile controls.

  Content: Hyperandrogenemia and its underlying causes form another group of menstrual disorders. Adolescent manifestations include acne, hirsutism, alopecia, oligo-/amenorrhea, pubertas praecox, and clitoral hypertrophy. Rapid virilization suggests a rare androgen-producing tumor. Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_02
  Name: Chronic hypertension
  Description: Hypertension identified at the booking visit or before 20 weeks, or already treated with antihypertensive medication when the woman is referred to maternity services. Its aetiology may be primary or secondary.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Blood pressure measurement
      Purpose: Assess blood pressure control during pregnancy and after birth.
      When indicated: At additional antenatal appointments according to individual needs; after birth, daily for the first 2 days, at least once between day 3 and day 5, and when clinically indicated following a treatment change.
      Interpretation: During treatment in pregnancy, the target is 135/85 mmHg. After birth, the aim is to keep blood pressure lower than 140/90 mmHg.
    - Test: Placental growth factor (PLGF)-based testing
      Purpose: Help rule out pre-eclampsia.
      When indicated: When pre-eclampsia is suspected between 20 weeks and 36 weeks and 6 days of pregnancy.
    - Test: Ultrasound for fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume assessment
      Purpose: Assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume.
      When indicated: At 28 weeks, 32 weeks and 36 weeks.
    - Test: Umbilical artery doppler velocimetry
      Purpose: Assess the fetal circulation.
      When indicated: At 28 weeks, 32 weeks and 36 weeks.
    - Test: Cardiotocography
      Purpose: Assess fetal status.
      When indicated: Only if clinically indicated.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Additional antenatal appointments depend on maternal and fetal needs; these may be weekly when hypertension is poorly controlled or every 2 to 4 weeks when well controlled. After birth, offer a treatment review at 2 weeks and a medical review at 6 to 8 weeks.
    Recommended tests:
      - Measure blood pressure daily for the first 2 days after birth and at least once between day 3 and day 5.
      - Measure blood pressure as clinically indicated if antihypertensive treatment changes after birth.
    Long term effects:
      - For women with chronic hypertension in a current or previous pregnancy, the table reports an approximately 1.7 times increased risk of a major adverse cardiovascular event and an approximately 1.8 times increased risk of stroke, relative to women without a hypertensive disorder during pregnancy.
    Survivorship notes: Continue antihypertensive treatment after birth if required, with review by a GP or specialist.

  Description: Hypertension first appearing after 20 weeks of pregnancy without significant proteinuria.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Full assessment in secondary care
      Purpose: Evaluate gestational hypertension and factors requiring closer assessment and follow-up.
      When indicated: At presentation, by a healthcare professional trained in managing hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
      Interpretation: Factors requiring additional assessment and follow-up include nulliparity, age 40 years or older, pregnancy interval of more than 10 years, family history of pre-eclampsia, multi-fetal pregnancy, BMI of 35 kg/m2 or more, gestational age at presentation, previous pre-eclampsia or gestational hypertension, and pre-existing vascular or kidney disease.
    - Test: Blood pressure measurement
      Purpose: Assess severity and response to treatment.
      When indicated: For hypertension, once or twice a week depending on blood pressure until it is 135/85 mmHg or less; for severe hypertension, every 15 to 30 minutes until it is less than 160/110 mmHg.
      Interpretation: Once antihypertensive treatment is given, the target is 135/85 mmHg or less.
    - Test: Dipstick proteinuria testing
      Purpose: Monitor for proteinuria.
      When indicated: Once or twice a week alongside blood pressure measurement for hypertension; daily during admission for severe hypertension.
      Interpretation: A result of 1+ or more prompts quantification with albumin:creatinine ratio or protein:creatinine ratio.
    - Test: Full blood count, liver function and renal function
      Purpose: Monitor maternal haematological, liver and kidney status.
      When indicated: At presentation and then weekly.
    - Test: Placental growth factor (PLGF)-based testing
      Purpose: Help rule out pre-eclampsia.
      When indicated: On 1 occasion if pre-eclampsia is suspected, between 20 weeks and 36 weeks and 6 days of pregnancy.
    - Test: Fetal heart auscultation
      Purpose: Assess fetal heart activity.
      When indicated: At every antenatal appointment.
    - Test: Ultrasound for fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume assessment
      Purpose: Assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume.
      When indicated: At diagnosis; if findings are normal, repeat every 2 to 4 weeks if clinically indicated. If severe hypertension persists, repeat every 2 weeks.
    - Test: Umbilical artery doppler velocimetry
      Purpose: Assess the fetal circulation.
      When indicated: At diagnosis; if findings are normal, repeat every 2 to 4 weeks if clinically indicated. In severe gestational hypertension, subsequent monitoring is determined by scan findings.
    - Test: Cardiotocography (CTG)
      Purpose: Assess fetal status.
      When indicated: For gestational hypertension, only if clinically indicated; for severe gestational hypertension, at diagnosis and subsequently if clinically indicated.
  Follow up:

      - Measure blood pressure as clinically indicated if antihypertensive treatment changes after birth.

      - After gestational hypertension in a previous or current pregnancy, hypertension of any type in a future pregnancy occurs in approximately 22% (1 in 5 women), pre-eclampsia in approximately 7% (1 in 14 women), gestational hypertension in between approximately 11% and 15% (up to 1 in 7 women), and chronic hypertension in approximately 3% (up to 1 in 34 women).

  Epidemiology: Hypertensive disorders affect around 8% to 10% of all pregnant women.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Chronic hypertension
      Distinguishing features: Hypertension present at the booking visit, before 20 weeks, or when the woman is already taking antihypertensive medication on referral to maternity services.
    - Name: Gestational hypertension
      Distinguishing features: New hypertension after 20 weeks without significant proteinuria.
    - Name: Pre-eclampsia
      Distinguishing features: New hypertension after 20 weeks accompanied by specified new-onset proteinuria, maternal organ dysfunction or uteroplacental dysfunction.
    - Name: Severe hypertension
      Distinguishing features: Blood pressure over 160 mmHg systolic or over 110 mmHg diastolic.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Blood pressure measurement
      Purpose: Identify hypertension and assess its severity.
      When indicated: During pregnancy and labour, and after birth when monitoring a hypertensive disorder.
      Interpretation: Hypertension is 140 mmHg systolic or higher, or 90 mmHg diastolic or higher; severe hypertension is over 160 mmHg systolic or over 110 mmHg diastolic.
  Follow up:
    Long term effects:
      - A history of a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy is associated with greater risk of hypertension and cardiovascular disease later in life.
      - The overall likelihood of a hypertensive disorder recurring in a future pregnancy is approximately 1 in 5.
    Survivorship notes: Women who have had a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy are advised to discuss cardiovascular risk reduction with their GP or specialist.

Document sections:
  Heading: Neonatal Outcomes
  Content: Because studies specifically examining neonatal outcomes after cesarean delivery on maternal request are limited, this discussion also considers cesarean delivery without labor. When birth occurs earlier than 39–40 weeks of gestation, elective cesarean delivery has a higher risk of neonatal respiratory morbidity than vaginal delivery, including transient tachypnea of the newborn, respiratory distress syndrome, and persistent pulmonary hypertension. Literature on elective cesarean delivery without labor also reports more complications related to prematurity among infants delivered by cesarean before 39 weeks of gestation. These include respiratory symptoms, adaptation problems such as hypothermia and hypoglycemia, and admission to neonatal intensive care. Given these potential complications, maternal-request cesarean delivery should not be performed before 39 weeks unless another indication warrants earlier birth. The 2006 National Institutes of Health consensus panel judged respiratory morbidity to be the only neonatal outcome with moderate-quality evidence; its risk varies with gestational age and is higher after cesarean than vaginal delivery. Evidence was poor for iatrogenic prematurity, neonatal hospital stay, fetal mortality, intracranial hemorrhage, neonatal asphyxia and encephalopathy, birth injury and laceration, and neonatal infection, limiting confidence in those results. Current evidence is insufficient to recommend cesarean delivery on maternal request over planned vaginal delivery on the basis of neonatal outcomes.

Document sections:
  Heading: 11.2 Epidemiology/aetiology/pathophysiology/risk factors
  Content: About 15% of couples seek infertility care after failing to conceive within 12 consecutive months. Difficulty conceiving a first child affects one in eight couples, and difficulty conceiving another affects one in six. A male-associated factor, usually accompanied by abnormal semen parameters, is identified in 50% of involuntarily childless couples. Every infertile couple should therefore have the male partner assessed by a urologist trained in male reproduction. Potential contributors include congenital or acquired urogenital abnormalities, genetic abnormalities, malignancy, urogenital infection, varicocele, raised scrotal temperature, endocrine or immunological factors, prior scrotal surgery and exposure to gonadotoxic radiotherapy or chemotherapy. Advanced paternal age is an additional risk factor. The female partner’s age and ovarian reserve may affect the choice and timing of assisted reproductive technology (ART) or surgery. Assessment after 6 months without conception when the female partner is older than 35 years remains debated. Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_03
  Name: Gestational hypertension
  Description: Hypertension first appearing after 20 weeks of pregnancy without significant proteinuria.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Full assessment in secondary care
      Purpose: Evaluate gestational hypertension and factors requiring closer assessment and follow-up.
      When indicated: At presentation, by a healthcare professional trained in managing hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
      Interpretation: Factors requiring additional assessment and follow-up include nulliparity, age 40 years or older, pregnancy interval of more than 10 years, family history of pre-eclampsia, multi-fetal pregnancy, BMI of 35 kg/m2 or more, gestational age at presentation, previous pre-eclampsia or gestational hypertension, and pre-existing vascular or kidney disease.
    - Test: Blood pressure measurement
      Purpose: Assess severity and response to treatment.
      When indicated: For hypertension, once or twice a week depending on blood pressure until it is 135/85 mmHg or less; for severe hypertension, every 15 to 30 minutes until it is less than 160/110 mmHg.
      Interpretation: Once antihypertensive treatment is given, the target is 135/85 mmHg or less.
    - Test: Dipstick proteinuria testing
      Purpose: Monitor for proteinuria.
      When indicated: Once or twice a week alongside blood pressure measurement for hypertension; daily during admission for severe hypertension.
      Interpretation: A result of 1+ or more prompts quantification with albumin:creatinine ratio or protein:creatinine ratio.
    - Test: Full blood count, liver function and renal function
      Purpose: Monitor maternal haematological, liver and kidney status.
      When indicated: At presentation and then weekly.
    - Test: Placental growth factor (PLGF)-based testing
      Purpose: Help rule out pre-eclampsia.
      When indicated: On 1 occasion if pre-eclampsia is suspected, between 20 weeks and 36 weeks and 6 days of pregnancy.
    - Test: Fetal heart auscultation
      Purpose: Assess fetal heart activity.
      When indicated: At every antenatal appointment.
    - Test: Ultrasound for fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume assessment
      Purpose: Assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume.
      When indicated: At diagnosis; if findings are normal, repeat every 2 to 4 weeks if clinically indicated. If severe hypertension persists, repeat every 2 weeks.
    - Test: Umbilical artery doppler velocimetry
      Purpose: Assess the fetal circulation.
      When indicated: At diagnosis; if findings are normal, repeat every 2 to 4 weeks if clinically indicated. In severe gestational hypertension, subsequent monitoring is determined by scan findings.
    - Test: Cardiotocography (CTG)
      Purpose: Assess fetal status.
      When indicated: For gestational hypertension, only if clinically indicated; for severe gestational hypertension, at diagnosis and subsequently if clinically indicated.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: After birth, offer women still receiving antihypertensive treatment a medical review 2 weeks after transfer to community care. Offer all women a medical review 6 to 8 weeks after birth.
    Recommended tests:
      - Measure blood pressure daily for the first 2 days after birth and at least once between day 3 and day 5.
      - Measure blood pressure as clinically indicated if antihypertensive treatment changes after birth.
    Long term effects:
      - After gestational hypertension in a previous or current pregnancy, hypertension of any type in a future pregnancy occurs in approximately 22% (1 in 5 women), pre-eclampsia in approximately 7% (1 in 14 women), gestational hypertension in between approximately 11% and 15% (up to 1 in 7 women), and chronic hypertension in approximately 3% (up to 1 in 34 women).

retrieved_chunks.text:
Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: endometriosis
  Description: A chronic, oestrogen-mediated inflammatory condition of uncertain cause in which tissue resembling endometrium occurs outside the uterus. Lesions commonly affect pelvic structures but may also occur outside the pelvis or be found incidentally during laparoscopy.
  Epidemiology: The guideline estimates that endometriosis affects 1 in 10 women and cites a World Health Organization estimate of 190 million women affected worldwide. Symptoms can begin in young women and persist after menopause. The reported average interval from symptom onset to confirmed diagnosis is 7-8 years.
  Clinical presentation: Presentations vary widely and do not reliably reflect the apparent extent of disease. Possible features include chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea that disrupts daily activities, deep dyspareunia, cyclical bowel symptoms—particularly dyschezia—cyclical urinary symptoms, and infertility. Fatigue, cyclical cough, haemoptysis, chest pain, pneumothorax, shoulder tip pain and scar swelling may also occur. Some women have no symptoms. Symptoms overlap with those of bowel and bladder disorders, musculoskeletal pain conditions and fibromyalgia.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: superficial peritoneal endometriosis
      Distinguishing features: Peritoneal disease may be missed on imaging, particularly when imaging findings are negative.
    - Name: ovarian endometrioma
      Distinguishing features: Ovarian disease that can be identified reliably with TVUS or MRI; other forms of endometriosis may coexist.
    - Name: deeply infiltrative endometriosis
      Distinguishing features: Disease extending beneath the peritoneum that may affect the uterosacral ligaments, pelvic side walls, rectovaginal septum, vagina, bowel, bladder or ureters.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Clinical history
      Purpose: Identify symptoms suggestive of endometriosis and support a presumptive diagnosis.
      When indicated: When endometriosis is suspected.
      Interpretation: A combination of symptoms, especially when cyclical, increases the likelihood of endometriosis; no symptom is specific to the disease.
    - Test: Abdominal and pelvic examination
      Purpose: Assess organ mobility, tenderness, posterior vaginal nodules and pelvic or abdominal masses.
      When indicated: Offer when symptoms suggest endometriosis; perform pelvic examination where appropriate.
      Interpretation: A normal examination does not exclude endometriosis, and examination alone cannot establish the diagnosis reliably.
    - Test: Speculum examination
      Purpose: Look for visible vaginal endometriotic lesions.
      When indicated: Where appropriate during clinical examination.
    - Test: Rectovaginal digital examination
      Purpose: Assess possible rectosigmoid infiltration or nodules and adnexal masses.
      When indicated: Consider where appropriate, with explicit consent and recognition that it may cause discomfort.
    - Test: TVUS
      Purpose: Investigate suspected endometriosis, particularly ovarian endometrioma or deeply infiltrative disease.
      When indicated: Offer as part of the investigation of suspected endometriosis.
      Interpretation: Negative imaging does not exclude endometriosis, particularly superficial peritoneal disease. In the Nisenblat et al. review, TVUS had 95% specificity and 65% sensitivity for superficial pelvic disease, 94% specificity and 79% sensitivity for deeply infiltrative disease, and 96% specificity and 95% sensitivity for ovarian endometriomas.
    - Test: Transabdominal ultrasound
      Purpose: Provide an alternative ultrasound approach.
      When indicated: Consider if transvaginal ultrasound is inappropriate or not tolerated.
    - Test: MRI
      Purpose: Assess the presence and extent of suspected deeply infiltrative lesions, including disease affecting the bowel, bladder or ureter.
      When indicated: Recommended for suspected deeply infiltrative disease involving the bowel, bladder or ureter; not recommended as the first-line diagnostic investigation.
      Interpretation: Negative imaging does not exclude endometriosis. The cited evidence reports 91% specificity and 95% sensitivity for endometriomas, and 72% specificity and 79% sensitivity for superficial peritoneal lesions.
    - Test: CT and PET-CT
      Purpose: The guideline discusses these imaging methods in relation to diagnosis; CT may have a role in planning surgery for deep disease involving the bladder, ureters and/or bowel.
      When indicated: Neither CT nor PET-CT is recommended to diagnose endometriosis.
      Interpretation: The evidence for diagnostic use is limited.
    - Test: Serum CA-125
      Purpose: The guideline evaluates, but does not recommend, its use for diagnosing endometriosis.
      When indicated: Do not use to diagnose endometriosis.
      Interpretation: An incidental result >35 IU/ml may be consistent with endometriosis, but disease can be present despite a result <35 IU/ml. A cited review reported pooled specificity 93% and sensitivity 52%; a negative result cannot rule out disease.
    - Test: Other endometrial, urinary and blood biomarkers
      Purpose: Investigated as possible diagnostic tests.
      When indicated: Diagnostic biomarkers are not recommended.
      Interpretation: The cited systematic reviews found no biomarker suitable to replace laparoscopy for diagnosis.
    - Test: Laparoscopy
      Purpose: Inspect the pelvis and abdomen for lesions, enable biopsy and provide an opportunity to classify disease.
      When indicated: Consider if empirical treatment is ineffective or inappropriate, including when imaging is negative.
      Interpretation: A negative result after thorough assessment has high negative predictive value, whereas an incomplete assessment can produce a false-negative result.
    - Test: Biopsy and histological examination
      Purpose: Confirm lesions suspected at laparoscopy; histology can also help exclude ovarian malignancy when an endometrioma is sampled or removed.
      When indicated: Take a biopsy of suspected lesions during diagnostic laparoscopy.
      Interpretation: Negative histology does not entirely exclude endometriosis.
  Staging:
    System: rASRM; ENZIAN; AAGL
    Additional rules: The guideline reports no agreed gold-standard classification. It describes rASRM as widely used but poorly reproducible, weakly correlated with pain and not inclusive of deep lesions in several organs. ENZIAN addresses deep and retroperitoneal disease and can be calculated from imaging for preoperative planning, but is not widely used and needs further evaluation for imaging-based application. AAGL can use imaging or operative findings, relates stages to surgical complexity and has not been fully validated. The guideline cites a proposed surgical classification toolbox using rASRM with ENZIAN and EFI where applicable.
  Prognostic tools:
    - Name: EFI
      Components:
      - Age
      - Previous pregnancy history
      - Surgical factors
      Interpretation: Predicts the likelihood of pregnancy following surgery for endometriosis and may help identify women who could benefit from ART. The guideline also describes its use when assessing prospects for natural or IUI conception.
  Follow up:
    Long term effects:
      - Persistent pain may contribute to central sensitisation.
      - Symptoms relapse after surgical treatment in 40-45% of women, and up to 30% undergo another procedure within five years of their first surgery.
    Survivorship notes: Endometriosis-related pain may disrupt daily life, work, mental and physical wellbeing, relationships and fertility. Symptom-free women do not necessarily need treatment.

Document sections:
  Heading: 5. How should an adnexal mass be managed in pregnant women?
  Content: Expertise-dependent US and MRI provide first-line detailed locoregional imaging; the usefulness of serum tumour markers remains unclear. Most functional cysts resolve spontaneously before 16 weeks of gestation, making observation reasonable. Surgery can be performed safely during pregnancy, preferably within 22 weeks. Document sections:
  Heading: 11.4.4.2.2 Microbiological findings
  Content: After urinary tract infection, including urethritis, has been excluded, > 106 peroxidase-positive white blood-cells (WBCs) per millilitre of ejaculate indicate inflammation. For suspected genitourinary infection, perform semen culture or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis for common urinary pathogens. Ejaculate concentrations > 103 CFU/mL indicate significant bacteriospermia. Deliver the sample to the laboratory the same day because elapsed time affects organism detection and the strains recovered. The ideal semen test for C. trachomatis is not established, although PCR is the most accurate reported method.

Historical data indicate that Ureaplasma urealyticum is pathogenic only above > 103 CFU/mL ejaculate; fewer than 10% of analysed samples exceeded that concentration. Normal urethral colonisation makes it difficult to interpret mycoplasma findings in ejaculate. A meta-analysis found no association of Ureaplasma parvum or Mycoplasma genitalium with male infertility, but reported relationships for U. urealyticum (OR: 3.03 95% CI: 1.02–8.99) and Mycoplasma hominis (OR: 2.8; 95% CI: 0.93– 3.64). Treatment is therefore not invariably recommended. Human papilloma virus (HPV) has been detected in semen in 20% of infertile populations and 8% of men in the general population. Systematic reviews associated seminal HPV with male infertility and poorer pregnancy outcomes, but prospective validation is needed to establish its clinical impact. Seminal Herpes Simplex virus (HSV)-2 may coincide with poorer sperm quality in infertile men than HSV-negative status; whether antiviral treatment improves fertility is unclear.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_03
  Name: Gestational hypertension
  Description: Hypertension first appearing after 20 weeks of pregnancy without significant proteinuria.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Full assessment in secondary care
      Purpose: Evaluate gestational hypertension and factors requiring closer assessment and follow-up.
      When indicated: At presentation, by a healthcare professional trained in managing hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
      Interpretation: Factors requiring additional assessment and follow-up include nulliparity, age 40 years or older, pregnancy interval of more than 10 years, family history of pre-eclampsia, multi-fetal pregnancy, BMI of 35 kg/m2 or more, gestational age at presentation, previous pre-eclampsia or gestational hypertension, and pre-existing vascular or kidney disease.
    - Test: Blood pressure measurement
      Purpose: Assess severity and response to treatment.
      When indicated: For hypertension, once or twice a week depending on blood pressure until it is 135/85 mmHg or less; for severe hypertension, every 15 to 30 minutes until it is less than 160/110 mmHg.
      Interpretation: Once antihypertensive treatment is given, the target is 135/85 mmHg or less.
    - Test: Dipstick proteinuria testing
      Purpose: Monitor for proteinuria.
      When indicated: Once or twice a week alongside blood pressure measurement for hypertension; daily during admission for severe hypertension.
      Interpretation: A result of 1+ or more prompts quantification with albumin:creatinine ratio or protein:creatinine ratio.
    - Test: Full blood count, liver function and renal function
      Purpose: Monitor maternal haematological, liver and kidney status.
      When indicated: At presentation and then weekly.
    - Test: Placental growth factor (PLGF)-based testing
      Purpose: Help rule out pre-eclampsia.
      When indicated: On 1 occasion if pre-eclampsia is suspected, between 20 weeks and 36 weeks and 6 days of pregnancy.
    - Test: Fetal heart auscultation
      Purpose: Assess fetal heart activity.
      When indicated: At every antenatal appointment.
    - Test: Ultrasound for fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume assessment
      Purpose: Assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume.
      When indicated: At diagnosis; if findings are normal, repeat every 2 to 4 weeks if clinically indicated. If severe hypertension persists, repeat every 2 weeks.
    - Test: Umbilical artery doppler velocimetry
      Purpose: Assess the fetal circulation.
      When indicated: At diagnosis; if findings are normal, repeat every 2 to 4 weeks if clinically indicated. In severe gestational hypertension, subsequent monitoring is determined by scan findings.
    - Test: Cardiotocography (CTG)
      Purpose: Assess fetal status.
      When indicated: For gestational hypertension, only if clinically indicated; for severe gestational hypertension, at diagnosis and subsequently if clinically indicated.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: After birth, offer women still receiving antihypertensive treatment a medical review 2 weeks after transfer to community care. Offer all women a medical review 6 to 8 weeks after birth.
    Recommended tests:
      - Measure blood pressure daily for the first 2 days after birth and at least once between day 3 and day 5.
      - Measure blood pressure as clinically indicated if antihypertensive treatment changes after birth.
    Long term effects:
      - After gestational hypertension in a previous or current pregnancy, hypertension of any type in a future pregnancy occurs in approximately 22% (1 in 5 women), pre-eclampsia in approximately 7% (1 in 14 women), gestational hypertension in between approximately 11% and 15% (up to 1 in 7 women), and chronic hypertension in approximately 3% (up to 1 in 34 women).
      - For women with gestational hypertension in a current or previous pregnancy, the table reports an approximately 1.5 to 3 times increased risk of a major adverse cardiovascular event and an approximately 2 to 4 times increased risk of later hypertension. Stroke risk may be increased.
    Survivorship notes: The community-care plan specifies who provides follow-up, how often blood pressure is checked, thresholds for reducing or stopping treatment, and when to refer for a primary-care blood pressure review.

Document sections:
  Heading: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome Clinical Features
  Content: A comprehensive clinical assessment is essential because history and examination inform 2 out of 3 diagnostic criteria and help identify alternative conditions. Relevant information includes menstrual and fertility history, obesity, and hyperandrogenic features. Under the 2023 International Evidence-Based PCOS Guidelines, irregular cycles are characterized as follows: cycles in the first year postmenarche are considered part of normal pubertal transition; within 1 to <3 years postmenarche, intervals <21 or >45 days are irregular; from 3 years postmenarche until perimenopause, intervals <21 or >35 days or <8 cycles per year are irregular; any cycle 1 year postmenarche with an interval >90 days is irregular; and primary amenorrhea by age 15 or >3 years post thelarche (breast development) is included. Hair loss may affect the vertex or crown or be diffuse; more severe hyperandrogenism may cause bitemporal loss and frontal hairline recession. Adolescents with severe acne or acne resistant to oral or topical antibiotics may have a 40% chance of developing PCOS. Persistent or worsening acne in females in their mid-20s to 30s calls for particular attention to hyperandrogenism. Hirsutism consists of coarse, dark terminal hair in a typically male distribution. Increased muscle mass, reduced breast size, voice deepening, and clitoromegaly are uncommon in PCOS; such virilization suggests elevated androgens and warrants investigation, especially for an ovarian or adrenal androgen-producing tumor. Hirsutism should be assessed objectively with the modified Ferrim-Gallwey scoring system. Depending on ethnicity, a modified Ferriman-Gallwey score (mFG) of 4 to 6 should be used for detection, while recognizing that self-treatment can obscure examination findings.

  Heading: Treatment
  Content: Timely recognition and a short interval between initial manifestations and definitive surgery are essential. Once rupture is diagnosed, immediate maternal stabilization and fetal delivery are imperative. After frank rupture, the interval before major fetal morbidity is generally only 10-37 minutes; when rupture is suspected, available resources should be mobilized rapidly for definitive surgical care. After delivery, maternal surgery is guided by rupture type and extent, bleeding severity, maternal condition, and wishes about future childbearing. Longitudinal tears generally bleed more heavily than transverse tears. Uterine repair as conservative surgical treatment should be reserved for women desiring future childbearing who have a low transverse rupture without extension into the broad ligament, cervix, or paracolpos; readily controlled bleeding; good general condition; and no clinical or laboratory evidence of developing coagulopathy. Hysterectomy should be considered the preferred treatment for uncontrollable uterine hemorrhage or multiple, longitudinal, or low-lying rupture sites. Clinicians should maintain strong suspicion, especially in high-risk patients, and act rapidly and decisively when uncertain.

Document sections:
  Heading: 6.2. Amenorrhea
  Content: Amenorrhea can have hormonal or organic causes and may be primary or secondary. Primary amenorrhea denotes no menarche by age 16; secondary amenorrhea means no menstruation for more than 90 days after previous periods. Pregnancy should be excluded before further investigation, and a previously regular cycle that becomes irregular warrants assessment. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (WHO I) occurs with pubertas tarda and is largely constitutional without pathological significance, although gonadal, hypothalamic, pituitary, or genetic disorders—including Sheehan syndrome and Kallmann syndrome—can cause it. Common adolescent causes of hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction (WHO II) are a high-risk constellation for polycystic ovary syndrome and central dysregulation associated with stress, anorexia, or competitive sport. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (WHO III), or premature ovarian insufficiency, involves loss of ovarian activity before age 40 years and affects approximately 1:10,000 patients under age 20. Potential causes are Turner syndrome, a Fragile X premutation, autoimmune predisposition, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or ovarian surgery. Organic amenorrhea (WHO IV) includes genital malformations such as Meier–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome and hymenal atresia, often first identified because of primary amenorrhea or dysmenorrhea. Reported incidences of the various causes differ so greatly by study and population that no general statement can be made. Absent follicular maturation can prevent adequate estrogenization and endometrial thickening, so bleeding does not occur. In the short term, estrogen deficiency can prevent pubertal onset and secondary sexual development; in the long term, it can impair bone, cognitive, and cardiovascular health. Girls with hypo- or hypergonadotropic hypogonadism consequently need treatment to induce puberty and sustain adequate estrogenization.

    - Timepoint: Prepregnancy or initial prenatal visit
      Method: Review detailed medical and obstetric history and the previous stillbirth workup; determine recurrence risk; perform diabetes screening and acquired thrombophilia testing with lupus anticoagulant and IgG and IgM for both anticardiolipin and b2-glycoprotein antibodies.

Main conclusion: Early recognition and treatment of ectopic pregnancy are essential to reduce the risk of rupture and severe hemorrhage. Management should reflect hemodynamic stability, implantation site, diagnostic findings, and the patient’s fertility goals, with urgent surgery when rupture is suspected.

Narrative summary: This educational review examines the presentation, diagnosis, and management of ectopic pregnancy rather than reporting a new clinical study. Ectopic pregnancy affects approximately 1% to 2% of pregnancies in the United States and accounts for 2.7% of pregnancy-related deaths. Approximately 97% occur in the fallopian tube. Lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding are common, while dizziness, fainting, shoulder pain, or severe pelvic pain may indicate rupture.

Evaluation combines serum β-hCG measurements with ultrasound, particularly TVUS. A β-hCG level >2000 mIU/mL without a visible intrauterine pregnancy is highly suggestive of ectopic pregnancy; the review also notes a suggested discriminatory cutoff of up to 3500 mIU/mL to avoid misdiagnosing a viable pregnancy. When pregnancy location remains uncertain, serial β-hCG measurements and repeat imaging may be needed.

Hemodynamic instability or suspected rupture requires urgent surgical intervention. For selected asymptomatic patients with low, declining β-hCG, expectant management may be considered; 88% of ectopic pregnancies with an initial β-hCG level of <200 mIU/mL resolved spontaneously. In appropriate candidates, methotrexate is a medical option, with reported success of approximately 70% to 95%; β-hCG monitoring continues until the level is undetectable. Surgical options include salpingostomy and salpingectomy. For cesarean scar ectopic pregnancy, expectant management is not recommended except in select cases of confirmed fetal demise, and systemic methotrexate alone is not recommended.

Document sections:
  Heading: 6.10. Endometriosis
  Content: Dysmenorrhea means painful menstruation. Primary dysmenorrhea occurs without a specific pathological condition; secondary dysmenorrhea occurs with a reproductive-system disorder causing menstrual cramps, such as endometriosis or fibroids. Endometriosis affects approximately 2% of adolescent women. It is an estrogen-dependent inflammatory condition involving functional endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity. Refractory pain, noncyclic lower abdominal pain, dysmenorrhea, dysuria, dyschezia, or dyspareunia makes it a likely diagnosis; increased absence from school or sport can also be a clue. Pain often accompanies nausea, vomiting, dyschezia, constipation, or vasovagal reactions. Definitive confirmation requires histology, but medication is first-line treatment. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for pain and hormonal treatment with progestogens or an extended-use contraceptive pill (off-label use) can be used to limit disease progression until childbearing is desired. GnRH analogs warrant great caution in adolescents because of adverse skeletal effects and long-term osteoporosis risk. Persistent symptoms may justify surgery, which should be performed at a highly experienced center to preserve ovarian reserve. Diagnosis appears delayed and treatment often inadequate in both adolescents and adults. Possible reasons include low ultrasonographic detection and reluctance to operate on adolescents. Clinical findings can nevertheless justify treatment without histological confirmation, and girls benefit from such treatment.

  Content: Fallopian tube torsion is isolated rotation of the tube without ovarian torsion, either along its middle segment or around its supporting ligaments. Pain can be acute or chronic, generalized or nonspecific, and may accompany nausea and vomiting. Missed torsion can destroy tubal function and lead to hydrosalpinx, necrosis, or resorption. Potential contributors include hydrosalpinx, segmental tubal agenesis with proximal hydrosalpinx, broad ligament or paratubal cysts, neoplasms, ectopic pregnancy, congenital anomalies, ovarian masses, infection, abnormal peristalsis or spasm, and external lesions such as adhesions. Imaging may show a dilated tube, an adjacent normal ovary, or a cystic mass separate from the ovary. Diagnosis is generally made during surgical exploration. Detorsion can prevent irreversible ischemic damage and loss of the tube.

Document sections:
  Heading: 6.2. Amenorrhea
  Content: Amenorrhea can have hormonal or organic causes and may be primary or secondary. Primary amenorrhea denotes no menarche by age 16; secondary amenorrhea means no menstruation for more than 90 days after previous periods. Pregnancy should be excluded before further investigation, and a previously regular cycle that becomes irregular warrants assessment. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (WHO I) occurs with pubertas tarda and is largely constitutional without pathological significance, although gonadal, hypothalamic, pituitary, or genetic disorders—including Sheehan syndrome and Kallmann syndrome—can cause it. Common adolescent causes of hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction (WHO II) are a high-risk constellation for polycystic ovary syndrome and central dysregulation associated with stress, anorexia, or competitive sport. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (WHO III), or premature ovarian insufficiency, involves loss of ovarian activity before age 40 years and affects approximately 1:10,000 patients under age 20. Potential causes are Turner syndrome, a Fragile X premutation, autoimmune predisposition, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or ovarian surgery. Organic amenorrhea (WHO IV) includes genital malformations such as Meier–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome and hymenal atresia, often first identified because of primary amenorrhea or dysmenorrhea. Reported incidences of the various causes differ so greatly by study and population that no general statement can be made. Absent follicular maturation can prevent adequate estrogenization and endometrial thickening, so bleeding does not occur. In the short term, estrogen deficiency can prevent pubertal onset and secondary sexual development; in the long term, it can impair bone, cognitive, and cardiovascular health. Girls with hypo- or hypergonadotropic hypogonadism consequently need treatment to induce puberty and sustain adequate estrogenization.

  Content: A comprehensive clinical assessment is essential because history and examination inform 2 out of 3 diagnostic criteria and help identify alternative conditions. Relevant information includes menstrual and fertility history, obesity, and hyperandrogenic features. Under the 2023 International Evidence-Based PCOS Guidelines, irregular cycles are characterized as follows: cycles in the first year postmenarche are considered part of normal pubertal transition; within 1 to <3 years postmenarche, intervals <21 or >45 days are irregular; from 3 years postmenarche until perimenopause, intervals <21 or >35 days or <8 cycles per year are irregular; any cycle 1 year postmenarche with an interval >90 days is irregular; and primary amenorrhea by age 15 or >3 years post thelarche (breast development) is included. Hair loss may affect the vertex or crown or be diffuse; more severe hyperandrogenism may cause bitemporal loss and frontal hairline recession. Adolescents with severe acne or acne resistant to oral or topical antibiotics may have a 40% chance of developing PCOS. Persistent or worsening acne in females in their mid-20s to 30s calls for particular attention to hyperandrogenism. Hirsutism consists of coarse, dark terminal hair in a typically male distribution. Increased muscle mass, reduced breast size, voice deepening, and clitoromegaly are uncommon in PCOS; such virilization suggests elevated androgens and warrants investigation, especially for an ovarian or adrenal androgen-producing tumor. Hirsutism should be assessed objectively with the modified Ferrim-Gallwey scoring system. Depending on ethnicity, a modified Ferriman-Gallwey score (mFG) of 4 to 6 should be used for detection, while recognizing that self-treatment can obscure examination findings.

    - Explicar beneficios, posibles efectos adversos y uso correcto de los métodos, y acordar la elección con la paciente conforme a sus preferencias y a los criterios de elegibilidad de la OMS.
    - Aplicar las categorías de selección del método según su significado: Categoría 1 permite utilizarlo en cualquier circunstancia; Categoría 2 favorece su uso en general; Categoría 3 aconseja no recomendarlo habitualmente, salvo que otras opciones más adecuadas no estén disponibles o no sean aceptadas; Categoría 4 indica no utilizarlo.
    - La edad, por sí sola, no contraindica la anticoncepción. Para prescribir anticonceptivos no se exige una analítica ni una citología, con la excepción señalada para el DIU.
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: 3 o 6 meses
      Method: Revisar el cumplimiento, los efectos secundarios y las dudas sobre el método.
  Supportive care:
    - Facilitar instrucciones orales y escritas, reiterar las indicaciones importantes y ofrecer la posibilidad de consultar dudas.
    - Registrar en la historia clínica el método elegido y su fecha de inicio, incluida la implantación del DIU o la inserción del implante subcutáneo.
