retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Assessment and management of endometriosis 2025__JC__000204
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Assessment and management of endometriosis 2025
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Background
  Content: Endometriosis is a chronic, estrogen-mediated inflammatory disorder of uncertain cause, defined by endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus. Deposits commonly affect pelvic structures including ovaries, fallopian tubes, peritoneum and uterosacral ligaments. Deeply infiltrative endometriosis (DIE) may affect bowel, bladder or ureter and impair organ function; disease can also occur outside the pelvis, involve nerve roots or be found incidentally during laparoscopy in an asymptomatic person. It mainly affects reproductive-age women, although symptoms can begin in youth or persist after menopause. Estimated prevalence is 1 in 10 women; the World Health Organization estimates 190 million affected women worldwide. Anatomical severity and symptom severity need not correspond. Symptoms are not specific and overlap with bowel, bladder, musculoskeletal and fibromyalgia-related conditions. Absent specific biomarkers, limited imaging sensitivity for peritoneal disease, limited awareness and normalisation of symptoms contribute to missed or delayed diagnosis. Pain may disrupt activities, employment, physical and mental well-being, relationships, sexual function and fertility. The reported average interval from symptom onset to confirmed diagnosis is 7-8 years. Persistent symptoms during that interval may impair quality of life, undermine the patient–physician relationship and contribute to central sensitisation. A multicentre study in Europe, the UK and USA estimated annual costs of €9579 per affected woman, predominantly from work absence. Treatment addresses pain with analgesia, medical disease suppression and/or surgery; infertility requires separate consideration.

Document sections:
  Heading: Clinical Practice
  Content: For suspected disease, clinicians may offer medical treatment without confirmed diagnosis after discussing adverse effects, pregnancy plans and past hormonal-treatment experiences. Goals are to lessen pain frequency and severity, improve quality of life and extend postoperative pain relief. Decide jointly, considering preferences, conception plans, adverse effects, cost and availability. Asymptomatic disease need not be treated. Recommend combined hormonal contraception—oral pill, vaginal ring or patch—or progestogens—oral pill, levonorgestrel intrauterine system, etonogestrel-releasing implant or medroxyprogesterone acetate depot injection—as first-line pain management and to prolong postoperative relief. Recommend continuous combined oral contraception. Reserve GnRH agonists for second line because of adverse effects and uncertainty about dose and duration; prescribe add-back hormones to counter hot flushes, vaginal dryness, bone loss and other treatment-induced menopausal symptoms. Reserve GnRH antagonists for second line because dose and duration lack consensus. Recommend aromatase inhibitors only for pain refractory to other options; they may be combined with oral contraceptives, progestogens or GnRH agonists and antagonists. Postoperative hormonal suppression may reduce recurrent pain.

Document sections:
  Heading: Hyperandrogenism Diagnostic Evaluation
  Content: In adult women, hirsutism, alopecia, and acne indicate clinical hyperandrogenism and can signal biochemical hyperandrogenism. Assessment should measure total and free testosterone; the calculated free androgen index can estimate free testosterone. If neither measure is elevated, androstenedione and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) may be considered, recognizing their lower specificity and the tendency of DHEA to decline with age. Laboratories should favor LC-MS/MS assays rather than direct immunoassays, including radiometric or enzyme-linked methods, for total or free testosterone because direct assays have limited accuracy, sensitivity, and precision in this setting. Androgen concentrations substantially above laboratory reference ranges should prompt consideration of ovarian or adrenal neoplasms, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing's syndrome, ovarian hyperthecosis—particularly after menopause—iatrogenic effects, and severe-insulin-resistance syndromes. Some androgen-secreting neoplasms cause only mild or moderate elevations, so the timing of onset and speed of progression are important clinical-history details.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: Management of Stillbirth
retrieved_chunks.text:
Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_02
  Name: previous stillbirth
  Description: A history of stillbirth affects recurrence counseling, surveillance, and planning in a subsequent pregnancy. The cause and gestational age of the earlier death, along with current maternal and fetal conditions, inform individualized care.
  Epidemiology: A systematic review and meta-analysis reported stillbirth in a subsequent pregnancy among 2.5% of women with a history of any stillbirth, versus 0.4% of women with a history of live birth (pooled OR, 4.83; 95% CI, 3.77–6.18). Evidence specifically addressing recurrence after an unexplained stillbirth is limited and conflicting. Two studies reported adjusted subsequent-stillbirth risks of 3.11 (95% CI, 0.72–13.50) and 1.00 (95% CI, 0.23–4.30) after a previous unexplained stillbirth. A retrospective analysis reported an adjusted risk of unexplained stillbirth after one previous stillbirth of 4.18 (95% CI, 1.36–12.89).
  Clinical presentation: Patients may experience anxiety during a subsequent pregnancy and require additional support.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: previous unexplained stillbirth
      Distinguishing features: The earlier stillbirth had no established cause despite evaluation; evidence to guide subsequent-pregnancy management is scarce.
    - Name: previous stillbirth at or after 32 0/7 weeks
      Distinguishing features: The earlier gestational age informs the recommended start of once or twice weekly antenatal surveillance.
    - Name: previous stillbirth before 32 0/7 weeks of gestation
      Distinguishing features: The timing of antenatal surveillance may be individualized.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: detailed medical and obstetric history and evaluation of previous stillbirth
      Purpose: Assess the prior evaluation and estimate recurrence risk.
      When indicated: Before pregnancy or at the initial prenatal visit.
      Interpretation: An identified cause or recurring maternal or obstetric condition may permit more specific recurrence counseling.
    - Test: genetic counseling
      Purpose: Address a familial genetic condition.
      When indicated: Before pregnancy or at the initial prenatal visit if a family genetic condition exists.
    - Test: Diabetes screen
      Purpose: Assess for diabetes.
      When indicated: Before pregnancy or at the initial prenatal visit.
    - Test: lupus anticoagulant as well as IgG and IgM for both anticardiolipin and b2-glycoprotein antibodies
      Purpose: Evaluate acquired thrombophilia.
      When indicated: Before pregnancy or at the initial prenatal visit.
    - Test: Dating ultrasonography
      Purpose: Establish pregnancy dating.
      When indicated: First Trimester.
    - Test: pregnancy-associated plasma protein A, human chorionic gonadotropin, and nuchal translucency
      Purpose: Provide first-trimester screening.
      When indicated: First Trimester, as an alternative to cell-free fetal DNA testing.
      Interpretation: The document states that this screening modifies risk but does not change management.
    - Test: cell-free fetal DNA testing
      Purpose: Provide a first-trimester screening option.
      When indicated: First Trimester, as an alternative to the other first-trimester screen listed.
    - Test: fetal sonographic anatomic survey
      Purpose: Assess fetal anatomy.
      When indicated: At 18–20 weeks.
    - Test: genetic screening or single marker alpha fetoprotein
      Purpose: Provide second-trimester screening.
      When indicated: Offer genetic screening if it was not done in the first trimester, or single marker alpha fetoprotein if first-trimester screening was already performed.
    - Test: sonographic screening for fetal growth restriction
      Purpose: Assess fetal growth.
      When indicated: After 28 weeks.
    - Test: antepartum fetal surveillance
      Purpose: Monitor a pregnancy after stillbirth.
      When indicated: For previous stillbirth at or after 32 0/7 weeks, once or twice weekly surveillance is recommended at 32 0/7 weeks or beginning 1–2 weeks before the gestational age of the previous stillbirth. For an earlier stillbirth, individualized timing may be considered.
      Interpretation: Testing can lead to intervention for abnormal, equivocal, or false-positive results; its potential harms and costs should be considered.
    - Test: fetal kick counting
      Purpose: Increase awareness of fetal movement patterns.
      When indicated: Specific recommendations cannot be made because evidence that it prevents stillbirth is insufficient.
      Interpretation: Reports of reduced movement warrant attentive, systematic assessment. A large randomized study of fetal movement awareness did not demonstrate a reduction in stillbirth rates and observed more inductions and hospital admissions.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Before pregnancy or at the initial prenatal visit, review the earlier stillbirth and recurrence risk. Provide first-trimester dating and screening, a fetal anatomic survey at 18–20 weeks, growth screening after 28 weeks, and antenatal surveillance according to the gestational age of the previous stillbirth. Planned delivery is at 39 0/7 weeks of gestation unless other maternal or fetal conditions dictate otherwise. Severe anxiety may warrant consideration of delivery at 37 0/7 weeks to 38 6/7 weeks after discussion of increased neonatal risks.
    Recommended tests:
      - Diabetes screen
      - lupus anticoagulant as well as IgG and IgM for both anticardiolipin and b2-glycoprotein antibodies
      - Dating ultrasonography
      - pregnancy-associated plasma protein A, human chorionic gonadotropin, and nuchal translucency or cell-free fetal DNA testing
      - fetal sonographic anatomic survey at 18–20 weeks
      - genetic screening if not performed in the first trimester, or single marker alpha fetoprotein if first-trimester screening was performed
      - sonographic screening for fetal growth restriction after 28 weeks
      - antepartum fetal surveillance
    Survivorship notes: Support and reassurance are included throughout subsequent-pregnancy care. Counseling should address modifiable risks, but a 2018 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to identify effective interventions that improve care after stillbirth. Delivery planning should weigh the risks of continuing pregnancy against maternal and neonatal risks of earlier delivery.   Heading: 5.4 What are the surgical, pharmacological or conservative treatment options for interstitial pregnancy?
  Content: Nonsurgical care is acceptable when stable (D). Reserve observation for low or markedly decreasing b-hCG where methotrexate might not improve outcome (D). Methotrexate is effective, but evidence cannot establish whether local or systemic administration is preferable (D). Laparoscopic cornual resection or salpingotomy is effective (D); hysteroscopic resection under laparoscopic or ultrasound guidance is another possible technique (D). Insufficient information on future-pregnancy safety and complications prevents recommending other nonsurgical methods (D). Initial serum b-hCG influences conservative-treatment success. In a case series of 42 women, initial values were lower after successful expectant or medical care than after unsuccessful care (3216 iu/l versus 15 900 iu/l; P < 0.05). Another series of 19 expectantly managed women reported 89.5% success. One observational study of 17 women receiving systemic methotrexate 50 mg/m2 reported no complications; another reported adverse effects in 40% of recipients. An Australian series of 13 pregnancies reported 91% success with single-dose intravenous methotrexate plus oral folinic acid rescue. Described local treatment includes ultrasound-guided aspiration of gestational-sac exocoelomic fluid followed by intrasaccular 25 mg methotrexate, with or without 0.2–0.4 mEq potassium chloride. Reported success is 91%, with fewer adverse effects and an option for simultaneous embryocide, but the technique is more demanding; embryocide has been reported to increase procedural success (Evidence level 3). Reported endoscopic approaches include electrocautery, an endoloop or encircling suture before evacuation. Moon et al. described haemostasis using 1 ampoule [20 U] vasopressin in 1000 ml normal saline [1000-fold], injecting 150–250 ml [0.02 U/ml] below the pregnancy. Other reports describe laparoscopic haemostatic sutures and a ‘purse-string’ resection technique. Hysteroscopic resection under laparoscopic and ultrasound guidance has been reported. A small series (n = 3) described ultrasound-guided dilatation and evacuation with polypectomy forceps followed by single-dose systemic methotrexate. Selective UAE with methotrexate has been used to limit bleeding, but future-pregnancy safety and complications remain uncertain. A reported 12-week case after failed systemic methotrexate was treated successfully with intra-amniotic etoposide, described as a topoisomerase II inhibitor used for gestational trophoblastic disease (Evidence level 3).

  Content: Interpret proteinuria alongside a complete clinical assessment of symptoms, signs and other findings relevant to pre-eclampsia. In secondary care, use an automated reagent-strip reader for initial dipstick screening; a result of 1+ or more should be quantified with an albumin:creatinine ratio or protein:creatinine ratio. Do not use the first morning urine void for quantification, and do not routinely collect urine over 24 hours. For protein:creatinine ratio, the threshold for significant proteinuria is 30 mg/mmol; if the result is 30 mg/mmol or above but diagnosis remains uncertain, consider a fresh sample and another clinical assessment. When albumin:creatinine ratio is used instead to diagnose pre-eclampsia in a pregnant woman with hypertension, apply a threshold of 8 mg/mmol and consider repeat testing on a new sample with clinical review if a result of 8 mg/mmol or above leaves diagnostic uncertainty. Document sections:
  Heading: Hormonal therapies as an adjuvant/pre-treatment to IVF
  Content: A proposed explanation for possible benefit from prolonged (3–6months) GnRH analogue suppression before IVF is reduced endometriosis-related inflammation affecting oocytes and endometrial receptivity. A Cochrane review of 8 RCTs involving 640 participants with endometriosis of any stage found uncertain effects of long-term GnRH treatment (minimum 3months), compared with no pretreatment before IVF or ICSI, on clinical pregnancy, miscarriage and live birth. Prolonged GnRH agonist treatment may excessively suppress the pituitary gland, potentially impairing ovarian response and luteal function. The review also found uncertain effects on mean oocyte and embryo numbers; underlying studies were very low quality and highly heterogeneous. An RCT involving 400 infertile women with minimal or mild disease found no improvement in embryo quality, implantation or clinical pregnancy after 3months of GnRH agonists following surgical cauterization and before ART. Because postoperative GnRH agonists reduce recurrence and endometrioma formation, they may have a role for symptomatic women awaiting ART. A small RCT of stimulated IUI compared daily Decapeptyl 0.1mg for 2weeks before stimulation (n=41, ‘long protocol’) with a single 3.75mg dose followed 4weeks later by daily Decapeptyl 0.1mg for 2weeks before stimulation (n=39, ‘ultralong protocol’); both groups included all disease stages. Clinical pregnancy did not differ between protocols for minimal or mild disease. For moderate or severe disease, clinical pregnancy was significantly higher with the ‘ultralong’ protocol (50%, 10/20) than with the ‘long’ protocol (19% 4/21). No studies compare long-term GnRH agonists with long-term combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) or endometrioma surgery before ART. Evidence about pregnancy outcomes with long-term continuous oral contraceptive pill or other progestins is limited and low quality. Evidence for aromatase inhibitors added to GnRH agonist pretreatment is likewise limited and low quality; a retrospective cohort of 126 women with endometriomas reported better IVF outcomes with daily Letrozole alongside GnRH agonists. Studies have shown Elagolix, an oral second generation GnRH receptor antagonist, to improve endometriosis-related dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia and non-menstrual pelvic pain. Its immediate pituitary gonadotrophin suppression is described as avoiding the initial GnRH agonist flare and providing an immediate effect. A double-blind randomised trial of Elagolix 200mg twice daily versus placebo for two weeks before IVF in patients with endometriosis was underway.

Document sections:
  Heading: Examination of the Stillborn Fetus
  Content: Examine the fetus promptly for dysmorphic findings and measure weight, length, and head circumference (1C Strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). Before 23 weeks, foot length may be especially helpful for estimating gestational age. Whole-body photographs without clothing, frontal and profile facial images, extremity and palm images, and close-ups of anomalies support later specialist review, particularly where a geneticist is unavailable. Offer fetal autopsy because it is among the most informative tests for cause of death (1A Strong recommendation, high-quality evidence); its yield is greater with dysmorphism, discordant growth measurements, anomalies, hydrops, or growth restriction. When families decline complete autopsy, options include partial autopsy, trained-pathologist gross examination, ultrasonography, and especially magnetic resonance imaging. Parents should have an opportunity to hold their baby and observe cultural or religious practices before autopsy. Wholebody X-ray in anterior–posterior and lateral views can reveal or clarify skeletal abnormalities. A full autopsy should follow published perinatal protocols, including measurements such as foot length and body weight to estimate gestational age, an estimate of time from death to delivery, investigation of developmental and intrinsic abnormalities, and evaluation for infection. Preferably, an experienced perinatal pathologist performs it and a clinician experienced in genetics and dysmorphology examines the fetus. The obstetric and relevant medical history and requests for additional tissue collection should be conveyed to pathology.

Document sections:
  Heading: History and Physical
  Content: Patients may have no symptoms; when symptoms occur, abnormal uterine bleeding is the most common. Abdominal pain, pelvic pain, and infertility may also occur. One in four reproductive-aged women with abnormal bleeding has an endometrial polyp in the cavity. Evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding should establish its cause and severity, associated symptoms, and comorbidities. A thorough medical and surgical history helps exclude other causes. No bleeding pattern is diagnostic of a polyp, but the bleeding history should be characterized; menorrhagia and intermenstrual spotting are reported most often. Tamoxifen, commonly used for breast cancer, can act as an agonist or antagonist in tissues bearing estrogen receptors. It has anticancer effects in breast tissue but carcinogenic effects in endometrial tissue. Chronic tamoxifen use is associated with endometrial polyps at an incidence of 20% to 35%. Hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms may also be associated with polyp formation, irregular bleeding, and ultrasound evidence of endometrial thickening. Clinical examination should include a general assessment, bimanual examination, and sterile speculum examination. The cervix and vaginal vault should be examined completely to exclude other structural explanations for symptoms. A pedunculated polyp may be visible at the external os.

Document sections:
  Heading: Cambios fisiológicos generales y locales durante la gestación
  Content: Las adaptaciones hormonales, mecánicas y nutritivas favorecen el desarrollo gestacional. Gran parte de la ganancia ponderal corresponde al útero y su contenido; se considera ideal 1 kg al mes. La volemia aumenta progresivamente y alcanza su máximo en la semana 34-36. Hay vasodilatación periférica, mayor flujo en útero, riñones, piel y mamas, y descenso de la presión coloidosmótica con edema. La tensión arterial disminuye durante el 1.er y 2.º trimestre, con mínimo alrededor de la semana 28 por menor resistencia periférica, y asciende en el tercero. La progesterona relaja el músculo liso vascular; la compresión uterina de la cava inferior eleva la presión venosa pélvica y de los miembros inferiores. El síndrome hipotensor por decúbito supino se resuelve colocando a la gestante en decúbito lateral izquierdo. El diafragma elevado desplaza el corazón superiormente y hacia la izquierda. Pueden ser fisiológicos el soplo sistólico funcional, el refuerzo del segundo ruido pulmonar o galope S3 y el desdoblamiento amplio del primer ruido; todo soplo diastólico es patológico. El ECG puede mostrar signos de hipertrofia y desviación del eje 15º a la izquierda. Aumentan la frecuencia cardiaca, que raramente supera 100 lpm, y el gasto cardiaco por mayor volumen sistólico y frecuencia. La expansión plasmática proporcionalmente superior al aumento eritrocitario ocasiona anemia dilucional, con hemoglobina de unos 11 g/dl y hematocrito en torno al 34 %. La leucocitosis leve es de 12.000 leucocitos/µl y raramente presenta desviación izquierda; puede alcanzar 20.000 en el puerperio. El aumento de fibrinógeno, tromboplastina y factores I, III, VII, VIII, IX y X, junto con menos plaquetas, favorece hipercoagulabilidad. La progesterona incrementa la sensibilidad respiratoria al CO2 y contribuye a hiperventilación con alcalosis respiratoria leve; aumentan el volumen de reserva respiratorio y la capacidad inspiratoria. Las encías pueden estar hipertróficas e hiperémicas y normalizarse tras el parto; el angiogranuloma gingival o épulis del embarazo puede sangrar, doler y requerir extirpación. La saliva aumenta y se acidifica. Náuseas y vómitos son más frecuentes en gestaciones múltiples y enfermedad trofoblástica gestacional. La relajación intestinal por progesterona reduce motilidad y ocasiona estreñimiento, atonía vesicular, litiasis o barro biliar, reflujo y pirosis, agravados por la presión intraabdominal. Aumentan fosfatasa alcalina (1,5 veces superior al límite de la normalidad), colesterol, triglicéridos y globulinas; disminuyen gammaglobulinas, albúmina y actividad de colinesterasa, sin modificación de transaminasas. Los riñones crecen ligeramente; la dilatación ureteral, mayor a la derecha, favorece crisis sin litiasis y desaparece 6-8 semanas posparto. El reflujo vesicoureteral favorece bacteriuria y el menor tono esfinteriano puede causar incontinencia. Aumentan flujo plasmático renal mediado por HPL, filtrado glomerular en un 40-50 % y reabsorción tubular; disminuyen creatinina, urea, ácido úrico y aminoácidos sanguíneos. Puede haber glucosuria sin hiperglucemia. Aparecen arañas vasculares, estrías y mayor pigmentación vulvar, púbica, umbilical, de línea alba, cara y cuello por estimulación de MSH mediada por progesterona. El metabolismo basal y consumo de oxígeno aumentan un 20 %. La primera mitad del embarazo es anabólica y la segunda catabólica, con resistencia a insulina inducida por lactógeno placentario para mantener el aporte fetal de glucosa. Aumentan lípidos totales, ácidos grasos libres, sodio y potasio; disminuyen calcio —que aumenta al final—, magnesio, hierro y fósforo. La caída de ácido fólico motiva su administración preconcepcional y durante organogénesis para prevenir defectos del tubo neural. Disminuyen LH y FSH; aumentan ACTH, MSH, progesterona, estrógenos y prolactina, cuya concentración crece hasta el parto y contribuye al equilibrio hidroelectrolítico fetal y a la secreción láctea. La oxitocina alcanza su máximo en el parto. Hay hiperplasia de islotes pancreáticos y mayor secreción de insulina y glucagón; aumentan actividad de aldosterona tras elevación de renina, cortisol y testosterona, así como T3, T4 y TGB, con posible bociogénesis. Ni el soplo diastólico ni la elevación de transaminasas o bilirrubina son hallazgos fisiológicos del embarazo.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Introducción
  Content: La endometriosis es una enfermedad benigna, crónica y dependiente del estrógeno, caracterizada por glándulas y estroma endometriales fuera de su ubicación habitual. Se relaciona con dolor pélvico crónico e infertilidad; suele localizarse en peritoneo pélvico, ovarios y tabique rectovaginal. León A, 2019, comunica una prevalencia aproximada del 11% en mujeres en edad reproductiva. Una estimación mundial sitúa la afectación en 10% de esas mujeres, equivalente a aproximadamente 190 millones según datos poblacionales de 2017; en México se estima que afecta a más de siete millones. Otras estimaciones indican entre 6 a 10% de las mujeres en edad reproductiva, entre 50 a 60% de las mujeres y adolescentes con dolor pélvico y hasta 50% de las mujeres con infertilidad. Según población y criterios diagnósticos, la prevalencia entre mujeres asintomáticas es aproximadamente de 2 a 50%. También puede presentarse antes de la menarquia o después de la menopausia. La variedad de síntomas, gravedad y casos asintomáticos dificulta estimar la prevalencia real; además, los datos epidemiológicos se restringen por la necesidad de cirugía y biopsia para el diagnóstico definitivo. El dolor puede ser cíclico o no cíclico e incluir menstruaciones dolorosas, dispareunia, dolor al defecar y disuria. También se describen fatiga y depresión. Frente a la población general femenina, la subinfertilidad o infertilidad es significativamente más frecuente en pacientes con endometriosis. Su origen se considera multifactorial: se proponen menstruación retrógrada, metaplasia celular y participación de células madre con propagación sanguínea y linfática. El estrógeno favorece inflamación, crecimiento y dolor, aunque su ausencia no siempre excluye endometriosis; también se consideran inmunidad alterada, influencias hormonales locales, genética y posibles contaminantes ambientales. La enfermedad suele permanecer en la cavidad abdominal, pero rara vez se han identificado lesiones en pulmón, cerebro y ojo. Los fenotipos tradicionalmente reconocidos son peritoneal, ovárico (endometrioma) y endometriosis profunda (DE). La elección terapéutica considera síntomas, edad, efectos adversos, localización y extensión, tratamientos anteriores y costo; habitualmente requiere manejo multidisciplinario. El 50% de las mujeres presenta recurrencia sintomática en un periodo de cinco años, con independencia del tratamiento. El abordaje puede ser médico o quirúrgico. No existe un sistema universal adoptado; se recomienda combinar rAFS, ENZIAN y EFI. El retraso diagnóstico y la recurrencia dificultan el manejo, que debe orientarse al síntoma motivo de consulta. Se investigan nuevas terapias para casos refractarios.

Document sections:
  Heading: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome Clinical Features
  Content: A comprehensive clinical assessment is essential because history and examination inform 2 out of 3 diagnostic criteria and help identify alternative conditions. Relevant information includes menstrual and fertility history, obesity, and hyperandrogenic features. Under the 2023 International Evidence-Based PCOS Guidelines, irregular cycles are characterized as follows: cycles in the first year postmenarche are considered part of normal pubertal transition; within 1 to <3 years postmenarche, intervals <21 or >45 days are irregular; from 3 years postmenarche until perimenopause, intervals <21 or >35 days or <8 cycles per year are irregular; any cycle 1 year postmenarche with an interval >90 days is irregular; and primary amenorrhea by age 15 or >3 years post thelarche (breast development) is included. Hair loss may affect the vertex or crown or be diffuse; more severe hyperandrogenism may cause bitemporal loss and frontal hairline recession. Adolescents with severe acne or acne resistant to oral or topical antibiotics may have a 40% chance of developing PCOS. Persistent or worsening acne in females in their mid-20s to 30s calls for particular attention to hyperandrogenism. Hirsutism consists of coarse, dark terminal hair in a typically male distribution. Increased muscle mass, reduced breast size, voice deepening, and clitoromegaly are uncommon in PCOS; such virilization suggests elevated androgens and warrants investigation, especially for an ovarian or adrenal androgen-producing tumor. Hirsutism should be assessed objectively with the modified Ferrim-Gallwey scoring system. Depending on ethnicity, a modified Ferriman-Gallwey score (mFG) of 4 to 6 should be used for detection, while recognizing that self-treatment can obscure examination findings.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_02
  Name: Uncomplicated cystitis
  Description: Acute, sporadic, or recurrent cystitis in nonpregnant women without relevant known urinary tract anatomical or functional abnormalities or comorbidities. Sexual intercourse, spermicide use, a new sexual partner, maternal UTI history, and childhood UTI history are risk factors.
  Epidemiology: Escherichia coli causes most cases.
  Clinical presentation: Dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency without vaginal discharge make the diagnosis highly likely. In elderly women, genitourinary symptoms do not necessarily indicate cystitis.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Focused symptom history
      Purpose: Assess lower urinary tract symptoms and the absence of vaginal discharge.
      When indicated: Suspected uncomplicated cystitis.
      Interpretation: Typical symptoms with no vaginal discharge support the diagnosis.
    - Test: Urine dipstick
      Purpose: Increase diagnostic confidence.
      When indicated: When the diagnosis is unclear.
      Interpretation: In patients with typical symptoms, urine testing adds only minimally to diagnostic accuracy.
    - Test: Urine culture
      Purpose: Investigate selected presentations or possible treatment failure.
      When indicated: Suspected acute pyelonephritis; atypical symptoms; pregnancy; symptoms that persist or recur within 4 wk after treatment completion.
      Interpretation: For symptoms persisting at treatment completion or returning within 2 wk after resolution, presume that the organism may not be susceptible to the original agent.
    - Test: Antimicrobial susceptibility testing
      Purpose: Inform selection of another antimicrobial.
      When indicated: Symptoms that persist at the end of treatment or resolve and recur within 2 wk.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Reassess if symptoms remain at the end of treatment or recur within 2 wk after resolving.
    Recommended tests:
      - Urine culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing if symptoms persist or recur within 2 wk; routine post-treatment urinalysis or culture is not indicated in asymptomatic patients.

  Content: Toda embarazada Rh negativa no sensibilizada debe recibir oferta de profilaxis anti-D y administración antenatal en la semana 28, salvo certeza completa de que la pareja es Rh negativa.   Heading: Clinical Examination
  Content: Offer examination, including pelvic examination when appropriate, to seek findings such as restricted organ mobility. A retrospective study of almost 800 infertile women with surgically confirmed disease identified poor uterine mobility as predictive. Vaginal examination can identify deep infiltration or nodules in the vagina, uterosacral ligaments or pouch of Douglas; speculum examination can show vaginal lesions. Rectovaginal examination may detect rectosigmoid infiltration, masses or adnexal masses/endometriomas. Significant findings can prompt earlier referral. retrieved_chunks.document_id: Ectopic Pregnancy StatPearls NCBI Bookshelf
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Etiology
  Content: An ectopic pregnancy is an embryo implanted outside the uterine cavity. The fallopian tube is the most frequent site, although implantation can occur in a cesarean scar, endocervical canal, ovary, or peritoneal cavity. Within the tube, the ampulla accounts for 70%; other possible sites include the cornua, fimbriae, and proximal isthmic segment. A heterotopic pregnancy combines an ectopic pregnancy with a normally developing pregnancy in the endometrial cavity. Tubal injury can impair transport and retain an oocyte or embryo; tubal ligation and other surgical changes can likewise alter tubal function. Extranubal implantation need not involve tubal dysfunction or customary risk factors. Recurrence risk is 10% after 1 previous ectopic pregnancy and >25% after 2 or more. Additional associated factors are tubal damage from gonorrhea, chlamydia, pelvic or tubal surgery, or endometriosis; pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) or complications of ascending infection; and infertility or assisted reproductive technology. With assisted reproduction, risk is higher with more embryo transfers, fresh rather than frozen transfers, and cleavage-stage (Day 3) transfers. IUD users have a lower overall risk of pregnancy, but 53% of pregnancies arising with an IUD are ectopic. Smoking is associated with increased risk through effects on tubal function. Women older than 35, those with congenital reproductive tract anomalies, and those with previous cesarean delivery—particularly after breech presentation—may have increased risk. Progesterone-only contraception carries a slightly higher risk than other contraceptive methods. Conversely, oral contraceptives, previous pregnancy termination, failure of emergency contraception, and cesarean delivery are described as not associated with increased risk.

Document sections:
  Heading: History and Physical
  Content: Patients may have no symptoms; when symptoms occur, abnormal uterine bleeding is the most common. Abdominal pain, pelvic pain, and infertility may also occur. One in four reproductive-aged women with abnormal bleeding has an endometrial polyp in the cavity. Evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding should establish its cause and severity, associated symptoms, and comorbidities. A thorough medical and surgical history helps exclude other causes. No bleeding pattern is diagnostic of a polyp, but the bleeding history should be characterized; menorrhagia and intermenstrual spotting are reported most often. Tamoxifen, commonly used for breast cancer, can act as an agonist or antagonist in tissues bearing estrogen receptors. It has anticancer effects in breast tissue but carcinogenic effects in endometrial tissue. Chronic tamoxifen use is associated with endometrial polyps at an incidence of 20% to 35%. Hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms may also be associated with polyp formation, irregular bleeding, and ultrasound evidence of endometrial thickening. Clinical examination should include a general assessment, bimanual examination, and sterile speculum examination. The cervix and vaginal vault should be examined completely to exclude other structural explanations for symptoms. A pedunculated polyp may be visible at the external os.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_03
  Name: Gestational hypertension
  Description: Hypertension first appearing after 20 weeks of pregnancy without significant proteinuria.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Full assessment in secondary care
      Purpose: Evaluate gestational hypertension and factors requiring closer assessment and follow-up.
      When indicated: At presentation, by a healthcare professional trained in managing hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
      Interpretation: Factors requiring additional assessment and follow-up include nulliparity, age 40 years or older, pregnancy interval of more than 10 years, family history of pre-eclampsia, multi-fetal pregnancy, BMI of 35 kg/m2 or more, gestational age at presentation, previous pre-eclampsia or gestational hypertension, and pre-existing vascular or kidney disease.
    - Test: Blood pressure measurement
      Purpose: Assess severity and response to treatment.
      When indicated: For hypertension, once or twice a week depending on blood pressure until it is 135/85 mmHg or less; for severe hypertension, every 15 to 30 minutes until it is less than 160/110 mmHg.
      Interpretation: Once antihypertensive treatment is given, the target is 135/85 mmHg or less.
    - Test: Dipstick proteinuria testing
      Purpose: Monitor for proteinuria.
      When indicated: Once or twice a week alongside blood pressure measurement for hypertension; daily during admission for severe hypertension.
      Interpretation: A result of 1+ or more prompts quantification with albumin:creatinine ratio or protein:creatinine ratio.
    - Test: Full blood count, liver function and renal function
      Purpose: Monitor maternal haematological, liver and kidney status.
      When indicated: At presentation and then weekly.
    - Test: Placental growth factor (PLGF)-based testing
      Purpose: Help rule out pre-eclampsia.
      When indicated: On 1 occasion if pre-eclampsia is suspected, between 20 weeks and 36 weeks and 6 days of pregnancy.
    - Test: Fetal heart auscultation
      Purpose: Assess fetal heart activity.
      When indicated: At every antenatal appointment.
    - Test: Ultrasound for fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume assessment
      Purpose: Assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume.
      When indicated: At diagnosis; if findings are normal, repeat every 2 to 4 weeks if clinically indicated. If severe hypertension persists, repeat every 2 weeks.
    - Test: Umbilical artery doppler velocimetry
      Purpose: Assess the fetal circulation.
      When indicated: At diagnosis; if findings are normal, repeat every 2 to 4 weeks if clinically indicated. In severe gestational hypertension, subsequent monitoring is determined by scan findings.
    - Test: Cardiotocography (CTG)
      Purpose: Assess fetal status.
      When indicated: For gestational hypertension, only if clinically indicated; for severe gestational hypertension, at diagnosis and subsequently if clinically indicated.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: After birth, offer women still receiving antihypertensive treatment a medical review 2 weeks after transfer to community care. Offer all women a medical review 6 to 8 weeks after birth.
    Recommended tests:
      - Measure blood pressure daily for the first 2 days after birth and at least once between day 3 and day 5.
      - Measure blood pressure as clinically indicated if antihypertensive treatment changes after birth.
    Long term effects:
      - After gestational hypertension in a previous or current pregnancy, hypertension of any type in a future pregnancy occurs in approximately 22% (1 in 5 women), pre-eclampsia in approximately 7% (1 in 14 women), gestational hypertension in between approximately 11% and 15% (up to 1 in 7 women), and chronic hypertension in approximately 3% (up to 1 in 34 women).
      - For women with gestational hypertension in a current or previous pregnancy, the table reports an approximately 1.5 to 3 times increased risk of a major adverse cardiovascular event and an approximately 2 to 4 times increased risk of later hypertension. Stroke risk may be increased.
    Survivorship notes: The community-care plan specifies who provides follow-up, how often blood pressure is checked, thresholds for reducing or stopping treatment, and when to refer for a primary-care blood pressure review.

  Heading: 3.9. Urethritis
  Content: Urethritis has infectious and noninfectious causes and should be distinguished from other lower-tract infections. Urethral infection is commonly sexually transmitted. Distinguish gonococcal urethritis (GU) from non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU). NGU is a nonspecific diagnosis with possible causes including Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum, and Trichomonas vaginalis. The causal contribution of Ureaplasma spp. is disputed; recent evidence suggests U. urealyticum, but not U. parvum, can cause NGU. Possible manifestations are mucopurulent or purulent discharge, dysuria, and urethral itching, although many infections cause no symptoms. Start empiric treatment at diagnosis for severe urethritis. With mild symptoms, delay treatment so nucleic acid amplification test results can guide selection. Assess and treat sexual partners at risk while protecting patient confidentiality. Table 12 sets out Strong diagnostic and treatment recommendations covering Gram staining, validated NAAT before empirical therapy, resistance assessment where gonorrhoea testing is positive, pathogen-directed treatment informed by local resistance, and partner treatment. Table 13 provides pathogen-specific and persistent-urethritis regimens and alternatives. Its note reports increasing evidence that intravenous ceftriaxone is safe and effective for gonorrhoeal infection and avoids the discomfort of intramuscular injection, despite the absence of randomised controlled trials.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 6. Menstrual Irregularities and Disorders in Adolescence 6.1. Dysfunctional, Juvenile Hypermenorrhea
  Content: Hypermenorrhea means bleeding lasting longer than 7 days with blood loss of more than 80 mL. It is a common adolescent gynecological complaint. Heavy blood loss can restrict school, sport, and social participation, reduce quality of life, and accompany increased depression; iron-deficiency anemia can cause serious health problems. During the first few years after menarche, anovulation associated with hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian immaturity often causes follicular persistence and increased uterine bleeding, a feature of normal pubertal development rather than necessarily a clinical problem. Persistent juvenile bleeding is attributed to insufficient GnRH and LH release and disrupted regulatory feedback, with irregular estrogen changes, a prolonged estrogen phase, or disturbed estrogen–progestogen balance. Differential diagnosis must include a bleeding disorder such as von Willebrand syndrome, platelet dysfunction, or factor 7 or 8 deficiency. Personal or family bleeding history strengthens suspicion. A coagulation disorder causes hypermenorrhea in 7–62% of cases; when present, managing bleeding can be difficult and calls for joint gynecological and hematological care to prevent recurrent bleeding that lowers hemoglobin (Hb). Hb should be measured because adolescents may struggle to judge blood loss; anemia-related tiredness, fatigue, and dizziness diminish quality of life. Affected girls often do not seek medical care or receive adequate diagnosis and treatment. Hormonal treatment is the preferred approach. Following sonographic assessment, an excessively thick endometrium can be treated with progestogen alone for 14 days, such as dydrogesterone 2 × 10 mg daily or medroxyprogesterone acetate 10 mg daily. With a thin endometrium, estrogenization followed by transformation is needed: options include estrogen alone for 10 days followed by an estrogen–progestogen combination, an oral contraceptive—which is most commonly used, particularly for prophylaxis—or norethisterone acetate 2.5–5 mg daily for 10 days. The latter has a partial estrogenic effect but is not freely available in every country. For acute bleeding that does not stop with usual dosing, a contraceptive pill containing at least 30 µg of ethinylestradiol can be given every 6–8 h until bleeding decreases, then reduced to two and subsequently one tablet daily. Individual contraindications and risks must be considered. Depending on risk, a progesterone-only pill can be used; acute heavy bleeding may require a higher progestogen dose, such as double the dose of desogestrel. Hospital admission is occasionally necessary, particularly when Hb is below 8 g/dL. Oral contraception and hormone replacement therapy can provide prophylaxis and can continue during overt anemia until Hb recovers, but hormone replacement therapy does not provide contraception. A levonorgestrel-containing IUD (intrauterine device) is another effective option with or without a coagulation disorder, without an increased expulsion rate reported in those with coagulation disorders. Insertion can be harder in adolescents, especially before sexual intercourse, and may require sedation. Heavy bleeding may also require iron replacement, transfusion, or tranexamic acid. Tranexamic acid is particularly relevant when hormones are declined or contraindicated and appears as effective as hormonal treatment for hypermenorrhea. Surgical curettage should be avoided to preserve the endometrium. Figure 5 illustrates marked endometrial thickening in a 12-year-old girl with juvenile hypermenorrhea. Treatment aims to stop bleeding, correct anemia, establish a regular cycle, and improve quality of life.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: postpartum haemorrhage
  Synonyms:
    - PPH
  Description: Bleeding after childbirth that requires prompt recognition and treatment. In the outcomes considered by the guideline, PPH is identified at blood loss ≥ 500 ml.
  Epidemiology: WHO estimates that about 14 million women experience PPH each year. Obstetric haemorrhage accounts for 27% of maternal deaths worldwide each year, and most of those deaths are due to PPH.
  Clinical presentation: Excessive postpartum blood loss may be accompanied by early warning signs such as tachycardia or hypotension.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Objective measurement of postpartum blood loss
      Purpose: Detect PPH and enable prompt treatment.
      When indicated: Routinely for all women giving birth; measurement is particularly important during the first few hours after birth.
      Interpretation: The guideline uses blood loss ≥ 500 ml to identify PPH among its priority outcomes. In a large trial, the treatment bundle was initiated at measured blood loss of 500 ml or greater, or 300 ml or greater when early warning signs of excessive blood loss were present; these trial triggers do not replace clinical judgement.
    - Test: Calibrated drape
      Purpose: Quantify postpartum blood loss objectively.
      When indicated: For women having a vaginal birth.
      Interpretation: Most available evidence on measurement after vaginal birth concerns calibrated drapes. Objective quantification is more likely to detect PPH than visual estimation, which is frequently inaccurate.
    - Test: Monitoring of vital parameters
      Purpose: Recognize early signs of excessive blood loss.
      When indicated: Regularly after birth, particularly during the first few hours.
      Interpretation: Tachycardia and hypotension are examples of early warning signs. The outcomes considered also include changes in heart rate, blood pressure and urine output.
    - Test: Examination of the genital tract
      When indicated: As part of the first-line PPH treatment bundle.
    - Test: Haemoglobin (Hb) concentration
      Purpose: Assess postpartum anaemia and the change in concentration before and after delivery among the outcomes considered by the guideline.
      Interpretation: Postpartum anaemia is defined among the priority outcomes as a haemoglobin (Hb) lower than 9 mg/dl.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Monitor regularly after birth, with particular attention to blood loss during the first few hours.
    Recommended tests:
      - Measurement of postpartum blood loss
      - Monitoring for early warning signs of excessive blood loss, including tachycardia and hypotension

Pregnancy and lactation: Embarazo
La hiperglicemia no controlada en la fase periconcepcional y durante el embarazo se asocia con un aumento del riesgo de anormalidades congénitas, pérdida del embarazo, hipertensión inducida por embarazo, preeclampsia y mortalidad perinatal. Es importante mantener el nivel de glucosa en sangre lo más cercano a la normalidad posible durante el embarazo, para reducir el riesgo de complicaciones relacionadas con la hiperglicemia para la madre y su hijo.
La metformina atraviesa la placenta en niveles que pueden ser tan elevados como las concetraciones de la madre.
Una gran cantidad de datos de mujeres embarazadas (más de 1000 resultados expuestos) de un estudio con una cohorte basada en registros y datos publicados (meta-análisis, estudios clínicos y registros) indican que no existe un aumento del riesgo de anormalidades congénitas ni toxicidad fetal/neonatal tras la exposición a metformina en la fase periconcepcional y/o durante el embarazo.
Existen una evidencia limitada e inconclusa del efecto de la metformina sobre los resultados de peso a largo plazo en los niños expuestos en el útero. La metformina parece no afectar al desarrollo motor y social hasta 4 años de edad en niños expuestos durante el embarazo, pese a que los datos sobre resultados a largo plazo son limitados.
Si es clínicamente necesario, se puede considerar el uso de metformina durante el embarazo y en la fase periconcepcional como un tratamiento adicional o como alternativa a la insulina.

Lactancia
La metformina se excreta en la leche materna. No se han observado efectos adversos en los recién nacidos/bebés con lactancia materna. Sin embargo, dado que la información disponible es limitada, la lactancia materna no se recomienda durante el tratamiento con metformina. La decisión de retirar la lactancia materna debe tomarse teniendo en cuenta los beneficios de la lactancia y el riesgo potencial de los efectos adversos en el niño.

Fertilidad
La fertilidad de ratas machos y hembras no se vio afectada por la metformina cuando ésta se administró a dosis tan altas como 600 mg/Kg/día, que es aproximadamente tres veces la dosis máxima diaria recomendada en humanos basándose en la comparación de la superficie corporal.

  Heading: 6. Adenomyosis: hysteroscopic treatment
  Content: Several hysteroscopic appearances have been linked to adenomyosis, but the method's diagnostic role is uncertain because it does not assess the deeper myometrium commonly involved. Hysteroscopic treatment has been proposed for focal or diffuse disease near the endometrium; it is not considered appropriate for deeper lesions. A focal lesion less than 1.5 cm and close to the endometrial cavity may be enucleated in an ambulatory setting with mechanical instruments or bipolar electrodes, similarly to a submucosal myoma. Resectoscopic treatment may be feasible for larger lesions or diffuse superficial disease, including in an office setting when a mini-resectoscope is available. Endometrial or endo-myometrial ablation may be performed for women who do not desire future pregnancy. Although medical therapy appears more effective for adenomyosis-related symptoms, improvement in dysmenorrhea and AUB is described in about 50% of hysteroscopically treated patients.

Conditions:

  Name: Hemorragia Postparto
  Synonyms:
    - HPP
  Description: La definición que el consenso considera más aceptada es cualquier pérdida sanguínea posparto que provoque signos de hipovolemia y/o inestabilidad hemodinámica. También recoge definiciones basadas en pérdida de >500ml tras parto vaginal, más de 1000ml tras cesárea, disminución de un 10% del hematocrito basal o pérdida de 500ml o más durante las 24 horas posteriores al parto. Sus causas se agrupan en las “4 T”: alteraciones del tono uterino, tejido placentario retenido o adherido, traumatismos genitales y trastornos de coagulación.
  Epidemiology: Permanece entre las tres principales causas de mortalidad materna mundial, especialmente en países en vías de desarrollo.
  Clinical presentation: Puede manifestarse con sangrado acompañado de hipovolemia o inestabilidad hemodinámica.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: hemorragia postparto primaria
      Distinguishing features: Ocurre en las primeras 24 hs. posteriores al nacimiento.
    - Name: hemorragia posparto secundaria
      Distinguishing features: Aparece después de 24 horas y hasta 12 semanas tras el parto; entre sus causas figuran los restos placentarios retenidos y/o la infección.
    - Name: HPP grave
      Distinguishing features: Se define por una pérdida de sangre de 1.000 ml o más dentro de las 24 horas posteriores al parto.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Cuantificación de la pérdida sanguínea
      Purpose: Determinar la magnitud de la hemorragia y orientar la intervención.
      When indicated: Ante sangrado posterior al parto.
      Interpretation: La estimación visual tiende a subestimar el volumen; el cálculo puede subestimarse hasta en un 50%. Debe relacionarse con los signos clínicos y los antecedentes individuales.
    - Test: Bolsa de recolección de sangre calibrada
      Purpose: Medir de forma objetiva la pérdida sanguínea posterior al parto.
      When indicated: Inmediatamente después del parto, cuando se emplee este método.
    - Test: Examen de la placenta expulsada
      Purpose: Comprobar que la expulsión fue completa y que la placenta está íntegra.
      When indicated: Durante la evaluación inicial de la hemorragia.
    - Test: Exploración del cuello uterino y la vagina con valvas
      Purpose: Identificar una posible fuente de sangrado en el tracto genital.
      When indicated: Durante la evaluación inicial de la hemorragia.
    - Test: Frecuencia cardiaca, tensión arterial, oximetría de pulso y diuresis horaria
      Purpose: Vigilar de forma continua la situación hemodinámica y la respuesta a la reanimación.
      When indicated: Durante la hemorragia y su tratamiento.
      Interpretation: A los 30 minutos, la estabilización del pulso con FC menor de 90 latidos por minuto, el aumento de la presión con TAS >100 mm de Hg, la mejoría del estado mental y una diuresis > 30 ml por hora son signos de respuesta hemodinámica.
  Staging:
    System: Clasificación según el momento de aparición
    Definitions:
      - Stage: hemorragia postparto primaria
        Description: Sangrado que ocurre durante las primeras 24 hs. después del nacimiento.
      - Stage: hemorragia posparto secundaria
        Description: Sangrado que aparece después de 24 horas y hasta 12 semanas después del parto.
    Additional rules: El documento también distingue la HPP grave por una pérdida de 1.000 ml o más en las 24 horas posteriores al parto.
  Prognostic tools:
    - Name: Índice de Choque
      Components:
      - frecuencia cardiaca

      - Group: normal en obstetricia
      Criteria: 0,7 a 0,9

      Criteria: valores superiores a 0,9

  Follow up:
    Schedule: Durante la reanimación se indica vigilancia continua; se reevalúa la respuesta hemodinámica a los 30 minutos y se mantienen controles clínicos en las fases de 20 a 60 minutos y de 60 minutos.

      - Monitorización de frecuencia cardiaca, tensión arterial, oximetría de pulso y diuresis horaria

      - Evaluación del estado de conciencia y del llenado capilar

retrieved_chunks.text:
Main conclusion: Early recognition and treatment of ectopic pregnancy are essential to reduce the risk of rupture and severe hemorrhage. Management should reflect hemodynamic stability, implantation site, diagnostic findings, and the patient’s fertility goals, with urgent surgery when rupture is suspected.

Narrative summary: This educational review examines the presentation, diagnosis, and management of ectopic pregnancy rather than reporting a new clinical study. Ectopic pregnancy affects approximately 1% to 2% of pregnancies in the United States and accounts for 2.7% of pregnancy-related deaths. Approximately 97% occur in the fallopian tube. Lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding are common, while dizziness, fainting, shoulder pain, or severe pelvic pain may indicate rupture.

Evaluation combines serum β-hCG measurements with ultrasound, particularly TVUS. A β-hCG level >2000 mIU/mL without a visible intrauterine pregnancy is highly suggestive of ectopic pregnancy; the review also notes a suggested discriminatory cutoff of up to 3500 mIU/mL to avoid misdiagnosing a viable pregnancy. When pregnancy location remains uncertain, serial β-hCG measurements and repeat imaging may be needed.

Hemodynamic instability or suspected rupture requires urgent surgical intervention. For selected asymptomatic patients with low, declining β-hCG, expectant management may be considered; 88% of ectopic pregnancies with an initial β-hCG level of <200 mIU/mL resolved spontaneously. In appropriate candidates, methotrexate is a medical option, with reported success of approximately 70% to 95%; β-hCG monitoring continues until the level is undetectable. Surgical options include salpingostomy and salpingectomy. For cesarean scar ectopic pregnancy, expectant management is not recommended except in select cases of confirmed fetal demise, and systemic methotrexate alone is not recommended.

  Decision rules:
    - Refer women and girls planning pregnancy or already pregnant to an epilepsy specialist team to review antiseizure medication options, and coordinate their care with specialist obstetrics and primary care.
    - Discuss the relative risks of poorly controlled seizures and medicine exposure during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Explain the importance of adherence and of not stopping medicine without medical supervision.
    - Consider closer review during pregnancy when the woman or girl has a learning disability, is aged under 16 years, has had a seizure within the past 12 months, has bilateral tonic-clonic seizures or has modifiable SUDEP risk factors.

Document sections:
  Heading: Epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (Doose syndrome)
  Content: This is a rare condition of young children for which accurate diagnosis and tertiary paediatric neurology advice are important. No treatment evidence was identified. Clinical experience supported levetiracetam and sodium valproate as first-line possibilities because they are used effectively for generalised epilepsy, including this syndrome. Sodium valproate needs caution, full benefit–risk discussion, MHRA safeguards and regular reassessment; the committee retained it as an option because alternatives are limited, treatment often starts young and most children outgrow seizures by their teenage years. Long-term sodium valproate may reduce bone mineral density and increase osteomalacia risk; consider supplementation for those at risk. Studies known to the committee and clinical experience supported a ketogenic diet as second-line alternative or add-on under a ketogenic diet team. In the absence of evidence, clinical experience identified clobazam, ethosuximide, topiramate and zonisamide as possible choices only after earlier options fail. Topiramate requires Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions for women and girls of childbearing potential. Do not use carbamazepine, gabapentin, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, pregabalin or vigabatrin because they increase seizure frequency in this syndrome. Consider withdrawing treatment after 2 seizure-free years in children. Further research is needed when first-line therapy fails or is intolerable. Major practice change is not expected.

Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 3: Adult. Chronic or progressive unilateral vision loss. Intraorbital mass-like lesion suspected or vascular lesion suspected. Initial imaging.
  Content: Many tumors, tumor-like conditions, systemic diseases, metastases, and high- or low-flow vascular malformations can involve the orbit. Distinguishing vascular from other lesions guides subsequent workup and care. Because the orbital space is restricted, either a soft-tissue or vascular mass may cause proptosis. Orbital-apex masses or inflammation characteristically produce vision loss with ophthalmoplegia. Orbital masses can be classified by location in the globe, optic nerve sheath complex, intraconal or extraconal space, bone, or multiple compartments. Benign lesions predominate, but malignant orbital tumors become more prevalent in adults older than 60 years of age. Among cysts, dermoid cysts are most common; excluding cysts, cavernous venous malformation is the commonest benign adult orbital mass, while non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the commonest malignant one. Imaging seeks to detect and characterize the causative orbital mass or vascular lesion, direct care, and sometimes establish a specific diagnosis.

question: First step in management of raised intracranial pressure-

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Best practices guidelines traumatic brain injury__JC__000299
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Best practices guidelines traumatic brain injury
retrieved_chunks.text:
Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_07
  Type: algorithm
  Title: Box 3. SIBICC I Tiers for ICP Treatment of Intracranial Hypertension for Patients with ICP Monitoring
  Source heading: Tiered Treatments
  Description: Step 1, Tier One: Target CPP 60–70 mm Hg; increase analgesia or sedation to reduce ICP; keep PaCO2 at 35–38 mm Hg/4.7–5.1 kPa; give intermittent boluses of mannitol (0.25–1.0 g/kg) or hypertonic saline; drain CSF through an existing EVD or consider EVD placement if monitoring began with a parenchymal probe; consider antiseizure prophylaxis for 1 week only unless continuation is indicated, and consider EEG monitoring. For either hyperosmolar agent, recommended limits are sodium 155 mEq/L and osmolality 320 mEq/L. Step 2, Tier Two: If further treatment is needed, maintain PaCO2 at 32–35 mm Hg/4.3–4.6 kPa; try neuromuscular paralysis in an adequately sedated patient and continue infusion only if the trial lowers ICP; perform a MAP Challenge to guide individualized MAP and CPP targets, returning MAP to baseline with impaired autoregulation or raising its target to lower ICP when autoregulation is intact. Step 3, Tier Three: If further escalation is appropriate, give pentobarbital or sodium thiopentone only if a test shows ICP benefit, titrating to ICP control without exceeding the dose producing burst suppression and avoiding hypotension; alternatively, perform secondary decompressive craniectomy or use active cooling for mild hypothermia at 35–36°C. Treatments within a tier have no prescribed rank, every lower-tier option need not be exhausted, and a tier can be bypassed when advantageous.
  Summary: Describes the SIBICC I escalation options for monitored intracranial hypertension.
  Clinical relevance: Structures treatment escalation according to relative risk and benefit while allowing patient-specific choices.

Document sections:
  Heading: Referral after a first seizure or remission and assessing risk of a second seizure
  Content: The committee considered rapid specialist referral important because epilepsy diagnosis is complex and errors can lead to inappropriate care. Evidence suggested adults with a mental health condition after a first seizure were almost 3 times more likely to have another seizure than the general population; those with sepsis were 4.5 times more likely than those without sepsis. Vascular-risk evidence did not show a risk difference, but the committee regarded diabetes, hypertension and atrial fibrillation as important potentially modifiable factors. Evidence about children's temperature and recurrence risk was unclear: febrile seizures generally do not predispose to later afebrile seizures, whereas afebrile seizures may increase recurrence risk. Individual risk assessment therefore also needs mental, physical and social factors. The committee did not recommend existing second-seizure prediction tools because poor discrimination between low and high risk could cause harm. Only about 25% of adults currently receive complete modifiable-risk assessment after a first seizure; changing this may modestly increase staff costs. The recommendations for children reflect existing practice.

Document sections:
  Heading: TIERED MANAGEMENT OF INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE
  Content: Treat raised ICP after severe TBI to limit secondary injury; untreated elevation can cause herniation, brainstem compression, reduced CPP, ischemia, or, in extreme cases, cessation of brain perfusion. Invasive monitors are currently preferred for accuracy and can detect expanding lesions, guide targeted treatment, calculate CPP and autoregulatory status, and provide waveform information about compliance. SIBICC developed three treatment tiers through a rigorous Delphi-based expert-consensus process to address gaps in evidence-based guidance. Treatments with more favorable risk–benefit profiles generally precede those with less favorable profiles, while clinicians retain discretion within tiers and can target suspected physiological disturbances. These algorithms are suggestions that can standardize care, not standards of practice; relevant disciplines should review and approve or adapt them locally. The full protocols cover ICP alone or ICP with low PbtO2, discouraged interventions, neurological worsening, and treatment weaning.

Document sections:
  Heading: 1.4 Assessment in the emergency department
  Content: For every emergency department arrival, stabilise airway, breathing and circulation (ABC) before addressing other injuries. Do not attribute reduced consciousness to intoxication until important traumatic brain injury has been excluded. Clinicians assessing head injury should be able to identify the listed risk factors for head and cervical spine CT, with training provided as necessary. A trained staff member should assess impaired consciousness, defined here as GCS less than 15, immediately. Consult the tranexamic acid recommendations for GCS 12 or less. For GCS 8 or less, involve an appropriately trained advanced-airway clinician early to assist resuscitation. [2003] [2023] A trained staff member should assess each emergency department presentation with head injury within a maximum of 15 minutes of hospital arrival, including initial categorisation of risk for clinically important brain or cervical spine injury. High-risk patients need full examination to identify imaging requirements for the head, cervical spine or other sites. Those initially classified as low risk need reassessment by an emergency department clinician. Base final imaging decisions on the relevant age-specific criteria after discussion with radiology. Reassess anyone returning with persistent symptoms from the original injury, discuss the case with a senior clinician experienced in head injury and consider CT. Treat pain to help avert raised intracranial pressure, with reassurance, fracture splinting and bladder catheterisation when required. Consider or suspect abuse, neglect or other safeguarding concerns as a possible cause or contributor. [2003, amended 2007] [2003, amended 2007 and 2023] [2003, amended 2023] [2007] [2023] Include a safeguarding-trained clinician in the initial assessment; document concerns and follow age-appropriate local safeguarding procedures. Use a consistent standard head-injury proforma across hospital departments for assessment and observation, with a separate form for people under 16 and space for extra details such as possible non-accidental injury. retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: ASSOCIATED CONDITIONS
  Content: Diuretics, antihistamines, anticholinergics, antidepressants, and systemic retinoids such as isotretinoin may aggravate symptoms. Frequently instilled eye medicines, for example more than four drops a day, can disturb tear-film maintenance, with preservatives contributing to epithelial breakdown. Low humidity, wind, drafts, air conditioning, heating, and reduced blinking during prolonged screen use, reading, or driving may worsen discomfort. External irritants and allergens may aggravate symptoms without being considered causes. Rosacea can worsen dry eye and ocular-surface disease. Although more frequently observed in fair skin, it occurs in all skin types; findings include facial erythema, telangiectasia, papules, pustules, enlarged sebaceous glands, and rhinophyma. Darker skin may obscure flushing and telangiectasia. Children may develop ocular manifestations before obvious skin disease, allowing misdiagnosis. Rosacea is more prevalent in women but can be more severe in men. Subtle signs can be overlooked, particularly in children presenting with recurrent blepharokeratoconjunctivitis, punctate erosions, peripheral keratitis, meibomian gland disease, or recurrent chalazia. Pediatric ocular disease often includes asymmetric corneal involvement with potentially sight-threatening impairment; skin manifestations are less frequent and atopy is common. Childhood styes are associated with increased adult rosacea risk. In Sjögren's syndrome, inflammatory infiltration of exocrine glands impairs salivary and tear production. About 10% of patients with clinically significant aqueous deficient dry eye have underlying primary Sjӧgren’s syndrome. Primary disease is multisystemic and increases lymphoma risk; about 5% of patients with Sjögren syndrome develop a lymphoid malignancy. A cited meta-analysis found the strongest rheumatic-disease association with lymphoid malignancy for primary Sjӧgren’s syndrome, reporting an incidence rate of 18.9% (95% CI, 9.4–37.9) and an increased incidence of 320 cases per 100,000 patient years. Ophthalmologists should therefore maintain strong suspicion and a low threshold for diagnostic serology in clinically significant dry eye. Infiltration or replacement of lacrimal secretory tissue in lymphoma, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, or amyloidosis can cause aqueous deficiency. Dry eye has also been reported with Epstein-Barr virus, human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1, HIV, hepatitis C, and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, with or without GVHD. One AIDS group had dry eye in 21%; diffuse infiltrative lymphadenopathy syndrome has been described in HIV, predominantly among children. Hepatitis C has been associated with decreased secretion and tear lactoferrin. Primary or persistent Epstein-Barr virus infection has been linked to gland enlargement, dry eye, and Sjögren’s syndrome. Chronic GVHD can cause lacrimal and conjunctival infiltration and fibrosis through T-cell interaction with fibroblasts. Ocular mucous membrane pemphigoid and Stevens-Johnson syndrome may destroy conjunctival goblet cells through inflammation and scarring. Atopy may contribute through blepharitis, conjunctival scarring, or antihistamines. Dry eye in younger patients or males warrants suspicion of an associated local or systemic disorder. Relevant eyelid or neurologic conditions include malposition, lagophthalmos, exophthalmos, thyroid-associated ocular disease, blepharitis, Parkinson disease, and Bell’s palsy; orbital or eyelid surgery, radiation, and injury may also contribute. Incomplete blinking was associated with a two-fold increase in evaporative dry eye, greater meibomian gland loss, poorer meibum, and thinner tear-film lipid layer. Greater screen exposure can reduce blinking and worsen ocular-surface disease in adults and children.

  Content: These seizures rapidly involve both cerebral hemispheres, causing loss of consciousness followed by muscle stiffening and rhythmic jerking. For time to treatment failure, evidence showed no medicine outperforming sodium valproate; it showed clear advantages over lacosamide, phenobarbital, carbamazepine and topiramate. No clear difference from other medicines was found for remission or time to first seizure. After sodium valproate, lamotrigine and levetiracetam performed next best on time to treatment failure, so the January 2025 update made all 3 first-line monotherapy options subject to MHRA restrictions. Discuss and review reproductive safety measures for women and girls and precautionary advice for boys and men taking sodium valproate. Adverse events were inconsistently reported, limiting comparisons, although careful titration or dose adjustment can manage many events. Evidence could not clearly rank add-on drugs. Lamotrigine, levetiracetam, perampanel and topiramate performed better than placebo for a 50% response rate; clobazam and sodium valproate were included on the basis of experience and established use despite no identified evidence for them. Levetiracetam and perampanel showed some evidence of greater seizure freedom than placebo, with substantial uncertainty. Brivaracetam might outperform placebo for more than 50% seizure-frequency reduction, while lacosamide was less effective than levetiracetam on that outcome. These 2 medicines, alongside phenobarbital, primidone and zonisamide, were included as possible second-line add-ons partly on clinical experience.   Content: Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS) is an uncommon sporadic neurocutaneous disorder, formerly categorized as a phakomatosis. Among its three variants, types 1 and 2 are suggested by a characteristic facial port-wine angioma, whereas type 3 has leptomeningeal angiomatosis without that readily visible feature. Seizures occur in 75 %–90 % of cases. Extensive pial angiomatosis causes seizures and can affect one lobe or much of a hemisphere; the epileptogenic cortex is presumed to extend beyond visible angiomatous plaques. retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Introduction
  Content: IIH involves raised cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure without an identified cause. Headache, visual disturbance and papilloedema are typical, while the rest of the neurological examination is generally normal. Headache is the most frequently reported symptom, occurring in 7599% of cases as printed in the document. Pseudotumour Cerebri Syndrome (PTCS) is another term that also covers secondary causes. Heinrich Quincke described the condition in the late nineteenth century and attributed it to excessive CSF production. Later names included ‘pseudotumor cerebri’ in 1904 and ‘benign intracranial hypertension’ in 1955; reports of visual loss made the description ‘benign’ inappropriate. Subsequent terminology included PTCS and IIH. The classical modified Dandy criteria suggest that IIH diagnosis requires symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (ICP), no focal neurological signs other than unilateral or bilateral sixth nerve palsies, increased CSF opening pressure with otherwise normal CSF, normal brain imaging without hydrocephalus, and no alternative explanation for raised ICP. Some authors consider these criteria sufficient. Friedman’s criteria provide an alternative. For definite IIH, they require A) papilloedema; B) a normal neurological examination apart from cranial nerve abnormalities; C) normal brain parenchyma without hydrocephalus, a mass, a structural lesion or abnormal meningeal enhancement on MRI with and without gadolinium in typical patients (female and obese), with MRI with and without gadolinium plus MRV for others; if MRI cannot be obtained or is contraindicated, contrast-enhanced CT may be used; D) normal CSF composition; and E) opening pressure of ≥280mm CSF in children, or 250mm CSF if the child is not sedated and not obese, measured during a properly performed lumbar puncture. Without papilloedema, IIH can still be diagnosed under these criteria when abducens nerve palsy and all of B-E are present. The document also describes diagnosis with B-E plus at least three of four imaging features: empty sella, flattening of the posterior globe, enlargement of the perioptic subarachnoid space with or without optic nerve tortuosity, and transverse venous sinus stenosis. A ‘probable’ diagnosis is possible with A-D and bilateral papilloedema when CSF pressure does not meet the diagnostic threshold in E. Diagnosis requires exclusion of underlying structural causes, including malignancy or autoimmune conditions. Potential imaging findings include secondary empty sella syndrome, flattened globes, abnormal optic nerve sheaths, optic nerve protrusion, posterior globe flattening and transverse sinus stenosis. A UK cohort reported IIH incidence of 0.71 per 100,000 among children aged 1-16 years, rising with age and weight to 4.18 per 100,000 in obese boys aged 12-15 years and 10.7 per 100,000 in obese girls of the same age. Other estimates for children range from 0.17 to 1.32 per 100,000. Treatment aims to protect vision and relieve headache. Weight control has been effective in adults. Drug treatment commonly involves acetazolamide or topiramate; a possible weight-loss benefit from topiramate has not yet been established in larger studies. Procedural options include CSF diversion, such as ventriculoperitoneal shunt (VPS) or lumboperitonral shunt, optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF), and venous sinus stenting (VSS). Choices depend on symptoms, the extent of visual loss and local availability. Lumbar puncture (LP) has been examined for both diagnosis and treatment, but doubts about its therapeutic efficacy have increased interest in surgery. How best to measure pressure and respond clinically to elevated measurements remains uncertain. With no randomised control trials of paediatric IIH management, this three-round Delphi study examined diagnosis, investigation and management to provide clinicians with recommendations from experienced professionals, following international adult consensus recommendations.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Abstract
  Content: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is the most frequent chronic complication of herpes zoster. It is a form of neuropathic pain that can substantially impair quality of life, particularly in older or immunocompromised people, despite the availability of vaccination. This review examines the effectiveness and safety of oral and topical medicines for PHN-related neuropathic pain. It draws on 49 scientific publications identified through PubMed, PubMedCentral, NCBI and Via Medica Journals and published between 2008–2024. Pharmacological treatment includes several oral and topical drug groups. Gabapentinoids and tricyclic anti-depressants are regarded as first-line options; lidocaine 5% patches have that position in some circumstances. Capsaicin 8% and opioids are considered second-line options. Because monotherapy relatively often fails to control pain, multimodal treatment is increasingly used. PHN remains difficult to manage, and the review emphasizes combining medicines with different mechanisms of action and selecting treatment according to the individual clinical situation.
