retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Chiang et al. 2021 International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity, Third Edition__JC__000006
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Chiang et al. 2021 International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity, Third Edition
retrieved_chunks.text:
Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)
  Description: A disorder of the developing retinal vasculature in premature infants. ICROP3 classifies each eye by the location of vascularization or disease, vascular changes, the appearance of the lesion at the vascular–avascular junction, and its circumferential extent. It also describes regression, reactivation, and late sequelae.
  Clinical presentation: Findings range from a demarcation line, ridge, or extraretinal neovascularization to partial or total retinal detachment. Posterior vessel dilation and tortuosity range continuously from normal through preplus disease to plus disease. After spontaneous regression or treatment, abnormalities may resolve incompletely, persist, or reactivate.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: preplus disease
      Distinguishing features: Retinal vascular dilation, tortuosity, or both are abnormal but do not reach the severity of plus disease.
    - Name: plus disease
      Distinguishing features: Posterior retinal vessels show dilation and tortuosity. Iris vascular engorgement, poor pupillary dilation, and peripheral vascular engorgement with vitreous haze can indicate advanced disease but are not required for this designation.
    - Name: persistent avascular retina (PAR)
      Distinguishing features: Vascularization remains incomplete after spontaneous or treatment-associated regression; the avascular area may be peripheral or posterior and is described by location and extent.
    - Name: reactivation
      Distinguishing features: Acute-phase vascular changes or lesions recur after regression. Findings can range from a new, self-limiting demarcation line to stage 3 disease with plus disease and need not follow the usual acute-stage sequence.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: ophthalmoscopy
      Purpose: Assess vascularization, vascular abnormalities, lesions, retinal detachment, and visibility of the optic disc.
      When indicated: During examination and classification of an eye at risk for or affected by ROP.
      Interpretation: Record zone, plus disease, stage, and extent for each eye; also note A-ROP if present. A visible optic disc distinguishes stage 5A from stage 5B and stage 5C.
    - Test: 28-diopter (D) lens
      Purpose: Estimate the temporal limit of zone I during ophthalmoscopy.
      When indicated: When assessing the retinal zone.
      Interpretation: With the nasal edge of the optic disc at one edge of the view, the temporal edge approximately marks the zone I limit.
    - Test: retinal photography
      Purpose: Document vascular and retinal findings.
      When indicated: When retinal imaging is used for assessment.
      Interpretation: Before 39 weeks’ postmenstrual age, the fovea may be difficult to identify; its position may instead be estimated from the macular center. Plus-disease assessment should not rely solely on vessels visible in narrow-angle photographs.
    - Test: OCT
      Purpose: Show features at the vascular–avascular junction and determine whether a partial detachment involves the fovea.
      When indicated: Particularly when foveal involvement is subtle or difficult to judge clinically.
      Interpretation: An attached fovea corresponds to stage 4A; foveal detachment corresponds to stage 4B.
    - Test: B-scan ultrasonography
      Purpose: Determine the extent of retinal detachment.
      When indicated: When fibrosis prevents visualization of the posterior pole.
      Interpretation: Can reveal total detachment and its funnel configuration despite an obstructed fundus view.
    - Test: fluorescein angiography
      Purpose: Characterize vascular abnormalities, avascular retina, leakage, or subtle neovascularization.
      When indicated: When additional vascular assessment is useful, including assessment of late abnormalities or possible reactivation.
      Interpretation: The illustrated findings include persistent avascular retina, leakage in incompletely regressed disease, and leakage at sites of reactivation.
    - Test: OCT angiography
      Purpose: Illustrate macular vascular abnormalities.
      Interpretation: The document illustrates an incompletely developed foveal contour and a poorly defined foveal avascular zone after ROP.
  Staging:
    System: ICROP3
    Definitions:
      - Stage: stage 1
        Description: A relatively flat, thin, white demarcation line lies within the retina at the vascular–avascular junction. Peripheral vessel dilation or tortuosity alone does not establish this stage.
      - Stage: stage 2
        Description: A ridge develops from the demarcation line, acquiring width and height. Isolated neovascular tufts called popcorn may lie behind it without constituting stage 3.
      - Stage: stage 3
        Description: Extraretinal neovascular tissue extends toward the vitreous from the ridge. Apparent flat neovascularization in zone I or posterior zone II also qualifies, even without an obvious ridge or demarcation line.
      - Stage: stage 4
        Description: Partial retinal detachment, which may be tractional or exudative.
      - Stage: stage 4A
        Description: Partial retinal detachment with the fovea remaining attached.
      - Stage: stage 4B
        Description: Partial retinal detachment involving the fovea. A posterior volcano-shaped tractional detachment remains stage 4B if the peripheral retina is attached.
      - Stage: stage 5
        Description: Total retinal detachment.
      - Stage: stage 5A
        Description: Total retinal detachment with an optic disc visible on ophthalmoscopy, suggesting an open funnel.
      - Stage: stage 5B
        Description: Total retinal detachment in which retrolental fibrovascular tissue or a closed funnel obscures the optic disc.
      - Stage: stage 5C
        Description: Findings of stage 5B accompanied by anterior segment abnormalities, such as marked anterior chamber shallowing, adhesions, or corneal opacification, suggesting a closed funnel.
    Additional rules: The most posterior vascularization or lesion determines the eye’s zone. Zone I extends from the optic disc center to a radius twice the estimated disc-center–to–foveal-center distance. Zone II extends from zone I to the nasal ora serrata, with comparable reach in other directions; posterior zone II extends 2 disc diameters beyond the zone I border. Zone III is the remaining peripheral crescent; its designation requires nasal vessels to reach the ora serrata and no ROP in the 2 nasal-most clock hours. A lesion entering a more posterior zone for 1 to 2 clock hours is classified by that zone with the qualifier “secondary to notch.” When stages coexist, use the most severe stage. Assess the preplus-to-plus spectrum using vessels within zone I rather than a quadrant count or only the narrow-angle photographic field. The document describes extent as 12 clock-hour sectors in Table 1 but as 30 sectors in the Extent section; these statements conflict. Document reactivated lesions with their zone and stage and the modifier “reactivated.”
  Follow up:
    Long term effects:
      - Late tractional, rhegmatogenous, or, rarely, exudative retinal detachment.
      - Retinoschisis that can extend into the macula and threaten visual field or acuity.
      - Persistent avascular retina, which is prone to thinning, holes, latticelike changes, and later retinal detachment.
      - Macular abnormalities, including a smaller foveal avascular zone and a blunted or absent foveal depression.
      - Persistent vessel tortuosity, straightened vascular arcades with macular dragging, a falciform retinal fold, abnormal branching, circumferential vascular connections, and telangiectatic vessels.
      - Vitreous hemorrhage.
      - Secondary angle-closure glaucoma later in life.
    Survivorship notes: Describe persistent avascular retina by location and extent. A late detachment without signs of active ROP is a sequela rather than reactivation. Reactivation is reported more often after anti-VEGF treatment than after spontaneous regression and rarely, if ever, after complete laser photocoagulation; current evidence places its most common occurrence after anti-VEGF injection between 37 and 60 weeks’ postmenstrual age, although later reactivation may occur.

  Content: The number of people with diabetes has increased across countries during the past 30 years alongside lifestyle changes. retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 4: Adult. Acute vision loss, retinal structural abnormality suspected. Initial imaging.
  Content: Acute vision loss from retinal detachment is an emergency because delayed treatment can result in permanent impairment. Rhegmatogenous detachment is the most common type: a neurosensory retinal break lets vitreous fluid enter the potential space between sensory and pigmented retina. Clinical assessment and dilated funduscopy establish the diagnosis, ordinarily without imaging. If vitreous hemorrhage or another obstacle obscures the posterior eye, ocular US may establish detachment. Exudative or serous detachment instead involves subretinal fluid without a neurosensory epithelial break. Inflammatory, infectious, neoplastic, vascular, or degenerative conditions can disrupt the blood-retinal barrier and cause it. Central retinal artery occlusion presents with abrupt, painless monocular vision loss and an afferent pupillary defect; clinical findings and funduscopy, rather than initial radiologic imaging, establish the diagnosis. IV fibrinolytic therapy may be given within the designated treatment window. For exudative detachment, imaging may identify an underlying choroidal mass or uveomeningeal syndrome after clinical diagnosis. Acute detachment often needs prompt treatment to prevent permanent vision loss.

Document sections:
  Heading: Natural History Staging of Angle-closure Disease5
  Content: Primary angle closure suspect denotes ITC with normal IOP and no glaucomatous optic neuropathy. In primary angle closure, IOP is elevated without glaucomatous optic neuropathy; lens opacity or retinal vascular pathology may coexist. Acute angle closure (AAC) crisis warrants rapid care distinct from routine management. Its post-crisis physical signs do not invariably determine long-term vision, although often-reversible current impairment may arise from lens opacity or an unresponsive dilated pupil following iris ischemia. Glaucomatous optic neuropathy at an acute presentation probably predates, rather than results from, a pressure elevation lasting hours or days. Primary angle closure glaucoma is the stage with glaucomatous optic neuropathy in an occluded-angle eye, defined by pre-laminar optic nerve head structural changes together with reproducible visual field loss.

Document sections:
  Heading: Clinical Features
  Content: Assessment of suspected disease should establish onset and course, which are usually insidious and gradual, and inquire about trauma, contact lenses, systemic illness, and medication use. Symptoms include blurred vision, irritation, redness, photophobia, tearing, and discharge. Pain is usually less pronounced than in bacterial or Acanthamoeba keratitis and does not track the clinical findings. Findings include circumcorneal ciliary hyperemia, corneal infiltration and edema, diminished corneal luster, and typically feathery ulcer margins. Grey or yellow stromal infiltration commonly extends past the ulcer edge. A grey infiltrative ring can appear as raised, fluffy lesions with dirty yellow or brown pigmentation; dense endothelial-level infiltration may form plaques. Multifocal satellite microabscesses occur in more than 10% of cases, and thick hypopyon occurs in more than half. Appearance varies with the causative species. Serrated or feathery margins, raised borders, satellites, and infiltrate color can assist clinical distinction from bacterial keratitis. Candida and other yeast-associated ulcers may have a collar-button configuration: typically a small ulcer with expanding stromal infiltration. Although they resemble bacterial ulcers, they progress more slowly, have more discrete stromal infiltration, and do not respond to topical antibiotics. The illustrated examples include early and advanced ulcers, satellite lesions, hypopyon, and subsequent corneal opacity and vascularization.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_04
  Name: Diabetic retinopathy
  Description: A diabetes-related eye condition that can be prevented or delayed by controlling hyperglycemia, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. Early disease may be asymptomatic.
  Epidemiology: It is the most common microvascular complication of diabetes and a leading global cause of preventable vision impairment and blindness. If current trends persist, the estimated number of affected people rises 1.2-fold, from 146 million in 2014 to 180.6 million in 2030.
  Clinical presentation: Early stages can have no symptoms; vision-threatening disease can result in vision impairment or blindness.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy
      Distinguishing features: Stages targeted for detection through systematic retinal screening and timely treatment.
    - Name: advanced proliferative diabetic retinopathy
      Distinguishing features: An advanced form listed among the indications for vitreoretinal surgery.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Systematic retinal screening
      Purpose: Detect diabetic retinopathy early, including its vision-threatening stages.
      When indicated: For people with diabetes, annually or biennially depending on the setting.
      Interpretation: Refer for assessment and treatment when indicated.
    - Test: Ophthalmoscopy
      Purpose: Examine the retina during diabetic retinopathy screening.
      When indicated: When screening is carried out by trained eye care personnel.
    - Test: Retinal imaging
      Purpose: Screen for diabetic retinopathy using local interpretation or centralized grading through telemedicine.
      When indicated: For people with diabetes undergoing retinal screening.
    - Test: Slit lamp examination
      Purpose: Assess retinal status when screening images are of poor quality.
      When indicated: For people referred from the English National Screening Programme because their retinal images are of poor quality.
    - Test: Optical coherence tomography (OCT)
      Purpose: Diagnose and monitor treatment for retinal disorders.
      When indicated: Where available; its cost limits availability in many low- and middle-income countries.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Retinal screening is described as annual or biennial, depending on the setting; longer-term care is needed for this chronic eye condition.
    Recommended tests:
      - Retinal examination through ophthalmoscopy or retinal imaging
    Long term effects:
      - Vision impairment or blindness may develop without early detection and timely management.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Mian et al. 2024 Corneal Edema and Opacification Preferred Practice Pattern®__JC__000292
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Mian et al. 2024 Corneal Edema and Opacification Preferred Practice Pattern®
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Management of Band Keratopathy
  Content: Band keratopathy involves hydroxyapatite deposits on the anterior Bowman’s layer and epithelial basement membrane associated with inflammation, local injury, or systemic hypercalcemia. It usually causes no symptoms, so debridement is reserved for glare, impaired vision, or pain caused by epithelial disruption. Deposits may be removed mechanically, chemically, or by combining both approaches: forceps can lift thick plaques, while finer material may require epithelial debridement followed by ethylene-diamine-tetra-acetic acid (EDTA) chelation. Studies support the safety and efficacy of alternative compounded EDTA sources where access is difficult. EDTA concentration and exposure time vary with calcium density and technique. A comparison reported mean healing times of 5–7 days after EDTA chelation versus 2–3 days for a similarly sized abrasion in normal eyes. Limiting EDTA exposure, including at the limbus, might hasten re-epithelialization. Slow healing increases the risk of stromal scarring and infection. When limbal stem cell deficiency, neurotrophic keratopathy, or severe dry eye coexists, amniotic membrane grafting or temporary tarsorrhaphy may support healing. With severe ocular surface disease, keratectomy risks may exceed its benefits. PTK is another option, but calcium ablates faster than adjacent tissue and may leave surface depressions and irregularities.

question: A boy presents with diplopia and restriction of eye movements following blunt trauma to his eye. X-ray reveals blow out fracture of orbit. Which pa of orbit is most likely damaged:

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Vision Loss__JC__000110
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Vision Loss
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 1: Adult. Acute posttraumatic visual defect. Suspect orbital injury. Initial imaging.
  Content: Orbital fractures most often follow assault or a direct blow, motor-vehicle collisions, falls, or sports injuries. They can occur alone or alongside zygomaticomaxillary complex, Le Fort II and III, or nasoethmoidal complex fractures. Diplopia can accompany depressed orbital-floor fractures, especially anterior- or middle-third injuries and small- to medium-sized defects with soft-tissue herniation. Fractures >2 cm are more likely to produce enophthalmos. Blowout injury can involve the lamina papyracea, but extraocular-muscle herniation and serious immediate complications are less common than with orbital-floor blowout fractures. Most orbital fractures can undergo delayed repair after swelling improves; CT can reveal injuries needing more urgent action, including trapdoor fractures and orbital compartment syndrome. Lateral- and superior-wall fractures carry increased traumatic optic neuropathy risk because blunt force can reach the optic canal and shear the nerve. With associated brain injury or obtundation, an afferent pupillary defect may be its sole clinical sign. Urgent diagnosis permits timely intervention when needed. Although optic-canal fractures increase nerve-injury risk, emergency surgery for traumatic optic neuropathy is generally reserved for a bone fragment impinging on the nerve, hematoma in the canal, or enlarging retrobulbar hematoma with proptosis. Severe proptosis with posterior globe tenting requires emergency orbital decompression to preserve vision. An orbital-apex fracture involving the superior orbital fissure can affect multiple traversing cranial nerves. Retrobulbar hematoma, emphysema, or a blow-in fracture can increase orbital mass effect and cause compartment syndrome and vision loss. Imaging evidence of retrobulbar bleeding does not sensitively predict subsequent compartment syndrome: diagnose it from clinical evidence of optic nerve compression. Extraocular-muscle entrapment after an orbital-floor fracture is likewise a clinical diagnosis; muscle herniation and altered contour have low positive predictive values for entrapment. Imaging aims to identify orbital injuries and complications early enough to guide timely care and prevent permanent visual loss.

  Heading: 1.1 Background
  Content: Glaucoma affects an estimated 80 million people worldwide and is a major cause of blindness. It is an intermittently progressive optic neuropathy that produces visual field defects attributable to injury at the pre-laminar optic nerve head. Lowering intraocular pressure slows or stops progression in the vast majority of cases. Secondary glaucoma arises from another ocular or systemic disorder, commonly neovascularization, uveitis or ocular trauma, and typically causes a marked pressure rise. Primary glaucoma has no such precipitating disease. Primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG) and primary open angle glaucoma (POAG) are distinguished by whether the iris obstructs the iridocorneal drainage angle. They differ in presentation and treatment; PACG depends more strongly on pressure, and its treatment aims to remove barriers to aqueous circulation. In primary angle-closure suspects (PACS), the iris contacts the trabecular meshwork, but intraocular pressure (IOP), optic nerve structure and visual function remain normal, without peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS). Primary angle-closure (PAC) involves current or previous IOP elevation and/or PAS, without glaucomatous optic nerve injury or visual field abnormality. PACG can arise without previously detected high IOP or PAS. Acute angle-closure (AAC) occurs when sudden complete trabecular obstruction produces extreme ocular hypertension; pain, abrupt visual reduction or loss, nausea and/or vomiting may be severe. Prompt presentation and suitable treatment have improved its outlook. PACG causes severe visual loss more often than POAG: approximately 60 million people worldwide have POAG versus 20 million with PACG, yet the numbers blinded by the two conditions are roughly equal. This greater threat has encouraged consideration of prevention.

Document sections:
  Heading: A B S T R A C T
  Content: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) is a persistent, progressive ocular inflammatory disease that can threaten vision and mainly affects children and young adults. Its prevalence ranges from <2 per 10,000 in the United States to as high as 1,100 per 10,000 in parts of Africa. Where VKC is uncommon, distinguishing it from other conditions can be difficult; treatment may begin only after disease progression and substantial impairment of quality of life. Although VKC was formerly regarded chiefly as an immunoglobulin E-mediated disorder, approximately 50% of affected patients lack allergic sensitization. Multiple inflammatory pathways contribute to its manifestations and characteristic conjunctival eosinophilic and fibroproliferative lesions. This review examines changes in understanding of VKC immunopathology, available and emerging treatments, their clinical implications, and priorities for research and practice.

  Content: Every patient should receive comprehensive medical eye assessment and follow-up at recommended intervals, including tear-film and ocular-surface evaluation, particularly before cataract or refractive surgery. Document sections:
  Heading: Presenting symptoms
  Content: Most cases are detected because parents or a paediatrician notice an abnormal-looking eye, such as a visibly small globe, marked nystagmus, strabismus, or an evident iris defect. Persistent poor vision can arise without RD through uncorrected refractive error, amblyopia, or foveal involvement and may become apparent when schooling begins. Acute visual deterioration, with or without pre-existing impairment, is most commonly due to newly occurring RD; sub foveal choroidal neovascular membrane is another possible cause. In children, visual disability may first be recognized when both eyes are affected, with an established RD in one and a more recent RD in the other; deterioration superimposed on poor baseline vision can be difficult for parents to detect. Small lesions sparing the disc and fovea may cause no symptoms unless RD develops. A large lesion can produce a yellow or white pupillary reflex, while a complicated cataract may also prompt recognition of an ocular problem.

Conditions:

  Name: Diabetic retinopathy
  Description: A diabetes-related eye condition that can be prevented or delayed by controlling hyperglycemia, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. Early disease may be asymptomatic.
  Epidemiology: It is the most common microvascular complication of diabetes and a leading global cause of preventable vision impairment and blindness. If current trends persist, the estimated number of affected people rises 1.2-fold, from 146 million in 2014 to 180.6 million in 2030.
  Clinical presentation: Early stages can have no symptoms; vision-threatening disease can result in vision impairment or blindness.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy
      Distinguishing features: Stages targeted for detection through systematic retinal screening and timely treatment.
    - Name: advanced proliferative diabetic retinopathy
      Distinguishing features: An advanced form listed among the indications for vitreoretinal surgery.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Systematic retinal screening
      Purpose: Detect diabetic retinopathy early, including its vision-threatening stages.
      When indicated: For people with diabetes, annually or biennially depending on the setting.
      Interpretation: Refer for assessment and treatment when indicated.
    - Test: Ophthalmoscopy
      Purpose: Examine the retina during diabetic retinopathy screening.
      When indicated: When screening is carried out by trained eye care personnel.
    - Test: Retinal imaging
      Purpose: Screen for diabetic retinopathy using local interpretation or centralized grading through telemedicine.
      When indicated: For people with diabetes undergoing retinal screening.
    - Test: Slit lamp examination
      Purpose: Assess retinal status when screening images are of poor quality.
      When indicated: For people referred from the English National Screening Programme because their retinal images are of poor quality.
    - Test: Optical coherence tomography (OCT)
      Purpose: Diagnose and monitor treatment for retinal disorders.
      When indicated: Where available; its cost limits availability in many low- and middle-income countries.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Retinal screening is described as annual or biennial, depending on the setting; longer-term care is needed for this chronic eye condition.
    Recommended tests:

question: Fluorescein stain is used in the eye to stain

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Amescua et al. 2024 Dry Eye Syndrome Preferred Practice Pattern®__JC__000206
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Amescua et al. 2024 Dry Eye Syndrome Preferred Practice Pattern®
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: OCULAR SURFACE DYE STAINING
  Content: Fluorescein, rose bengal, and lissamine green help assess ocular-surface abnormalities. Fluorescein penetrates epithelium where intercellular junctions are sufficiently disrupted; use a saline-moistened strip or 1% to 2% sodium fluorescein and examine with slit lamp and cobalt blue illumination. Staining may become clearer after about 2 minutes and with a yellow filter. Mild staining can occur in normal eyes, particularly in the morning; dry eye often produces exposure-zone punctate or blotchy staining, more readily seen on cornea than conjunctiva. Rose bengal may be applied with a moistened strip or 1% solution; advise patients that it can irritate, so topical anesthetic is typically used first. Leave saline against the strip for at least a minute before application. Rose bengal stains conjunctiva more intensely than cornea, highlighting cells lacking mucus coating and tear debris; a red-free filter can aid viewing. Lissamine green has a staining pattern resembling rose bengal with less irritation, but waiting 1 to 2 minutes reduces visibility; unlike fluorescein, it is not recommended to assess corneal epithelial disease. Diffuse corneal and conjunctival staining commonly accompanies viral keratoconjunctivitis or medicamentosa. Inferior corneal and bulbar conjunctival staining is typical of staphylococcal blepharitis, meibomian gland disease, lagophthalmos, or exposure; superior bulbar conjunctival staining is typical of superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis. Interpalpebral corneal and bulbar conjunctival staining commonly accompanies aqueous deficiency.

question: Wavelength of Femtosecond laser is

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Salgado et al. 2024 Update on Femtosecond Laser Assisted Cataract Surgery A Review__JC__000114
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Salgado et al. 2024 Update on Femtosecond Laser Assisted Cataract Surgery A Review
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Technology Femtosecond Lasers
  Content: Femtosecond lasers produce pulses lasting on the order of 10−15 s. Their near-infrared output at 1053 nm creates tissue photodisruption while avoiding effects such as the thermal injury associated with earlier lasers. Power, repetition rate, and spot size permit further adjustment of the laser–tissue interaction. Photodisruption proceeds through plasma formation, shock-wave generation, and cavitation. Tissue separation occurs through ablation and cleaving, with pulse energy chiefly determining their relative contributions. The threshold for photodisruption varies with tissue characteristics, numerical aperture (NA), and wavelength. Higher-energy pulses produce more tissue ablation through expanding gas bubbles; lower-energy pulses ablate less tissue and rely more on cleaving, requiring higher frequencies and closer spot spacing.

  Heading: People with diabetes
  Content: The number of people with diabetes has increased across countries during the past 30 years alongside lifestyle changes. Diabetic retinopathy is the most common diabetic microvascular complication and a leading preventable cause of vision impairment and blindness. If existing trends persist, a cited estimate projects a 1.2-fold rise in affected people, from 146 million in 2014 to 180.6 million in 2030. Most associated vision impairment can be avoided through risk-factor control, early identification and timely treatment. Many national and international professional societies have long endorsed systematic retinal screening of people with diabetes to detect vision-threatening disease, annually or biennially according to setting, followed by treatment when needed. Lower-cost retinal cameras and artificial-intelligence approaches may improve access and quality closer to home.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Visual Acuity (VA)
  Content: VA measures visual resolution and remains the most important visual measure for children with CNS tumours. Assess best-corrected VA (BCVA) in each eye, at far and near distances if possible, and report the threshold optotype detail in logMAR, from 0.0 for normal vision to 2.0. A change of 0.2 LogMAR VA or more is clinically relevant. If quantitative measurement is infeasible, fixation observations can help establish whether vision is present; document Hand Motion (HM), counting fingers (CF), Light Perception (LP) or No Light Perception (NLP), as appropriate. Testing depends on age and cooperation: Teller Acuity preferential looking Cards (TAC) are commonly used for infants and preverbal children, whereas Lea symbols, Cardiff Acuity Test, Kays Picture Chart and later HOTV or Snellen charts suit older children.

Changing VA test methods can slightly overestimate or underestimate longitudinal results. Because vision develops rapidly over the first 2-3 years and reaches full potential only after 5 years of age, age-specific normal ranges should be used in young children.

Document sections:
  Heading: Management of Band Keratopathy
  Content: Band keratopathy involves hydroxyapatite deposits on the anterior Bowman’s layer and epithelial basement membrane associated with inflammation, local injury, or systemic hypercalcemia. It usually causes no symptoms, so debridement is reserved for glare, impaired vision, or pain caused by epithelial disruption. Deposits may be removed mechanically, chemically, or by combining both approaches: forceps can lift thick plaques, while finer material may require epithelial debridement followed by ethylene-diamine-tetra-acetic acid (EDTA) chelation. Studies support the safety and efficacy of alternative compounded EDTA sources where access is difficult. EDTA concentration and exposure time vary with calcium density and technique. A comparison reported mean healing times of 5–7 days after EDTA chelation versus 2–3 days for a similarly sized abrasion in normal eyes. Limiting EDTA exposure, including at the limbus, might hasten re-epithelialization. Slow healing increases the risk of stromal scarring and infection. When limbal stem cell deficiency, neurotrophic keratopathy, or severe dry eye coexists, amniotic membrane grafting or temporary tarsorrhaphy may support healing. With severe ocular surface disease, keratectomy risks may exceed its benefits. PTK is another option, but calcium ablates faster than adjacent tissue and may leave surface depressions and irregularities.

gold_answer: Duration of type II diabetes mellitus

retrieved_chunks.document_id: Lim et al. 2025 Diabetic Retinopathy Preferred Practice Pattern®
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: RISK FACTORS
  Content: Diabetes duration is a major DR risk factor. In type 1 diabetes, retinopathy affects approximately 25% after 5 years, almost 60% after 10 years, and 80% after 15 years. WESDR found PDR in approximately 50% of people aged 30 and younger after 20 years of type 1 diabetes. LALES and Proyecto VER found PDR in 18% of participants with diabetes for more than 15 years, without a difference between diabetes types. The Singapore Eye Disease Study identified Indian ethnicity, diabetes duration, HbA1c, serum glucose, and systolic blood pressure as independent predictors of any DR; lower diastolic pressure, total cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol were associated with lower odds. In a Canadian First Nations study, elevated HbA1c predicted two-step DR progression (HR =1.42; P < 0.0001), as did systolic blood pressure (HR = 1.24 per 10 mmHg; P = 0.009). Among people older than 30 with type 2 diabetes of known duration less than 5 years, DR occurred in 40% using insulin and 24% not using it; with documented duration up to 19 years, corresponding rates were 84% and 53%. PDR developed in 2% with type 2 diabetes for less than 5 years and 25% with duration of 25 years or more. Differences between historical cohorts may reflect changing glucose and hypertension care. Glycemia and blood pressure are principal modifiable risks; once DR exists, glycemic control appears more predictive of progression than duration. An HbA1c target of 7% or lower is recommended for most patients, with possible benefit from 6.5% in selected patients. Higher HbA1c corresponds to greater DME risk. The VISS Study associated long-term weighted HbA1c from type 1 diagnosis to 30+ years with PDR and nephropathy and proposed HbA1c 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) or lower, as near normal as possible, to avoid PDR and macroalbuminuria. In a prospective cohort of 3322 people with type 2 diabetes followed for 10 to 25 years, diagnosis at ages 15 up to age 40 carried adjusted OR 2.8 for DR versus diagnosis at ages 60 to under 70. Hypertension treatment remains important. A meta-analysis found modest DR-prevention benefit from lowering blood pressure for up to 5 years, especially with hypertension and type 2 diabetes, but little evidence that lowering it slows DR progression without hypertension. Large studies suggest lipid management may reduce progression and treatment need; findings about age, diabetes type, clotting, renal disease, inactivity, inflammatory markers, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are less consistent. Ophthalmologists should encourage adherence to care for all medical aspects of diabetes. DR is more prevalent among patients receiving dialysis; an association was reported with systolic, but not diastolic, pressure, fasting glucose, HbA1c, and high HDL cholesterol. A 2018 meta-analysis found lipid-lowering agents protective against DR progression and possibly DME onset, without an effect on acuity or hard exudates. A 2023 Cochrane review found that fenofibrate probably did not change DR progression across type 2 diabetes patients with and without existing DR but probably reduced progression in those with DR (I+, Moderate Quality). A later trial associated fenofibrate with a 27% reduction in progression or treatment among patients with early DR, with equivalent effects by diabetes type. A study suggested omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, docosahexaenoic acid, and eicosapentaenoic acid might relate to less severe DR; a systematic review found that nutraceutical evidence needs further research (III, Insufficient quality). Evidence on genetic and epigenetic explanations of differing progression is conflicting: one study found associations of longer duration and higher HbA1c with PDR in haplogroup H (P = 0.0001 and P = 0.011, respectively), but not haplogroup UK; a larger study did not reproduce that association. One study associated HMGA1 rs139876191 carriage with significantly lower PDR risk and proposed reduced VEGF A expression as an explanation. A meta-analysis of 13 studies associated VEGF variants rs2010963, rs833061, and rs699947 with NPDR or PDR. In a type 2 diabetes study, patients with metabolic syndrome versus those without it had more albuminuria (40.8% vs. 21.8%; P < 0.001), retinopathy (37.9% vs. 28.6%; P < 0.001), coronary disease (19.4% vs. 11.6%; P < 0.001), cerebrovascular disease (5.8% vs. 3.2%; P = 0.014), and ankle-brachial index less than 0.9 or 1.3 or higher (6.1% vs. 3.0%; P = 0.015). These outcomes tended to rise with the number of syndrome components (all P for trend < 0.05); screening may help identify higher-risk patients. In 50,254 eyes, baseline NPDR features predicted 5-year PDR progression: IRMA versus venous beading carried HR = 1.77; P = 0.0013 for PDR, and dot-blot hemorrhages in 4-quadrants carried HR = 3.84; P = 0.0095 for vitreous hemorrhage. Protocol S associated worse baseline PDR with worsening despite anti-VEGF or PRP (64% [high-risk PDR or worse] vs. 23% [moderate PDR or better]; HR = 3.97; P < 0.001). Within its PRP group, worsening was more frequent after pattern scan than conventional single-spot PRP (60% vs. 39%; HR = 2.04; P = 0.008), regardless of spot count. OCT and OCTA have identified additional progression biomarkers.

Document sections:
  Heading: 1. Introduction
  Content: Retinoblastoma is the most frequent childhood ocular malignancy and affects approximately 1 in 15,000–20,000 live births. Without timely treatment, it can be fatal. In high-income countries, diagnosis generally precedes invasion of the optic nerve, choroid, sclera, or orbit, and disease-free survival approaches 100%. In low-and-middle-income countries, particularly in Africa, invasive presentation is more common, increasing local and distant metastatic risk and substantially lowering survival. Treatment aims to preserve life, prevent metastasis, retain the eye, and maximize vision, although protocols differ between centers. Before the 1990 s, enucleation and external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) predominated but could cause vision loss and serious adverse effects. Subsequent approaches improved disease-free survival, globe salvage, and, in selected cases, vision preservation. Plaque radiotherapy, cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, and transpupillary thermotherapy contributed to this change, while chemotherapy delivered by different routes had a particularly important role. The authors searched PubMed for English-language articles dating back to January 1, 1960, targeting publications from January 1, 1990, to January 31, 2024. Search terms covered retinoblastoma, chemotherapy, intravenous chemotherapy, chemoreduction, intra-arterial chemotherapy, ophthalmic artery chemosurgery, intravitreal chemotherapy, intracameral chemotherapy, and periocular chemotherapy. Their aim was to summarize current knowledge and emerging chemotherapy trends in retinoblastoma.

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Galor et al. 2023 TFOS Lifestyle Impact of lifestyle challenges on the ocular surface__JC__000420
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Galor et al. 2023 TFOS Lifestyle Impact of lifestyle challenges on the ocular surface
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 4.3.2. Eye rubbing, DED, and keratoconus
  Content: Prolonged or vigorous rubbing may alter ocular tissues and contribute to DED or keratoconus [195]. Reported associations also include corneal ectasia, conjunctivitis, glaucoma, iris and posterior-capsule complications, intraocular-lens dislocation, retinal detachment, and extrusion of implanted silicone oil [197]. Ocular allergy may be connected through rubbing or keratoconus, but evidence conflicts; one systematic review and meta-analysis of keratoconus and allergic eye disease was retracted in 2022 [204]. Among 61 patients with vernal keratoconjunctivitis and corneal ectasia, n = 53 had keratoconus and pathological rubbing was frequent [205]. DED with allergic conjunctivitis and asthma in children have also been linked to ocular allergy [206,207]. Contact lenses and chemical irritants can provoke rubbing by stimulating ocular-surface nociceptors; removal-relief rubbing associated with contact lenses may partly contribute to DED among long-term wearers [208,209,210,211,285]. Psychiatric conditions accompanied by chronic fatigue or stress have also been linked to rubbing [209]. Among 212 institutionalized patients, including Trisomy 21 (n = 30), neonatal asphyxia (n = 15), and pregnancy-related infection (n = 9), 7.5% (n = 16) had keratoconus and were more likely to rub their eyes than those without keratoconus (p = 0.008) [212]. A 2021 systematic review pooling six case-control studies associated rubbing with keratoconus (OR 6.46, 95% CI 4.12–10.1), but found heterogeneous studies with limited methodological quality and called for standardized measurement of rubbing frequency, force, and technique [213].

Document sections:
  Heading: Examination
  Content: Every patient should receive comprehensive medical eye assessment and follow-up at recommended intervals, including tear-film and ocular-surface evaluation, particularly before cataract or refractive surgery. Symptoms suggestive of dry eye warrant additional relevant tests. External and slit-lamp examinations document signs, tear quality, quantity, and stability, and alternative causes. External assessment may inspect skin for scleroderma, rosacea, or seborrhea; lids for closure, position, blinking, inflammation, secretions, or spasm; everted lids for tarsal conjunctival inflammation, allergy, or fibrosis; lacrimal-gland enlargement, proptosis, cranial nerves, and hand findings associated with systemic disease. Slit-lamp assessment addresses tear-meniscus height, debris, viscosity, mucus, foaming, and tear breakup; eyelash disorders; meibomian-gland openings, expressibility, atrophy, secretion, and lid-margin changes; punctal position, patency, or plugs; tarsal and bulbar conjunctival inflammation, scarring, staining, or other abnormalities; and corneal drying, dye staining, epithelial defects, filaments, thinning, infiltrates, ulcers, scarring, neovascularization, or prior surgery. Conjunctival lissamine green staining may assist early recognition of Sjögren’s syndrome.

question: Most common cause of orbital cellulitis is?

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Vision Loss__JC__000126
retrieved_chunks.document_id: Vision Loss
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 2: Adult. Acute vision loss. Infection or inflammatory disorder suspected. Initial imaging.
  Content: Orbital infection can cause cellulitis, subperiosteal abscess, or orbital abscess and is an ophthalmologic emergency because of potential visual loss and intracranial complications, including meningitis, cerebritis, intracranial abscess, and cavernous sinus thrombosis. Pain and swelling near the orbit, reduced acuity, and ophthalmoplegia may occur. Infection most commonly spreads from adjacent structures, often from bacterial paranasal sinus disease. Clinical and imaging differentiation of periorbital from postseptal disease helps determine whether inpatient IV antibiotics are needed. Subperiosteal abscess usually needs surgical drainage. Acute invasive fungal sinusitis can also cause orbital complications; it is aggressive, associated with high mortality, and typically affects immunocompromised patients. Orbital inflammation can be idiopathic or secondary to granulomatous, inflammatory, or autoimmune disease, including sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease, or Graves’ disease. Its manifestations and risk of visual loss depend on the cause and affected orbital structures. Cellulitis, orbital inflammatory syndrome, and lymphoproliferative lesions may overlap clinically and radiologically. Imaging seeks to define disease extent and complications, particularly abscess, to guide intervention and avert lasting vision loss, intracranial extension, or cavernous sinus thrombosis.

Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 3: Adult. Chronic or progressive unilateral vision loss. Intraorbital mass-like lesion suspected or vascular lesion suspected. Initial imaging.
  Content: Many tumors, tumor-like conditions, systemic diseases, metastases, and high- or low-flow vascular malformations can involve the orbit. Distinguishing vascular from other lesions guides subsequent workup and care. Because the orbital space is restricted, either a soft-tissue or vascular mass may cause proptosis. Orbital-apex masses or inflammation characteristically produce vision loss with ophthalmoplegia. Orbital masses can be classified by location in the globe, optic nerve sheath complex, intraconal or extraconal space, bone, or multiple compartments. Benign lesions predominate, but malignant orbital tumors become more prevalent in adults older than 60 years of age. Among cysts, dermoid cysts are most common; excluding cysts, cavernous venous malformation is the commonest benign adult orbital mass, while non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the commonest malignant one. Imaging seeks to detect and characterize the causative orbital mass or vascular lesion, direct care, and sometimes establish a specific diagnosis.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_04
  Name: Diabetic retinopathy
  Description: A diabetes-related eye condition that can be prevented or delayed by controlling hyperglycemia, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. Early disease may be asymptomatic.
  Epidemiology: It is the most common microvascular complication of diabetes and a leading global cause of preventable vision impairment and blindness. If current trends persist, the estimated number of affected people rises 1.2-fold, from 146 million in 2014 to 180.6 million in 2030.
  Clinical presentation: Early stages can have no symptoms; vision-threatening disease can result in vision impairment or blindness.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy
      Distinguishing features: Stages targeted for detection through systematic retinal screening and timely treatment.
    - Name: advanced proliferative diabetic retinopathy
      Distinguishing features: An advanced form listed among the indications for vitreoretinal surgery.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Systematic retinal screening
      Purpose: Detect diabetic retinopathy early, including its vision-threatening stages.
      When indicated: For people with diabetes, annually or biennially depending on the setting.
      Interpretation: Refer for assessment and treatment when indicated.
    - Test: Ophthalmoscopy
      Purpose: Examine the retina during diabetic retinopathy screening.
      When indicated: When screening is carried out by trained eye care personnel.
    - Test: Retinal imaging
      Purpose: Screen for diabetic retinopathy using local interpretation or centralized grading through telemedicine.
      When indicated: For people with diabetes undergoing retinal screening.
    - Test: Slit lamp examination
      Purpose: Assess retinal status when screening images are of poor quality.
      When indicated: For people referred from the English National Screening Programme because their retinal images are of poor quality.
    - Test: Optical coherence tomography (OCT)
      Purpose: Diagnose and monitor treatment for retinal disorders.
      When indicated: Where available; its cost limits availability in many low- and middle-income countries.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Retinal screening is described as annual or biennial, depending on the setting; longer-term care is needed for this chronic eye condition.
    Recommended tests:
      - Retinal examination through ophthalmoscopy or retinal imaging
    Long term effects:
      - Vision impairment or blindness may develop without early detection and timely management.

Condition or topic: Fungal keratitis

Clinical background: Fungal keratitis is a major cause of microbial corneal infection that can lead to blindness, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions. Fungi rarely invade an intact cornea, but trauma, especially involving vegetable matter, immunosuppression, topical steroid use, and ocular surface disease can increase susceptibility. More than a million cases are estimated to occur each year; the risk of perforation is about 10%, and more than half of affected patients lose vision and live with monocular blindness. Diagnosis can be difficult to confirm in the laboratory, while the availability and effectiveness of antifungal treatments pose additional challenges. Prolonged, intensive topical treatment may be insufficient.

Document sections:
  Heading: Variant 1: Adult. Acute posttraumatic visual defect. Suspect orbital injury. Initial imaging.
  Content: Orbital fractures most often follow assault or a direct blow, motor-vehicle collisions, falls, or sports injuries. They can occur alone or alongside zygomaticomaxillary complex, Le Fort II and III, or nasoethmoidal complex fractures. Diplopia can accompany depressed orbital-floor fractures, especially anterior- or middle-third injuries and small- to medium-sized defects with soft-tissue herniation. Fractures >2 cm are more likely to produce enophthalmos. Blowout injury can involve the lamina papyracea, but extraocular-muscle herniation and serious immediate complications are less common than with orbital-floor blowout fractures. Most orbital fractures can undergo delayed repair after swelling improves; CT can reveal injuries needing more urgent action, including trapdoor fractures and orbital compartment syndrome. Lateral- and superior-wall fractures carry increased traumatic optic neuropathy risk because blunt force can reach the optic canal and shear the nerve. With associated brain injury or obtundation, an afferent pupillary defect may be its sole clinical sign. Urgent diagnosis permits timely intervention when needed. Although optic-canal fractures increase nerve-injury risk, emergency surgery for traumatic optic neuropathy is generally reserved for a bone fragment impinging on the nerve, hematoma in the canal, or enlarging retrobulbar hematoma with proptosis. Severe proptosis with posterior globe tenting requires emergency orbital decompression to preserve vision. An orbital-apex fracture involving the superior orbital fissure can affect multiple traversing cranial nerves. Retrobulbar hematoma, emphysema, or a blow-in fracture can increase orbital mass effect and cause compartment syndrome and vision loss. Imaging evidence of retrobulbar bleeding does not sensitively predict subsequent compartment syndrome: diagnose it from clinical evidence of optic nerve compression. Extraocular-muscle entrapment after an orbital-floor fracture is likewise a clinical diagnosis; muscle herniation and altered contour have low positive predictive values for entrapment. Imaging aims to identify orbital injuries and complications early enough to guide timely care and prevent permanent visual loss.

Document sections:
  Heading: 1. Introduction
  Content: Retinoblastoma is the most frequent childhood ocular malignancy and affects approximately 1 in 15,000–20,000 live births. Without timely treatment, it can be fatal. In high-income countries, diagnosis generally precedes invasion of the optic nerve, choroid, sclera, or orbit, and disease-free survival approaches 100%. In low-and-middle-income countries, particularly in Africa, invasive presentation is more common, increasing local and distant metastatic risk and substantially lowering survival. Treatment aims to preserve life, prevent metastasis, retain the eye, and maximize vision, although protocols differ between centers. Before the 1990 s, enucleation and external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) predominated but could cause vision loss and serious adverse effects. Subsequent approaches improved disease-free survival, globe salvage, and, in selected cases, vision preservation. Plaque radiotherapy, cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, and transpupillary thermotherapy contributed to this change, while chemotherapy delivered by different routes had a particularly important role. The authors searched PubMed for English-language articles dating back to January 1, 1960, targeting publications from January 1, 1990, to January 31, 2024. Search terms covered retinoblastoma, chemotherapy, intravenous chemotherapy, chemoreduction, intra-arterial chemotherapy, ophthalmic artery chemosurgery, intravitreal chemotherapy, intracameral chemotherapy, and periocular chemotherapy. Their aim was to summarize current knowledge and emerging chemotherapy trends in retinoblastoma.

Document sections:
  Heading: OCULAR SURFACE DYE STAINING
  Content: Fluorescein, rose bengal, and lissamine green help assess ocular-surface abnormalities. Fluorescein penetrates epithelium where intercellular junctions are sufficiently disrupted; use a saline-moistened strip or 1% to 2% sodium fluorescein and examine with slit lamp and cobalt blue illumination. Staining may become clearer after about 2 minutes and with a yellow filter. Mild staining can occur in normal eyes, particularly in the morning; dry eye often produces exposure-zone punctate or blotchy staining, more readily seen on cornea than conjunctiva. Rose bengal may be applied with a moistened strip or 1% solution; advise patients that it can irritate, so topical anesthetic is typically used first. Leave saline against the strip for at least a minute before application. Rose bengal stains conjunctiva more intensely than cornea, highlighting cells lacking mucus coating and tear debris; a red-free filter can aid viewing. Lissamine green has a staining pattern resembling rose bengal with less irritation, but waiting 1 to 2 minutes reduces visibility; unlike fluorescein, it is not recommended to assess corneal epithelial disease. Diffuse corneal and conjunctival staining commonly accompanies viral keratoconjunctivitis or medicamentosa. Inferior corneal and bulbar conjunctival staining is typical of staphylococcal blepharitis, meibomian gland disease, lagophthalmos, or exposure; superior bulbar conjunctival staining is typical of superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis. Interpalpebral corneal and bulbar conjunctival staining commonly accompanies aqueous deficiency.

  Content: Selected men may be offered sphincterotomy for emptying, with mandatory counseling about its high failure risk and possible further intervention. Urethral bulking agents may be offered for stress incontinence, with counseling that benefit is modest and cure uncommon (both Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C).       Purpose: Assess the urinary tract after a first infection when indicated.

Document sections:
  Heading: b.- Embolización de las arterias uterinas
  Content: La embolización de las arterias uterinas (EAU) es mínimamente invasiva y se plantea como alternativa a operaciones más invasivas. Se ha comunicado eficacia y alta satisfacción en mujeres con leiomiomas. Frente a las técnicas quirúrgicas citadas, se describe como menos costosa y asociada a recuperación más breve y menos dolor. Sus efectos secundarios habituales son dolor pélvico, náuseas y fiebre por necrosis isquémica; aproximadamente el 5 % presenta complicaciones importantes, entre ellas hemorragia, reintervención e infección. También se ha comunicado deterioro de función ovárica después de EAU. En adenomiosis sintomática, varios estudios observaron mejoría clínica sostenida. Entre sus limitaciones figuran posible recrecimiento temprano de la adenomiosis y disponibilidad restringida. El dolor puede prolongarse un máximo de 1 a 2 meses, similar al posterior a la escisión laparoscópica. La intervención requiere radiólogos calificados.

question: Which of the following is/are a complication of urethral stricture?

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__EAUN Guideline Urethral intermittent catheterisation in adults 2024__JC__000354
retrieved_chunks.document_id: EAUN Guideline Urethral intermittent catheterisation in adults 2024
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 15.2 Contraindications
  Content: Suspected or confirmed urethral rupture, UTI or false passage are listed contraindications. Injury to urethral epithelium can heal with scarring and stricture formation. Male strictures commonly cause obstructive voiding symptoms and may follow IC, infection, trauma, lichen sclerosus, prostate-cancer treatment such as radiotherapy, or an unidentified cause. UK Hospital Episode Statistics and similar US data suggest male incidence rises from about 10 in every 100,000 up to 25 years to 40 in every 100,000 by the age of 65 years and > 100 in every 100,000 over 65 years. Female urethral strictures affect 0.1–1% of women with voiding complaints and can cause irritative as well as obstructive symptoms. In a review by Chakraborty et al., 53.48% of surgically treated female strictures were presumed idiopathic and 91.29% had a prior intervention. Smith et al. attributed 8% of female strictures to inflammation and infection and 6.6% to trauma. Male strictures may occur anywhere, particularly in the bulbar urethra (50 %) and at the meatus. In selected patients, intermittent dilatation is established as palliative management of refractory strictures and can reduce recurrence up to 68%. Diversion, such as a continent stoma or ileal conduit, is required if reconstruction is impossible or repair attempts fail. A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to determine which of dilatation, endoscopic urethrotomy or urethroplasty best balances effectiveness, adverse effects and costs. A small RCT (n=49) comparing CISC with repeated sounds dilatation reported a statistically significant improvement in flow rate and QoL among patients performing CISC.

  Content: Urinary leakage is the characteristic finding; it is generally painless and constant, although position-dependent leakage can be intermittent. Intraoperative recognition of genitourinary or gastrointestinal injury occurs in only about half of cases. VVF assessment generally combines history and direct-visualisation examination with selected imaging or laboratory investigations. Late-excretory-phase contrast CT can identify fistulae, ureteric integrity and possible urinoma; MRI, particularly T2-weighted imaging, can also provide diagnostic detail. retrieved_chunks.document_id: EAU Guidelines on Urethral Strictures 2023
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 6.3.5.1.4 Extirpative surgery and urinary diversion for non-traumatic posterior urethral stenosis
  Content: In complex or recurrent disease, severe necrosis, calcification or morbidity—particularly severe pain—may make LUT reconstruction inappropriate or impossible. Intractable haematuria and fistulation are other reasons to abandon the urethral outlet. Such patients commonly have previous pelvic irradiation or high-energy prostate cancer treatment and multiple prior treatment attempts. Preserving the bladder requires adequate capacity, compliance and function, as well as healthy distal ureters. The last-resort option is continent or incontinent urinary diversion, with or without cystectomy; selection depends largely on bladder capacity, local symptoms, performance status and patient expectations. Cystectomy at diversion can relieve otherwise unmanageable bladder pain, spasms and haematuria, especially after pelvic radiotherapy. In Sack et al.’s study of fifteen patients, satisfaction was 100%, and the overwhelming majority would have undergone surgery an average of thirteen months earlier. Faris et al. reported that 27% also needed bowel diversion because of intractable gastrointestinal morbidity. Improved QoL and high satisfaction after diversion, and palliation of pain, spasms and haematuria by cystectomy, each have LE 3. Perform diversion for recurrent or complex disease with reduced bladder capacity and/or incapacitating local symptoms (Weak); perform cystectomy during diversion for intractable bladder pain, spasms and/or haematuria (Weak).

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: Clinical Practice
  Content: Offer surgery as one option for endometriosis-associated pain. Before surgery, discuss the procedure, expected effect on symptoms, risks, benefits and possible need for another operation. Use laparoscopy rather than laparotomy unless contraindicated, and consider excision instead of ablation for pain. For endometrioma, consider ovarian cystectomy or CO2 laser vaporisation rather than drainage with coagulation to reduce recurrence and pain. Minimise ovarian injury, particularly with recurrent endometrioma or concern about ovarian reserve.

For women who no longer intend to conceive and have not benefited from conservative treatment, hysterectomy with or without ovarian removal may be considered. If hysterectomy is chosen, the guideline favours total over sub-total hysterectomy because endometriosis may persist in or near a retained cervix. All visible lesions should be excised during hysterectomy. Women should understand that hysterectomy does not necessarily eliminate symptoms. If a woman with previous endometriosis needs menopausal hormone therapy (MHT), a continuous oestrogen-progestogen regimen is advised.

question: Hematuria with dysmorphic RBC are seen in

retrieved_chunks.chunk_id: json__Lee et al. 2025 Comparison of Urinary Red Blood Cell Distribution ( URDspan__JC__000113

retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 1 | Introduction
  Content: Hematuria means RBCs are present in urine and may be visible or detectable only microscopically. It is a fundamental manifestation of glomerulonephritis (GN); microscopic assessment of urinary sediment is presented as its most effective detection method. Birch et al. proposed in 1979 that urinary RBC morphology could distinguish glomerular from non-glomerular origins. Passage through glomeruli can damage RBC membranes and produce dysmorphic RBCs (dRBCs). Shichiri et al. reported in 1988 that erythrocytes were smaller in glomerular than in non-glomerular disease, and Hyodo et al. later proposed an RBC size range of 4–6 μm for discriminating the origins. Compared with blood, urine has much less albumin and more urea; this environment increases membrane vulnerability and changes RBC shape. High urea concentrations particularly favor burr-cell formation. Passage across the glomerular basement membrane may produce acanthocytes through membrane injury. RBCs in renal disease are also more susceptible to factors including iron deficiency, osmotic lysis, shape distortion, and vesicle formation. Reliable recognition of urinary dRBCs requires an experienced observer, and observer-dependent interpretation may explain differences between laboratories. The authors consider continuing education in RBC morphology essential and mention deep learning for microscopy as another possible approach. Instrument-measured small-RBC fractions are easier to obtain and less dependent on interpretation, making them potentially more objective and standardized. The fully automated UF-5000 uses fluorescence flow cytometry to classify urine particles and reports morphological RBC information, including non-lysed RBCs, lysed RBCs, large RBCs, small RBCs, and RBC-Info. Its classification uses forward scatter light (FSC), side scatter light (SSC), side fluorescence light (SFL), and depolarized side scattered light (DSS). A small RBC has FSC intensity < 70; a non-lysed RBC has a strong FSC signal and morphological stability indicated by SSC. URD is the small-RBC count divided by the non-lysed-RBC count. Earlier studies investigated possible clinical uses, but most were single-center studies. Reported cutoffs for distinguishing glomerular from non-glomerular hematuria varied from 30.1% to 40.5% for small RBCs and from 0% to 30.0% for dRBCs. The authors therefore considered a multicenter assessment using the same equipment necessary for clinical application. Across four hospitals, they collected urine microscopy findings, urine measures, serum markers, and kidney-function information to compare institutional dRBC and URD measurements and cutoffs and assess their clinical significance.

Document sections:
  Heading: PSA Testing
  Content: PSA is secreted by prostate epithelial cells; its protease activity liquefies coagulated ejaculate and promotes sperm motility. How it enters the circulation is unknown. Commercial serum assays perform similarly when appropriately used apart from small calibration differences, but results from differently calibrated assays cannot be directly exchanged. Repeat an unusually high result, especially near an evaluation threshold; in one study, approximately 25% initially measuring 4 to 10 ng/mL had a normal repeat result. PSA is not specific to cancer: most people with elevated values do not have prostate cancer, and no low value eliminates risk. Total PSA >10 ng/mL corresponds to greater than 67% likelihood of biopsy-detectable cancer; about 18% with PSA 4 to 10 ng/mL have a subsequent positive biopsy. In PCPT data from 18,882 participants, end-of-study biopsy identified cancer in 15% with PSA of 4.0 ng/mL or less and normal DRE. At 3.1 ng/mL, sensitivity for any prostate cancer was about 32% and specificity about 87%. Appropriate PSA testing alone can advance diagnosis by 5 to 10 years, with variation across studies, populations, and protocols. After PSA testing was introduced, detection shifted toward early organ-confined disease and away from metastasis at diagnosis. Population-screening studies have demonstrated survival benefits using PSA, sometimes alongside DRE or other tests.

Document sections:
  Heading: 3.1 Epidemiology
  Content: UC is the second most frequent urological malignancy in developed countries and can arise in the lower urinary tract or the pyelocaliceal cavities and ureter. Bladder cancer (BC) constitutes 90–95% of UC, whereas UTUC constitutes 5–10%; estimated annual incidence in Western countries is almost two cases per 100,000 inhabitants. Incidence has increased over recent decades, possibly because detection improved and populations aged. Incidence peaks at 70–90 years, and UTUC occurs twice as often in men. In an international retrospective registry of 2,380 people diagnosed between 2014 and 2019 at 101 centres in 29 countries, 70.5% were men, 53.3% were current or former smokers, and 53% received a diagnosis after symptoms, chiefly visible haematuria. A meta-analysis of 44 studies estimated UTUC incidence among people with visible and non-visible haematuria at 0.75% and 0.17%, respectively. Approximately two-thirds of patients presenting with UTUC have muscle-invasive disease at diagnosis, versus 15–25% with newly diagnosed BC; population studies from Germany and England suggest muscle-invasive UTUC accounts for approximately half of recent incident cases. Approximately 9% present with metastases. Pyelocaliceal tumours occur approximately twice as frequently as ureteral tumours; multifocality occurs in approximately 10–20%, and concomitant upper-tract carcinoma in situ in between 11% and 36%. Concurrent BC occurs in 17%; previous BC was recorded in 41% of American men and 4% of Chinese men. These differences, alongside genetic and epigenetic factors, may help explain more advanced, higher-grade presentations in Asian patients. After treatment, bladder recurrence occurs in 29%, varying with patient, tumour and treatment characteristics, versus 2–5% recurrence in the contralateral upper tract. UTUC and BC differ substantially in frequencies of common genomic changes, although tumours in a person with both cancers are often clonally related. UTUC genomic profiling can inform bladder-recurrence risk and identify Lynch syndrome-associated tumours. Among 82 patients given intravesical bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) for high-risk BC and imaged regularly between years 1 and 3, 13% developed asymptomatic UTUC; another series of 307 patients without routine upper-tract imaging reported 25% UTUC after BC. A multicentre cohort of n = 402 followed for 50 month reported 7.5% UTUC among NMIBC recipients of BCG; intravesical recurrence and a non-papillary tumour at transurethral resection of the bladder (TURB) predicted UTUC. Following radical cystectomy for MIBC, 3–5% develop metachronous UTUC.

Document sections:
  Heading: 4.8.4.3 Management of ureteric fistulae
  Content: Higher-risk operations require surgeons able to protect ureteric blood supply and promptly recognise injury. An intraoperative injury should be repaired immediately using debridement, adequate vascularity, a tension-free anastomosis and internal stenting. After relevant abdominal or pelvic surgery, unexpectedly slow recovery, fluid leakage or pelvicalyceal dilatation should raise suspicion of delayed upper-tract injury. No operative approach has proved superior; consensus favours established tissue-repair principles and experienced teams. Options include internal or external drainage, nephrostomy and stenting, and repair early (< 2 weeks) or later (> 3 months) when needed. Functional and anatomical imaging after repair should detect ureteric stricture or declining renal function. Early postoperative UVF, chiefly following hysterectomy, is the most frequent upper-tract fistula presentation in urological practice. In an RCT of 3,141 women undergoing open or laparoscopic gynaecological surgery, prophylactic ureteric stents did not alter the low injury risk (1%). Selected endoscopic approaches include retrograde or antegrade stenting with nephrostomy, or ureteroscopic realignment, but long-term success is unknown. Distal antegrade ureteric occlusion plus nephrostomy often palliates terminal malignant-fistula leakage. Failure or secondary stricture after endoluminal treatment usually calls for abdominal repair, potentially including end-to-end anastomosis, reimplantation with psoas hitch or Boari flap, or bowel replacement. Document sections:
  Heading: 5.5 Urinary cytology
  Content: Cytology of voided urine or bladder washings detects exfoliated malignant cells with sensitivity 84% for HG/G3 tumours and 16% for LG/G1 tumours; CIS sensitivity ranges from 28–100%. A report using the Paris system found sensitivity 46% for HG disease. Cytology complements cystoscopy for HG/G3 disease but is not intended to detect LG tumours. Positive voided cytology can indicate UC anywhere in the tract, while a negative result cannot exclude it. Interpretation varies by reader and can be impaired by sparse cells, infection, stones or intravesical treatment, although experienced practitioners achieve specificity exceeding 90%. Digital image processing with artificial intelligence in the VisioCyt test raised HG sensitivity up to 92%. The Paris System 2022 (2nd Edn.) uses the full diagnostic categories No adequate diagnosis possible (No diagnosis), Negative for UC (Negative), Atypical urothelial cells (Atypia), Suspicious for HG UC (Suspicious), and High-grade/G3 UC (Malignant). Its terminology emphasizes HG/G3 detection, and retrospective studies have validated it. A prospective study suggested pre-TURB risk stratification: cytology negative for HG had 93% specificity for LG disease; an HG-positive result predicted HG disease with 92% specificity and 91% PPV. One cytospin slide is usually sufficient. Suspicious cytology warrants repeat investigation because the underlying risk of an HG lesion is 24-53%. Adjunctive voided cytology for HG detection and reporting with the Paris System 2nd Edn. each have a Strong recommendation. Obtain at least 25 mL of fresh or adequately fixed urine; first-morning urine is unsuitable because cytolysis is frequent (Strong).

  Content: For asymptomatic patients, the EAU favours initial US because it avoids radiation, costs less and can identify hydronephrosis and stones in the calyces, renal pelvis and pelvic-ureteric or vesico-ureteric junctions. retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 6.8. High Risk for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
  Content: An adolescent symptom constellation can indicate high risk for future PCOS. In adults, Rotterdam criteria confirm PCOS when two of three features are present: oligo-/amenorrhea, hyperandrogenemia or signs of androgenization, and sonomorphological evidence of polycystic ovaries. These criteria should not be applied in adolescence, and PCOS should not be diagnosed until 8 years after menarche. Blood androgen concentrations reach adult female levels only at ages 12–15, and clear cut-offs are lacking. Androgens originate in the adrenal cortex, periphery, and adipose tissue. Polycystic ovarian appearance is unsuitable as an adolescent diagnostic criterion because around 33% of girls of this age have it on sonography; its presence alone does not establish PCOS. Oligomenorrhoea together with hyperandrogenemia appears to signal increased later PCOS risk. Adolescents should therefore be classified as high risk and followed closely without premature diagnostic labeling or distress. Individualized monitoring is important because associated risks include metabolic syndrome, impaired glucose tolerance, type II diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, arterial hypertension, sterility, endometrial cancer, and depression. The Ferriman–Gallwey score permits patient assessment of body hair in hirsutism; Figure 6 illustrates pronounced hirsutism and obesity permagna in a 16-year-old girl at high risk for PCOS. Possible laboratory findings include LH/FSH quotient >>2, Homa index >2.5, abnormal oral glucose tolerance or HbA1c, elevated AMH, and, with obesity, low SHBG or dyslipidemia. Normal 17-OH progesterone helps distinguish this constellation from congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH). None of these additional laboratory abnormalities is a diagnostic criterion. Diagnosis requires exclusion of other hyperandrogenemia causes. Etiology remains largely uncertain, although genetic and environmental contributions appear possible. Several mechanisms may lead to anovulation; the proposed “two-hit” theory combines predisposition with a trigger such as insulin resistance. PCOS treatment should be multidisciplinary. An anti-androgen contraceptive pill is the primary treatment for cycle disturbance; oral contraception is also preferred for acne, hirsutism, and regular endometrial transformation during amenorrhea. Cyproterone acetate, dienogest, chlormadinone acetate, and drospirenone are described as potent antiandrogenic progestins. Lowering androgens improves acne and hirsutism, although visible improvement in hair growth can take a good 6–9 months. With obesity, exercise and nutritional counseling are important aspects of lifestyle change; collaboration with dieticians or an obesity center can help, and multidisciplinary care improves treatment success. Metformin is an insulin sensitizer that can support weight reduction, particularly with insulin resistance and BMI over 25 kg/m2. Its dose is increased gradually to a maximum of 2000 mg daily to limit gastrointestinal effects such as diarrhea, and it works only in combination with exercise. Dermatological support may help acne; laser treatment can be tried for distressing hirsutism, and eflornithine cream can slow facial hair growth and reduce shaving frequency. Marked obesity, thrombophilia-related coagulation disorder, arterial hypertension, or nicotine use may contraindicate oral contraception; progestogen-only preparations such as cyproterone acetate or drospirenone can then be tried. Individual contraceptive needs must be considered. Without endometrial transformation during amenorrhea, hyperplasia may arise. Given metabolic risk, close OGTT monitoring, weight and blood-pressure checks even in slim girls, and lipid assessment are sensible to enable timely referral for treatment.

Document sections:
  Heading: Abstract
  Content: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most frequent malignancy in white populations. European multidisciplinary experts updated guidance on its diagnosis and treatment and distinguish ‘easy-to-treat’ from ‘difficult-to-treat’ BCC using the EADO clinical classification. Clinical and dermatoscopic findings generally establish the diagnosis, but uncertain lesions require histopathological confirmation. Complete surgical removal is first-line treatment. Micrographically controlled surgery shall be offered for high-risk or recurrent tumours and those at critical anatomical sites. Topical or destructive treatments can be considered for low-risk superficial BCC; photodynamic therapy is effective for superficial and low-risk nodular BCC. A multidisciplinary tumour board should discuss difficult-to-treat cases. Patients with locally advanced or metastatic BCC should be offered the Hedgehog inhibitors vismodegib or sonidegib. Anti-PD1 treatment with cemiplimab is a second-line option after progression, contraindication or intolerance to Hedgehog inhibitors. Radiotherapy is an alternative when surgery is unsuitable or declined, particularly in older patients; electrochemotherapy may be offered if surgery or radiotherapy is contraindicated. Gorlin syndrome requires regular skin examinations for early detection and treatment. Long-term follow-up is recommended for high-risk BCC, multiple BCCs and Gorlin syndrome.
