Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_19
  Name: Varicocele
  Description: A common congenital venous abnormality that can be associated with impaired testicular growth, sub-fertility, discomfort or hypogonadism.
  Epidemiology: Present in almost 15% of the general male population, 25% of men with abnormal semen analysis and 35-40% of men presenting with infertility. Reported incidence is 35–44% in primary infertility and 45–81% in secondary infertility.
  Clinical presentation: It may be palpable or visible, cause pain or discomfort, and accompany abnormal semen parameters. Worsening semen parameters are associated with greater grade and age.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Subclinical
      Distinguishing features: Neither palpable nor visible at rest or with Valsalva manoeuvre, but detectable with a special test such as Doppler US.
    - Name: Grade 1
      Distinguishing features: Palpable during Valsalva manoeuvre.
    - Name: Grade 2
      Distinguishing features: Palpable at rest.
    - Name: Grade 3
      Distinguishing features: Visible and palpable at rest.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Physical examination
      Purpose: Establish the clinical diagnosis and grade.
      When indicated: Suspected varicocele.
      Interpretation: Palpability and visibility at rest or during Valsalva manoeuvre distinguish the stated grades.
    - Test: Scrotal Doppler US
      Purpose: Assess reflux, vein diameter and persistent or recurrent varicocele.
      When indicated: Inconclusive examination or persistently unsatisfactory semen analysis after repair.
      Interpretation: A maximum diameter > 3 mm while upright and during Valsalva manoeuvre, together with reflux lasting > 2 seconds, correlates with clinically significant varicocele.
    - Test: Semen analysis
      Purpose: Assess fertility-related semen abnormalities.
      When indicated: Infertility evaluation or assessment after repair.
    - Test: Testicular volume assessment using Lambert’s formula
      Purpose: Estimate volume in patients with infertility and/or varicocele.
      When indicated: Assessment of testicular size.
      Interpretation: The stated formula is V=L x W x H x 0.71.
    - Test: Further abdominal and retroperitoneal assessment
      Purpose: Investigate underlying pathology or congenital anomalies.
      When indicated: Isolated clinical right varicocele.

  Heading: Assessing pre-eclampsia
  Content: A professional trained in pregnancy-related hypertensive disorders should assess pre-eclampsia. Perform a complete clinical assessment at every antenatal visit and offer admission for observation or intervention if maternal or fetal wellbeing raises concern. Examples include sustained systolic pressure of 160 mmHg or higher; a new, persistent rise in creatinine to 90 micromol/litre or more, 1 mg/100 ml or more; alanine transaminase over 70 IU/litre or twice the upper limit of normal; platelets under 150,000/microlitre; impending eclampsia or pulmonary oedema; other severe features; suspected fetal compromise; or other concerning clinical findings. retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 3.1 Epidemiology
  Content: UC is the second most frequent urological malignancy in developed countries and can arise in the lower urinary tract or the pyelocaliceal cavities and ureter. Bladder cancer (BC) constitutes 90–95% of UC, whereas UTUC constitutes 5–10%; estimated annual incidence in Western countries is almost two cases per 100,000 inhabitants. Incidence has increased over recent decades, possibly because detection improved and populations aged. Incidence peaks at 70–90 years, and UTUC occurs twice as often in men. In an international retrospective registry of 2,380 people diagnosed between 2014 and 2019 at 101 centres in 29 countries, 70.5% were men, 53.3% were current or former smokers, and 53% received a diagnosis after symptoms, chiefly visible haematuria. A meta-analysis of 44 studies estimated UTUC incidence among people with visible and non-visible haematuria at 0.75% and 0.17%, respectively. Approximately two-thirds of patients presenting with UTUC have muscle-invasive disease at diagnosis, versus 15–25% with newly diagnosed BC; population studies from Germany and England suggest muscle-invasive UTUC accounts for approximately half of recent incident cases. Approximately 9% present with metastases. Pyelocaliceal tumours occur approximately twice as frequently as ureteral tumours; multifocality occurs in approximately 10–20%, and concomitant upper-tract carcinoma in situ in between 11% and 36%. Concurrent BC occurs in 17%; previous BC was recorded in 41% of American men and 4% of Chinese men. These differences, alongside genetic and epigenetic factors, may help explain more advanced, higher-grade presentations in Asian patients. After treatment, bladder recurrence occurs in 29%, varying with patient, tumour and treatment characteristics, versus 2–5% recurrence in the contralateral upper tract. UTUC and BC differ substantially in frequencies of common genomic changes, although tumours in a person with both cancers are often clonally related. UTUC genomic profiling can inform bladder-recurrence risk and identify Lynch syndrome-associated tumours. Among 82 patients given intravesical bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) for high-risk BC and imaged regularly between years 1 and 3, 13% developed asymptomatic UTUC; another series of 307 patients without routine upper-tract imaging reported 25% UTUC after BC. A multicentre cohort of n = 402 followed for 50 month reported 7.5% UTUC among NMIBC recipients of BCG; intravesical recurrence and a non-papillary tumour at transurethral resection of the bladder (TURB) predicted UTUC. Following radical cystectomy for MIBC, 3–5% develop metachronous UTUC.

      Conditions for use: Consider an intracavernous combination where available, with its unlicensed status made clear.
    - Name: Trimix
      Summary: A combination of papaverine 8-16 mg, phentolamine 0.2-0.4 mg and alprostadil 10-20 μg. The guideline reports efficacy reaching 92% and less penile pain than alprostadil monotherapy, but it has never been licensed for ED.
      Conditions for use: Consider a combination injection where available, with its unlicensed status and fibrosis risk made clear.
    - Name: InvicorpTM
      Summary: Combines vasoactive intestinal peptide (25 μg) with phentolamine mesylate (1-2 mg Invicorp). Clinical studies report effectiveness in > 80% of men with ED, including previous non-responders, with little penile pain and a virtually negligible risk of priapism.

      Reason: Its high incidence of adverse effects has led to its abandonment as monotherapy; papaverine is not licensed for ED.
    - Name: Phentolamine monotherapy
      Reason: It produces a poor erectile response as monotherapy and is not licensed for ED.
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: After initiation and during close follow-up
      Method: Assess erection quality, pain, prolonged erections, priapism, fibrosis, satisfaction and continued participation in the injection programme.
      Interpretation: Most reported discontinuations of intracavernous pharmacotherapy occur within the first two to three months.
  Supportive care:
    - Provide office-based injection training, careful counselling and close follow-up.
    - For alprostadil-related pain, the guideline describes sodium bicarbonate or local anaesthesia as possible measures.

Document sections:
  Heading: Context
  Content: The lower urinary tract comprises bladder and urethra and coordinates urine storage and expulsion under central and peripheral nervous-system control. Neurological disease affecting the brain, suprasacral or sacral spinal cord, or peripheral nerves can produce characteristic patterns of bladder and sphincter dysfunction; the nature of the injury also matters. Childhood neurological damage often stems from congenital conditions such as spina bifida or sacral agenesis. Stroke, spinal cord injury and cauda equina compression can cause relatively stable injury, whereas dementia, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis and peripheral neuropathy can cause progressive damage. Table 1 groups example neurological conditions by lesion site and likelihood of progression. Because the neural centres governing urinary, bowel and sexual function are close, dysfunctions often coexist and warrant a holistic rather than isolated urinary approach. Neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction can impair storage, emptying or both; storage symptoms include increased frequency and incontinence. Urinary symptoms can cause embarrassment, social isolation and difficulty with daily activities. Incontinence can result from overactive bladder, urethral sphincter dysfunction or both. Risks include markedly more urinary tract infections and loss of renal function from elevated bladder pressures, infection or kidney stones. Medical treatment often does not restore normal urinary function, and medicines, intermittent self-catheterisation, indwelling catheters, pads and appliances can affect quality of life. Families and carers may face physical, psychological, relationship and social pressures. Costs arise from supplies, medicines, operations, care and professional support, as well as effects on employment, follow-up and long-term surveillance. The full guideline contains 3 algorithms outlining the clinical approach. For recommended uses outside UK marketing authorisation at publication, prescribers should follow relevant professional guidance, take responsibility for the decision, and obtain and document informed consent.

  Content: Ovarian lesions account for most abdominal masses in pediatric girls and span functional cysts through malignant tumors. Cysts constitute 60% of pediatric ovarian lesions. Neoplasms are grouped by origin into germ cell, sex cordstromal, and epithelial tumors. Incidence, causes, and presentation vary by age: germ cell tumors predominate among childhood and adolescent ovarian neoplasms, whereas epithelial tumors predominate in adults. Document sections:
  Heading: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJO)
  Content: Prenatal screening ultrasonography (US) and postnatal imaging have increased detection of hydronephrosis and lowered the age at pyeloplasty. Prenatal hydronephrosis is identified in up to 4.5% of screening ultrasounds; UPJO occurs in 1 per 1000–2000 newborns. UPJO is more common in males, involves the left kidney in up to 67% of cases, and is bilateral in up to 10%. Urinary tract US assesses hydronephrosis severity, pelvocalyceal dilation, and renal cortical thinning at birth. In 1993, the Society for Fetal Urology (SFU) proposed a standardized US grade based on urinary tract dilation and parenchymal thickness. The urinary tract dilation (UTD) classification introduced in 2014 assesses six parameters: anterior–posterior renal pelvic diameter, urinary tract dilatation, parenchymal thickness, parenchymal appearance, ureteral status, and bladder status. The first postnatal US should occur more than 48 h after birth to avoid underestimating dilation. In addition to US, 99mTc-MAG3 is recommended for neonatal renography and visualization of kidneys when renal function is impaired. Functional immaturity of neonatal kidneys can produce increased residual cortical activity when the radiopharmaceutical and furosemide are administered together in an F0 study; activity may remain at up to 50% or more of its peak. This phenomenon resolves after the age of 3 months.

Document sections:
  Heading: 1 | Introduction
  Content: Hematuria means RBCs are present in urine and may be visible or detectable only microscopically. It is a fundamental manifestation of glomerulonephritis (GN); microscopic assessment of urinary sediment is presented as its most effective detection method. Birch et al. proposed in 1979 that urinary RBC morphology could distinguish glomerular from non-glomerular origins. Passage through glomeruli can damage RBC membranes and produce dysmorphic RBCs (dRBCs). Shichiri et al. reported in 1988 that erythrocytes were smaller in glomerular than in non-glomerular disease, and Hyodo et al. later proposed an RBC size range of 4–6 μm for discriminating the origins. Compared with blood, urine has much less albumin and more urea; this environment increases membrane vulnerability and changes RBC shape. High urea concentrations particularly favor burr-cell formation. Passage across the glomerular basement membrane may produce acanthocytes through membrane injury. RBCs in renal disease are also more susceptible to factors including iron deficiency, osmotic lysis, shape distortion, and vesicle formation. Reliable recognition of urinary dRBCs requires an experienced observer, and observer-dependent interpretation may explain differences between laboratories. The authors consider continuing education in RBC morphology essential and mention deep learning for microscopy as another possible approach. Instrument-measured small-RBC fractions are easier to obtain and less dependent on interpretation, making them potentially more objective and standardized. The fully automated UF-5000 uses fluorescence flow cytometry to classify urine particles and reports morphological RBC information, including non-lysed RBCs, lysed RBCs, large RBCs, small RBCs, and RBC-Info. Its classification uses forward scatter light (FSC), side scatter light (SSC), side fluorescence light (SFL), and depolarized side scattered light (DSS). A small RBC has FSC intensity < 70; a non-lysed RBC has a strong FSC signal and morphological stability indicated by SSC. URD is the small-RBC count divided by the non-lysed-RBC count. Earlier studies investigated possible clinical uses, but most were single-center studies. Reported cutoffs for distinguishing glomerular from non-glomerular hematuria varied from 30.1% to 40.5% for small RBCs and from 0% to 30.0% for dRBCs. The authors therefore considered a multicenter assessment using the same equipment necessary for clinical application. Across four hospitals, they collected urine microscopy findings, urine measures, serum markers, and kidney-function information to compare institutional dRBC and URD measurements and cutoffs and assess their clinical significance.

  Content: Testicular germ cell tumour (TGCT) is the most common cancer in Caucasian men aged 15-40 years and affects approximately 1% of sub-fertile men.   Content: Suspected or confirmed urethral rupture, UTI or false passage are listed contraindications. Injury to urethral epithelium can heal with scarring and stricture formation. Male strictures commonly cause obstructive voiding symptoms and may follow IC, infection, trauma, lichen sclerosus, prostate-cancer treatment such as radiotherapy, or an unidentified cause. UK Hospital Episode Statistics and similar US data suggest male incidence rises from about 10 in every 100,000 up to 25 years to 40 in every 100,000 by the age of 65 years and > 100 in every 100,000 over 65 years. Female urethral strictures affect 0.1–1% of women with voiding complaints and can cause irritative as well as obstructive symptoms. In a review by Chakraborty et al., 53.48% of surgically treated female strictures were presumed idiopathic and 91.29% had a prior intervention. Smith et al. attributed 8% of female strictures to inflammation and infection and 6.6% to trauma. Male strictures may occur anywhere, particularly in the bulbar urethra (50 %) and at the meatus. In selected patients, intermittent dilatation is established as palliative management of refractory strictures and can reduce recurrence up to 68%. Diversion, such as a continent stoma or ileal conduit, is required if reconstruction is impossible or repair attempts fail. A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to determine which of dilatation, endoscopic urethrotomy or urethroplasty best balances effectiveness, adverse effects and costs.   Heading: 3.2 Epidemiology
  Content: Among males, incidence rises sharply after 55 years of age; mean age is 45.1, and estimated overall incidence is 229-627 per 100,000 males. The anterior urethra accounts for 92.2% of affected sites, particularly the bulbar urethra (46.9%). Among females with refractory lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), 2-29% have bladder outflow obstruction (BOO), of whom 4-20% have a urethral stricture; true FUS therefore affects 0.08-5.4% of women with refractory LUTS. Incidence increases markedly after 64 years of age. Following hypospadias repair, meatal stenosis or stricture is reported in 1.3-20% of cases, varying with severity and technique; incidence is significantly higher in well-resourced countries, where repair is more frequent. Up to 18% of all strictures involve the meatus or fossa navicularis, commonly following failed hypospadias repair (FHR), lichen sclerosus (LS), trauma or instrumentation, or without identified cause. Meatal stenosis after neonatal circumcision is reported in less than 0.2% of children. Strictures affect 2-56% of female-to-male (FtM) transgender patients (‘transmen’) and 4-40% of male-to-female (MtF) transgender patients (‘transwomen’); in transwomen, they arise almost exclusively at the neomeatus.

Document sections:
  Heading: 10.2.1 Stuttering (recurrent or intermittent) priapism
  Content: Stuttering, intermittent, or recurrent priapism consists of repeated painful prolonged erections that resolve spontaneously between episodes. Episodes resemble recurrent ischaemic priapism but are generally shorter; their frequency and duration vary, and one can develop into prolonged ischaemic priapism. Robust epidemiological evidence is lacking. Recurrent episodes occur in 42-64% of men with SCD. Among adolescents and young men, reported priapism incidence is 35%, of whom 72% have a stuttering-priapism history. Causes resemble those of ischaemic priapism: SCD is most common, but idiopathic and neurologically associated cases occur. Acute ischaemic priapism, particularly lasting more than 4 hours, increases subsequent risk. Proposed mechanisms include inflammation, cellular adhesion, NO metabolism, vascular reactivity, and coagulation. An androgen association is disputed; lowering serum testosterone to hypogonadal levels is one proposed means of suppressing androgen-related triggers of recurrence.

KUB X-ray can establish radiopacity but need not be obtained when NCCT is planned. The AUA recommends NCCT before PCNL (AUA: strong recommendation) and when choosing between SWL and URS (AUA: conditional recommendation); US alone is discouraged for the latter decision. Suspected substantial renal injury may warrant a DTPA or MAG-3 renogram to guide care (AUA: conditional recommendation). The EAU advises testing serum creatinine, uric acid, ionised calcium, sodium, potassium, blood cell counts and C-reactive protein, plus coagulation when intervention is intended (EAU: strong recommendation). Both organisations strongly recommend urine culture and microscopy before intervention.

  Heading: 1.2 Assessment of proteinuria in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
  Content: Interpret proteinuria alongside a complete clinical assessment of symptoms, signs and other findings relevant to pre-eclampsia. In secondary care, use an automated reagent-strip reader for initial dipstick screening; a result of 1+ or more should be quantified with an albumin:creatinine ratio or protein:creatinine ratio. Do not use the first morning urine void for quantification, and do not routinely collect urine over 24 hours. For protein:creatinine ratio, the threshold for significant proteinuria is 30 mg/mmol; if the result is 30 mg/mmol or above but diagnosis remains uncertain, consider a fresh sample and another clinical assessment. When albumin:creatinine ratio is used instead to diagnose pre-eclampsia in a pregnant woman with hypertension, apply a threshold of 8 mg/mmol and consider repeat testing on a new sample with clinical review if a result of 8 mg/mmol or above leaves diagnostic uncertainty.   Heading: 10.1.3.1.3 Aspiration ± irrigation with 0.9% w/v saline solution in combination with intracavernous injection of pharmacological agents.
  Content: Combining aspiration, with or without irrigation, and intracavernous medication is considered standard care for ischaemic priapism. Sympathomimetic or α-adrenergic agents used include phenylephrine, etilephrine, ephedrine, epinephrine, norepinephrine, and metaraminol; reported resolution reaches up to 80%. Intracavernous adrenaline alone has also been described sporadically. Reported resolution with prior aspiration or irrigation plus a sympathomimetic ranges from 80 to 100%, versus 58% with sympathomimetic injection alone. Phenylephrine and other intracavernous sympathomimetics may cause headache, dizziness, hypertension, reflex bradycardia, tachycardia, palpitations, and, sporadically, subarachnoid haemorrhage. Monitor blood pressure and pulse during administration. Because hypertension and serious cardiovascular or neurological complications have been reported, the Guidelines Panel considers these drugs contraindicated in malignant or poorly controlled hypertension. Data also suggest a hypertensive crisis when sympathomimetics are combined with monoamine oxidase inhibitors; do not combine them.

Document sections:
  Heading: 8.2.3.2 Surgical treatment
  Content: Conservative care may resolve painful erections in most men but produces substantial straightening in only a small proportion. Surgery seeks to correct curvature so penetrative intercourse is possible and is indicated for substantial deformity with intercourse difficulty and sexual bother. Disease should be stable for 3-6 months, or surgery should occur more than 9-12 months after PD onset. Once stable, failed conservative or medical treatment, extensive plaques or patient preference may also prompt surgery. Before reconstruction, document plaque size and position, curvature, hinge or hourglass deformity, penile length and ED status. Discuss intended benefits and risks to enable informed choice: shortening, ED, numbness, delayed orgasm, recurrent or residual curvature, palpable knots or stitches, possible circumcision and further penile wasting after shortening surgery. Procedure selection considers length, curvature and erectile function, including response to ED drugs, as well as expectations. Patients should understand that the primary aim is a functionally straight penis. Options comprise tunical shortening, tunical lengthening and penile prosthesis implantation, potentially with additional straightening for concurrent ED and residual curvature. Degloving with circumcision to prevent postoperative phimosis is described as the standard approach, although modifications exist; one study suggested circumcision may be unnecessary with a normal preoperative foreskin. Non-degloving approaches have been described to avoid ischaemic and lymphatic complications after subcoronal circumcision. No standardised questionnaire evaluates surgical outcomes. Prospective evidence is sparse and low-level; most outcomes come from retrospective, usually non-comparative and non-randomised single-centre studies or expert opinion, so they require caution.

Transurethral, endoscopic and percutaneous approaches have comparable SFRs and shorter operations, admissions and catheterisation than open cystolithotomy. Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_04
  Name: Pre-eclampsia
  Description: New hypertension, over 140 mmHg systolic or over 90 mmHg diastolic, after 20 weeks of pregnancy together with 1 or more newly occurring findings: proteinuria, maternal organ dysfunction or uteroplacental dysfunction.
  Epidemiology: The guideline states that less than 1 woman in every million who gives birth now dies from pre-eclampsia.
  Clinical presentation: Possible symptoms include severe headache, blurred vision or flashing before the eyes, severe pain below the ribs, vomiting, and sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet. Maternal organ dysfunction may affect the kidneys, liver, nervous system or blood. Uteroplacental findings may include fetal growth restriction, abnormal umbilical artery doppler waveform analysis or stillbirth.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Severe pre-eclampsia
      Distinguishing features: Pre-eclampsia with severe hypertension unresponsive to treatment or accompanied by specified persistent symptoms, worsening blood results, impaired fetal growth or abnormal doppler findings.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Full clinical assessment
      Purpose: Evaluate maternal and fetal wellbeing and determine whether hospital surveillance is needed.
      When indicated: At every antenatal appointment, by a healthcare professional trained in managing hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
      Interpretation: Concerning findings include sustained systolic blood pressure of 160 mmHg or higher; a new, persistent rise in creatinine to 90 micromol/litre or more, 1 mg/100 ml or more; a rise in alanine transaminase to over 70 IU/litre, or twice upper limit of normal range; a fall in platelet count to under 150,000/microlitre; impending eclampsia or pulmonary oedema; other severe features; or suspected fetal compromise.
    - Test: Automated reagent-strip reading device for dipstick proteinuria screening
      Purpose: Screen for urinary protein in secondary care.
      When indicated: During assessment of a pregnant woman for proteinuria.
      Interpretation: A screening result of 1+ or more calls for quantification with albumin:creatinine ratio or protein:creatinine ratio. For the definition of pre-eclampsia, dipstick proteinuria is at least 1 g/litre [2+].
    - Test: Urine protein:creatinine ratio
      Purpose: Quantify proteinuria.
      When indicated: After a positive dipstick result of 1+ or more; a first morning urine void should not be used for quantification.
      Interpretation: 30 mg/mmol or more indicates significant proteinuria. If the result is 30 mg/mmol or above and diagnosis remains uncertain, consider testing a new sample alongside clinical review.
    - Test: Urine albumin:creatinine ratio
      Purpose: Provide an alternative measure of proteinuria when diagnosing pre-eclampsia in a pregnant woman with hypertension.
      When indicated: After a positive dipstick result of 1+ or more; a first morning urine void should not be used for quantification.
      Interpretation: The diagnostic threshold is 8 mg/mmol. If the result is 8 mg/mmol or above and diagnosis remains uncertain, consider testing a new sample alongside clinical review.
    - Test: 24-hour urine collection
      Purpose: Quantify proteinuria.
      When indicated: Not for routine use; the guideline notes that it may be more appropriate on rare occasions, such as in women with renal complications.
    - Test: Placental growth factor (PLGF)-based testing
      Purpose: Help rule out pre-eclampsia.
      When indicated: For suspected pre-eclampsia between 20 weeks and 36 weeks and 6 days of pregnancy.
    - Test: Serum creatinine
      Purpose: Assess renal involvement and monitor maternal condition.
      When indicated: During assessment and subsequent blood-test monitoring.
      Interpretation: Creatinine of 90 micromol/litre or more, 1.02 mg/100 ml or more, is a renal-insufficiency criterion in the definition of pre-eclampsia.
    - Test: Liver transaminases
      Purpose: Assess liver involvement and monitor maternal condition.
      When indicated: During assessment and subsequent blood-test monitoring.
      Interpretation: Alanine aminotransferase or aspartate aminotransferase over 40 IU/litre is a liver-involvement criterion in the definition of pre-eclampsia.
    - Test: Platelet count
      Purpose: Assess haematological involvement and monitor maternal condition.
      When indicated: During assessment and subsequent blood-test monitoring.
      Interpretation: A count below 150,000/microlitre is a thrombocytopenia criterion in the definition of pre-eclampsia.
    - Test: Full blood count, liver function and renal function
      Purpose: Monitor maternal haematological, liver and kidney status.
      When indicated: Twice a week with hypertension or 3 times a week with severe hypertension.
    - Test: Fetal heart auscultation
      Purpose: Assess fetal heart activity.
      When indicated: At every antenatal appointment.
    - Test: Ultrasound for fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume assessment
      Purpose: Assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume.
      When indicated: At diagnosis and, if normal, every 2 weeks.
    - Test: Umbilical artery doppler velocimetry
      Purpose: Assess the fetal circulation and uteroplacental dysfunction.
      When indicated: At diagnosis if conservative management is planned; repeat fetal growth, amniotic fluid or umbilical artery doppler assessment every 2 weeks according to findings.
      Interpretation: An abnormal umbilical artery doppler waveform may indicate uteroplacental dysfunction.
    - Test: Cardiotocography (CTG)
      Purpose: Assess fetal status.
      When indicated: At diagnosis; subsequently if clinically indicated, including a change in fetal movement, vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain or deterioration in maternal condition.
  Prognostic tools:
    - Name: fullPIERS
      Interpretation: May help guide place-of-care and intervention decisions at any time during pregnancy by predicting adverse maternal outcomes; it does not predict outcomes for babies.
    - Name: PREP-S
      Interpretation: May help guide place-of-care and intervention decisions only up to 34 weeks of pregnancy by predicting adverse maternal outcomes; it does not predict outcomes for babies.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: After transfer to community care, offer a review at 2 weeks to women who remain on antihypertensive treatment. Offer all women a medical review 6 to 8 weeks after birth. Persistent proteinuria of 1+ or more at that review calls for a further kidney-function review at 3 months.
    Recommended tests:
      - For women who received no antihypertensive treatment, measure blood pressure at least 4 times a day while admitted, at least once between day 3 and day 5 after birth, and on alternate days until normal if it was abnormal on days 3 to 5.
      - For women who received antihypertensive treatment, measure blood pressure at least 4 times a day while admitted and every 1 to 2 days for up to 2 weeks after transfer to community care, until treatment has stopped and hypertension has resolved.
      - Ask about severe headache and epigastric pain whenever blood pressure is measured after birth.
      - For mild or moderate hypertension, or after step-down from critical care, measure platelet count, transaminases and serum creatinine 48 to 72 hours after birth or step-down; do not repeat normal measurements at that time. Repeat abnormal results as clinically indicated until normal.
      - Perform a urinary reagent-strip test 6 to 8 weeks after birth; assess kidney function at 3 months if proteinuria remains 1+ or more.
    Long term effects:
      - After pre-eclampsia in a previous or current pregnancy, hypertension of any type in a future pregnancy occurs in approximately 20% (1 in 5 women), and pre-eclampsia in up to approximately 16% (1 in 6 women). If birth was at 28 to 34 weeks, the reported recurrence of pre-eclampsia is approximately 33% (1 in 3 women); if birth was at 34 to 37 weeks, it is approximately 23% (1 in 4 women).
      - No evidence was identified for recurrence after birth at less than 28 weeks; the committee considered the risk likely to be at least as high as, if not higher than, after birth between 28 and 34 weeks.
      - After pre-eclampsia in a previous or current pregnancy, the table reports future gestational hypertension in between approximately 6 and 12% (up to 1 in 8 women) and chronic hypertension in approximately 2% (up to 1 in 50 women).
      - For women with pre-eclampsia in a current or previous pregnancy, the table reports an approximately 1.5 to 3 times increased risk of a major adverse cardiovascular event, an approximately 2 times increased risk of cardiovascular mortality, an approximately 2 to 3 times increased risk of stroke, and an approximately 2 to 5 times increased risk of later hypertension.
    Survivorship notes: If neither proteinuria nor hypertension is present at the postnatal review at 6 to 8 weeks, the guideline states that the relative risk of end-stage kidney disease remains increased but its absolute risk is low, and no further follow-up is necessary. Consider specialist kidney assessment if kidney function is abnormal at 3 months. Women are advised to reach and maintain a BMI of 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m2 before a subsequent pregnancy; recurrence becomes more likely when the inter-pregnancy interval exceeds 10 years.

Document sections:
  Heading: Context
  Content: LUTS encompass storage, voiding and post-micturition symptoms. Possible causes involve abnormal structure or function of the prostate, urethra, bladder or sphincters. In men, the most common cause is benign prostate enlargement (BPE), which obstructs the bladder outlet; BPE arises from an increase in prostate cell numbers called benign prostatic hyperplasia. Other possible causes include detrusor weakness or overactivity, prostate inflammation (prostatitis), urinary tract infection, prostate cancer and neurological disease. Categorising symptoms as voiding, storage or post-micturition helps identify their source. Voiding symptoms comprise a weak or intermittent stream, straining, hesitancy, terminal dribbling and incomplete emptying. Storage symptoms comprise urgency, frequency, urgency incontinence and nocturia. Post-micturition dribbling is the main post-micturition symptom and is common and bothersome. LUTS usually do not cause severe illness but can substantially impair quality of life or indicate serious urogenital disease. They impose a major burden on ageing men: age is an important risk factor, prevalence rises with age, and bothersome LUTS occur in up to 30% of men older than 65 years. This represents a large population that might need treatment.

  Description: Following PFUI, partial injury or unsuccessful early realignment can leave a non-obliterative membranous stenosis. Complete disruption can leave an obliterative distraction defect in which dense fibrosis separates the urethral ends.
  Epidemiology: Motor vehicle accidents are described as the main cause of blunt posterior urethral injury associated with pelvic fracture.
  Clinical presentation: The resulting posterior obstruction may occur alongside sexual dysfunction or urinary incontinence attributable to the original injury.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: non-obliterative stenosis
      Distinguishing features: A residual lumen remains after partial injury or unsuccessful early realignment.
    - Name: obliterative stenosis
      Distinguishing features: A complete injury leaves separated urethral ends with intervening fibrotic tissue.
    - Name: pelvic fracture urethral injury (PFUI)
      Distinguishing features: Pelvic-fracture-associated posterior urethral injury that can result in a distraction defect.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Retrograde urethrography (RUG) and voiding cystourethrography (VCUG)

    - Test: Retrograde urethroscopy and antegrade cystoscopy

    - Test: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)

      Interpretation: In a cited study, the MRI-measured pubo-urethral stump angle predicted the need for a more elaborate approach.
    - Test: Sexual-function assessment
      Purpose: Document function after injury and during recovery.
      When indicated: Assessment before and after reconstructive surgery.
      Interpretation: Normal erectile function may return during the first two years after trauma.

Document sections:
  Heading: Absence seizures
  Content: Absence seizures are generalised events involving impaired awareness, cessation of activity or speech, and blank staring. They can occur alone or in childhood absence epilepsy, juvenile absence epilepsy or juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Treatment evidence concerned children and young people; the committee extrapolated it to adults because pathophysiology is similar. Limited evidence suggests ethosuximide may improve absence-seizure outcomes and remission, and it may benefit cognition; clinical experience supports its first-line use. Sodium valproate may increase remission and appeared to produce fewer adverse events than other reviewed medicines. Lamotrigine and levetiracetam also appeared effective. Following January 2025 MHRA changes, all 3 are second-line monotherapy or add-on options for absence seizures, with sodium valproate reproductive precautions. Long-term sodium valproate can lower bone mineral density and increase osteomalacia risk; consider supplementation in those at risk. Some other medicines may aggravate seizures. For absence seizures accompanied by, or at risk of, other seizure types, evidence linked sodium valproate to greater remission and good tolerability. After the January 2025 update, sodium valproate, levetiracetam and lamotrigine are all first-line monotherapy or add-on options, subject to sodium valproate precautions. Ethosuximide may improve absence outcomes and remission and is a possible second-line add-on, but should not be the sole medicine when other seizure types coexist because it controls only absence seizures. For some women and girls able to have children, sodium valproate remains an option only after thorough discussion, unsuccessful alternatives and adherence to MHRA safety advice through shared decision making. Prescribing order may change and sodium valproate requires additional counselling, clinical assessment and administration.

Document sections:
  Heading: 3.5. Uncomplicated pyelonephritis
  Content: Uncomplicated pyelonephritis is confined to nonpregnant, premenopausal women without known relevant urological abnormalities or comorbidities. Typical features are fever (>38 C), chills, flank pain, nausea, vomiting, or costovertebral-angle tenderness, with or without cystitis symptoms. Routine diagnostic testing should include urine white and red blood cells and nitrite; every case also requires urine culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Upper-tract ultrasound should exclude obstruction or renal stones in patients with previous urolithiasis, impaired renal function, or high urine pH. Consider contrast-enhanced computed tomography or excretory urography if fever persists after 72 h of treatment, or immediately upon clinical deterioration. In pregnancy, ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is preferred when investigating complicating factors to avoid fetal radiation exposure. Rapid imaging-based distinction from potentially obstructive pyelonephritis matters because obstruction can quickly lead to urosepsis. Only fluoroquinolones and cephalosporins can be recommended for empiric oral treatment. Oral cephalosporins produce significantly lower blood and urine concentrations than intravenous administration. Avoid nitrofurantoin, oral fosfomycin, and pivmecillinam because efficacy data are insufficient. A short outpatient antibiotic course has been shown to achieve clinical and microbiological success equivalent to longer courses, but carries more recurrence within 4–6 wk; local policy and resistance patterns should guide its use. Patients needing admission should initially receive intravenous treatment, such as a fluoroquinolone, an aminoglycoside with or without ampicillin, or an extended-spectrum cephalosporin or penicillin. Reserve carbapenems and novel broad-spectrum agents for early culture evidence of multidrug-resistant organisms; choose according to local resistance and refine using susceptibility findings. Signs of urosepsis warrant empiric coverage for extended-spectrum b-lactamase–producing organisms. Patients improving after parenteral treatment who can take oral fluids may change to oral therapy. Pregnant patients with mild symptoms may be managed as outpatients with suitable parenteral agents if close follow-up is feasible; more severe illness generally requires hospitalisation and supportive care. Following improvement, parenteral therapy may be changed to oral treatment for a total duration of 7–10 d. Men with febrile UTI, pyelonephritis, recurrent infection, or suspected complicating factors should receive at least 2 wk, preferably with a fluoroquinolone, because prostatic involvement is frequent. Tables 5 and 6 provide suggested empiric oral and parenteral regimens, respectively, with doses, durations where given, and qualifications.

Document sections:
  Heading: 3.14. Genitourinary tuberculosis
  Content: Tuberculosis (TB) is common worldwide, but its extrapulmonary form, genitourinary TB (GUTB), is often underestimated by urologists, especially in non-endemic areas such as Europe. GUTB accounted for 4.6% of extrapulmonary TB cases in the EU between 1997 and 2017. It can involve any genitourinary organ and is almost always secondary to bloodstream spread of chronic latent TB infection (LTBI). Risk factors include primary TB or LTBI, diabetes, older age, low body mass index, cancer-related comorbidity, immunosuppression including human immunodeficiency virus, renal failure, and socioeconomic disadvantage. Estimated lifetime reactivation risk is up to 15%. No single test establishes GUTB: diagnosis requires clinical suspicion grounded in history and supported by microbiology, molecular and histological testing, and imaging. Symptoms are commonly nonspecific, including haematuria, increased urinary frequency, difficulty voiding, and abdominal, lumbar, or suprapubic pain. Women may also have menstrual irregularity or pelvic pain. Infertility may lead patients to present, but infertility and TB are not considered in detail. Table 17 presents Strong and Weak diagnostic recommendations. Combination drug treatment is first-line. For newly diagnosed extrapulmonary TB, the World Health Organisation advises daily treatment for 6 mo: an initial 2 mo with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, then 4 mo with isoniazid and rifampicin. Multidrug-resistant TB, defined here by resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid, calls for individualised treatment with at least five effective TB drugs during the intensive phase, including pyrazinamide and four core second-line drugs. Table 18 details treatment regimens, doses, drug groups, and selection restrictions. More than 50% of patients may need ablative, endoscopic, or reconstructive surgery because infection can be destructive and diagnosis delayed. In one cited source, 26.9% of GUTB cases had a nonfunctioning unilateral kidney and 7.4% had renal failure. High-quality evidence on surgery is scarce, so the panel could not make a definitive recommendation for surgical intervention. Assess each patient individually and base the decision to operate on disease location, progression, extent, and genitourinary damage.

  Heading: Treatment
  Content: Timely recognition and a short interval between initial manifestations and definitive surgery are essential. Once rupture is diagnosed, immediate maternal stabilization and fetal delivery are imperative. After frank rupture, the interval before major fetal morbidity is generally only 10-37 minutes; when rupture is suspected, available resources should be mobilized rapidly for definitive surgical care. After delivery, maternal surgery is guided by rupture type and extent, bleeding severity, maternal condition, and wishes about future childbearing. Document sections:
  Heading: 3.14. Genitourinary tuberculosis
  Content: Tuberculosis (TB) is common worldwide, but its extrapulmonary form, genitourinary TB (GUTB), is often underestimated by urologists, especially in non-endemic areas such as Europe. GUTB accounted for 4.6% of extrapulmonary TB cases in the EU between 1997 and 2017. It can involve any genitourinary organ and is almost always secondary to bloodstream spread of chronic latent TB infection (LTBI). Risk factors include primary TB or LTBI, diabetes, older age, low body mass index, cancer-related comorbidity, immunosuppression including human immunodeficiency virus, renal failure, and socioeconomic disadvantage. Estimated lifetime reactivation risk is up to 15%. No single test establishes GUTB: diagnosis requires clinical suspicion grounded in history and supported by microbiology, molecular and histological testing, and imaging. Symptoms are commonly nonspecific, including haematuria, increased urinary frequency, difficulty voiding, and abdominal, lumbar, or suprapubic pain. Women may also have menstrual irregularity or pelvic pain. Infertility may lead patients to present, but infertility and TB are not considered in detail. Table 17 presents Strong and Weak diagnostic recommendations. Combination drug treatment is first-line. For newly diagnosed extrapulmonary TB, the World Health Organisation advises daily treatment for 6 mo: an initial 2 mo with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, then 4 mo with isoniazid and rifampicin. Multidrug-resistant TB, defined here by resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid, calls for individualised treatment with at least five effective TB drugs during the intensive phase, including pyrazinamide and four core second-line drugs. Table 18 details treatment regimens, doses, drug groups, and selection restrictions. More than 50% of patients may need ablative, endoscopic, or reconstructive surgery because infection can be destructive and diagnosis delayed. In one cited source, 26.9% of GUTB cases had a nonfunctioning unilateral kidney and 7.4% had renal failure. High-quality evidence on surgery is scarce, so the panel could not make a definitive recommendation for surgical intervention. Assess each patient individually and base the decision to operate on disease location, progression, extent, and genitourinary damage.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: Taman et al. 2025 Vasopressor Use in Acute Spinal Cord Injury Current Evidence and Clinical Implications
retrieved_chunks.text:
Document sections:
  Heading: 3.3. Vasopressor and Inotrope Selection
  Content: Vasopressors and inotropes address hemodynamic disturbance in acute SCI by supporting systemic pressure and cord perfusion. Norepinephrine and phenylephrine chiefly raise vascular resistance through alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction; dobutamine chiefly increases contractility through beta-1 stimulation and thereby raises cardiac output. Dopamine and epinephrine combine pressor and inotropic actions that depend on dose and receptor activity. Vasopressors are generally used for MAP support, whereas inotropes are reserved for cardiac dysfunction. Table 2 compares the agents' receptor actions, physiological effects, adverse effects, access requirements, precautions, interactions, and patient-specific uses.

Norepinephrine is often used first in acute SCI. Its strong alpha-adrenergic action increases peripheral resistance and opposes the severe hypotension of neurogenic shock; mild beta-adrenergic action can slightly increase heart rate and contractility. Its ability to maintain or lower ITP can support SCPP. In a cited comparison with dopamine, norepinephrine increased SCPP by 2 mmHg without a difference in MAP effects. Its vasoconstriction warrants caution in peripheral vascular disease because ischemia could worsen. Prolonged use requires central venous access to avoid local necrosis from peripheral administration. Animal experiments found better restoration of cord flow and oxygenation with norepinephrine than with phenylephrine, but application of that finding to humans is uncertain.

Dopamine acts on dopaminergic, beta-adrenergic, and alpha-adrenergic receptors according to dose. Low doses dilate renal and mesenteric vessels and might lower systemic pressure; moderate doses increase heart rate and contractility and can help when cardiac dysfunction coexists; higher doses increase vascular resistance. It has been associated with higher ITP, lower SCPP, and potentially worse neurological outcomes, as well as more arrhythmias, particularly in older patients. Higher complication rates, including myocardial injury and arrhythmias, make it generally less favored, especially for elderly patients. Prolonged treatment requires central access, and pheochromocytoma is a contraindication.

Epinephrine strongly stimulates beta and alpha receptors, substantially increasing heart rate, cardiac output, and systemic resistance. Its risks include tachyarrhythmias and greater myocardial oxygen demand. Because of these effects and its extensive adverse-effect profile, it is generally reserved for persistent refractory hypotension when other vasopressors do not achieve stability; careful monitoring is needed.

Phenylephrine selectively stimulates alpha-1 receptors, raising systemic resistance with little heart-rate effect. It does not improve cardiac output through beta-adrenergic action, limiting usefulness when myocardial function is impaired. It is often reserved for patients in whom other vasopressors are contraindicated or whose tachyarrhythmias restrict norepinephrine use. Prolonged administration requires central access because extravasation can injure tissue. Although generally tolerated, it warrants caution with severe bradycardia or heart block. Experimental evidence suggests norepinephrine may improve cord perfusion and oxygenation more effectively than phenylephrine.

Dobutamine chiefly activates beta-1 receptors to increase contractility and cardiac output. Weak alpha-1 activity causes limited vasoconstriction, while beta-2 activity causes mild vasodilation. Vasodilation, tachyarrhythmia risk, and increased myocardial oxygen demand require caution with substantial cardiac risk. Because it does not substantially increase systemic resistance, it has limited value alone for hypotension from neurogenic shock. It is often paired with a vasopressor when cardiac output needs improvement. Central venous access is generally unnecessary unless doses are high or treatment is prolonged. It is preferred for heart failure or significant myocardial dysfunction and may restore cardiac output and cord oxygenation better than norepinephrine in those patients.

Document sections:
  Heading: 3.5. Uncomplicated pyelonephritis
  Content: Uncomplicated pyelonephritis is confined to nonpregnant, premenopausal women without known relevant urological abnormalities or comorbidities. Typical features are fever (>38 C), chills, flank pain, nausea, vomiting, or costovertebral-angle tenderness, with or without cystitis symptoms. Routine diagnostic testing should include urine white and red blood cells and nitrite; every case also requires urine culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Upper-tract ultrasound should exclude obstruction or renal stones in patients with previous urolithiasis, impaired renal function, or high urine pH. Consider contrast-enhanced computed tomography or excretory urography if fever persists after 72 h of treatment, or immediately upon clinical deterioration. In pregnancy, ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is preferred when investigating complicating factors to avoid fetal radiation exposure. Rapid imaging-based distinction from potentially obstructive pyelonephritis matters because obstruction can quickly lead to urosepsis. Only fluoroquinolones and cephalosporins can be recommended for empiric oral treatment. Oral cephalosporins produce significantly lower blood and urine concentrations than intravenous administration. Avoid nitrofurantoin, oral fosfomycin, and pivmecillinam because efficacy data are insufficient. A short outpatient antibiotic course has been shown to achieve clinical and microbiological success equivalent to longer courses, but carries more recurrence within 4–6 wk; local policy and resistance patterns should guide its use. Patients needing admission should initially receive intravenous treatment, such as a fluoroquinolone, an aminoglycoside with or without ampicillin, or an extended-spectrum cephalosporin or penicillin. Reserve carbapenems and novel broad-spectrum agents for early culture evidence of multidrug-resistant organisms; choose according to local resistance and refine using susceptibility findings. Signs of urosepsis warrant empiric coverage for extended-spectrum b-lactamase–producing organisms. Patients improving after parenteral treatment who can take oral fluids may change to oral therapy. Pregnant patients with mild symptoms may be managed as outpatients with suitable parenteral agents if close follow-up is feasible; more severe illness generally requires hospitalisation and supportive care. Following improvement, parenteral therapy may be changed to oral treatment for a total duration of 7–10 d. Men with febrile UTI, pyelonephritis, recurrent infection, or suspected complicating factors should receive at least 2 wk, preferably with a fluoroquinolone, because prostatic involvement is frequent. Tables 5 and 6 provide suggested empiric oral and parenteral regimens, respectively, with doses, durations where given, and qualifications.

  Heading: STATEMENT FOURTEEN
  Content: Stable moderate-risk NLUTD warrants an annual focused history, examination, symptom assessment, and renal function assessment, with upper tract imaging every 1-2 years (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Two systematic reviews and seven observational studies informed the statement; aggregate bias risk was very serious. This category includes patients requiring CIC or indwelling drainage, or with elevated PVR, but without dangerous UDS findings. Annual encounters can identify complications, catheter difficulties, and treatment response. Serum creatinine is convenient but may be misleadingly low with reduced muscle mass; a meaningful rise from baseline deserves assessment even within the normal range. A 24-hour creatinine clearance is more sensitive but burdensome; Cystatin C is less influenced by muscle mass, although cost limits use. Renal US every 1-2 years assesses asymptomatic stones and other findings; existing equivalent interval imaging may suffice. Reported recurrent renal stone rates in long-term SCI studies were 34-64%, and bladder stone recurrence reached 23%, supporting lifelong vigilance. Nuclear renal scanning is more useful for suspected obstruction or deteriorating function than as a substitute for US because it detects stones poorly. The optimal US frequency is uncertain. In one series, 48 SCI patients using CIC with initially safe UDS were followed for a mean of 6.8 years using annual US: 6% developed mild/moderate hydronephrosis and 13% renal calculi, without severe hydronephrosis or new scarring or thinning. Another US study included 1005 SCI patients, 313 with tetraplegia and 692 with paraplegia, examined a mean 32.5 +/- 49.2 months after injury: renal stones occurred in 6%, hydronephrosis in 5.5%, renal atrophy in 1.2%, and bladder trabeculation in 35.1%. Clinicians may extend imaging to every two years for reliably help-seeking patients stable over longer periods and should consider travel burden when arranging tests.

Main conclusion: The authors consider the new EANM/EANO/RANO/SNMMI guidelines an important step toward consistent, evidence-based, and safe use of SSTR-targeted PET imaging and radiopharmaceutical therapy for meningioma. They also emphasize that adequately designed, controlled prospective multicenter trials are needed to support wider clinical adoption.

Narrative summary: This editorial examines the clinical role of SSTR-targeted imaging and radiopharmaceutical therapy for meningioma and the newly developed EANM/EANO/RANO/SNMMI practice guidelines. Although surgery cures most meningiomas, 20%–25% recur and require further treatment. Most meningiomas express SSTRs, particularly SSTR2, providing a basis for the use of radiolabeled SSTR ligands.

The authors describe increasing use of SSTR-targeted PET for differential diagnosis, assessment of tumor extent, surgical and radiotherapy planning, distinguishing recurrence from treatment-related changes, and prognostication. Its use for disease monitoring has also been proposed. Evidence for radiopharmaceutical therapy remains limited to small case series and small, uncontrolled prospective trials. An interim analysis of an ongoing single-arm phase II trial reported that its predefined progression-free survival rate at the 6-mo threshold was met; the analysis also identified [68Ga]Ga-DOTATATE PET as a potentially useful biomarker of treatment response. The first randomized trial of [177Lu]Lu-DOTATATE for recurrent meningioma, LUMEN-1 (NCT06326190), was scheduled to begin enrolling patients in the first quarter of 2025.

The guidelines address PET indications, acquisition, interpretation, and reporting, alongside procedures for radiopharmaceutical therapy. The authors expect them to improve standardization and patient access while stressing the need for adequately designed, controlled prospective multicenter trials before these approaches can be effectively integrated into routine neuro-oncology practice.

Document sections:
  Heading: 1 | Introduction
  Content: Hematuria means RBCs are present in urine and may be visible or detectable only microscopically. It is a fundamental manifestation of glomerulonephritis (GN); microscopic assessment of urinary sediment is presented as its most effective detection method. Birch et al. proposed in 1979 that urinary RBC morphology could distinguish glomerular from non-glomerular origins. Passage through glomeruli can damage RBC membranes and produce dysmorphic RBCs (dRBCs). Shichiri et al. reported in 1988 that erythrocytes were smaller in glomerular than in non-glomerular disease, and Hyodo et al. later proposed an RBC size range of 4–6 μm for discriminating the origins. Compared with blood, urine has much less albumin and more urea; this environment increases membrane vulnerability and changes RBC shape. High urea concentrations particularly favor burr-cell formation. Passage across the glomerular basement membrane may produce acanthocytes through membrane injury. RBCs in renal disease are also more susceptible to factors including iron deficiency, osmotic lysis, shape distortion, and vesicle formation. Reliable recognition of urinary dRBCs requires an experienced observer, and observer-dependent interpretation may explain differences between laboratories. The authors consider continuing education in RBC morphology essential and mention deep learning for microscopy as another possible approach. Instrument-measured small-RBC fractions are easier to obtain and less dependent on interpretation, making them potentially more objective and standardized. The fully automated UF-5000 uses fluorescence flow cytometry to classify urine particles and reports morphological RBC information, including non-lysed RBCs, lysed RBCs, large RBCs, small RBCs, and RBC-Info. Its classification uses forward scatter light (FSC), side scatter light (SSC), side fluorescence light (SFL), and depolarized side scattered light (DSS). A small RBC has FSC intensity < 70; a non-lysed RBC has a strong FSC signal and morphological stability indicated by SSC. URD is the small-RBC count divided by the non-lysed-RBC count. Earlier studies investigated possible clinical uses, but most were single-center studies. Reported cutoffs for distinguishing glomerular from non-glomerular hematuria varied from 30.1% to 40.5% for small RBCs and from 0% to 30.0% for dRBCs. The authors therefore considered a multicenter assessment using the same equipment necessary for clinical application. Across four hospitals, they collected urine microscopy findings, urine measures, serum markers, and kidney-function information to compare institutional dRBC and URD measurements and cutoffs and assess their clinical significance.

  Heading: 3.5. Uncomplicated pyelonephritis
  Content: Uncomplicated pyelonephritis is confined to nonpregnant, premenopausal women without known relevant urological abnormalities or comorbidities. Typical features are fever (>38 C), chills, flank pain, nausea, vomiting, or costovertebral-angle tenderness, with or without cystitis symptoms. Routine diagnostic testing should include urine white and red blood cells and nitrite; every case also requires urine culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Upper-tract ultrasound should exclude obstruction or renal stones in patients with previous urolithiasis, impaired renal function, or high urine pH. Consider contrast-enhanced computed tomography or excretory urography if fever persists after 72 h of treatment, or immediately upon clinical deterioration.   Content: Primary amenorrhea is the main manifestation of genital malformations.   Heading: 4.8.4.3 Management of ureteric fistulae
  Content: Higher-risk operations require surgeons able to protect ureteric blood supply and promptly recognise injury. An intraoperative injury should be repaired immediately using debridement, adequate vascularity, a tension-free anastomosis and internal stenting. After relevant abdominal or pelvic surgery, unexpectedly slow recovery, fluid leakage or pelvicalyceal dilatation should raise suspicion of delayed upper-tract injury. No operative approach has proved superior; consensus favours established tissue-repair principles and experienced teams. Options include internal or external drainage, nephrostomy and stenting, and repair early (< 2 weeks) or later (> 3 months) when needed. Functional and anatomical imaging after repair should detect ureteric stricture or declining renal function. Early postoperative UVF, chiefly following hysterectomy, is the most frequent upper-tract fistula presentation in urological practice. In an RCT of 3,141 women undergoing open or laparoscopic gynaecological surgery, prophylactic ureteric stents did not alter the low injury risk (1%). Selected endoscopic approaches include retrograde or antegrade stenting with nephrostomy, or ureteroscopic realignment, but long-term success is unknown. Distal antegrade ureteric occlusion plus nephrostomy often palliates terminal malignant-fistula leakage. Failure or secondary stricture after endoluminal treatment usually calls for abdominal repair, potentially including end-to-end anastomosis, reimplantation with psoas hitch or Boari flap, or bowel replacement. Nephrectomy is a last resort, particularly with poor function on the affected side and a normal opposite kidney.

Edema caused by inflammation or pressure can resolve when its cause resolves.   Heading: 4.2.1 Epidemiology, aetiology, pathophysiology
  Content: SUI means involuntary urinary loss during effort or physical exertion and has substantial social and economic consequences. The estimated number of US women with UI rises from 18.3 million in 2010 to 28.4 million in 2050. SUI prevalence appears highest at ages 45–59 years. Evidence about ethnicity is inconsistent, although several studies find more SUI among white women than African American or Asian American women. Positive associations include parity, obesity, previous hysterectomy or pelvic surgery, diabetes mellitus, pulmonary disease and physical activity level. A meta-analysis of six studies involving 3,678 cases found three times the SUI risk with metabolic syndrome. Two frequently overlapping mechanisms are inadequate bladder-neck and urethral support causing hypermobility, and intrinsic sphincter weakness associated with trauma, radiotherapy, surgery, neurological disease or ageing. Under the vaginal hammock hypothesis, pelvic support normally helps compress and close the urethra; support damage can instead allow downward urethral movement and bladder-neck funnelling during raised abdominal pressure. Nearly all treatments address both mechanisms, but most tend to work better when some urethral hypermobility is present than with isolated sphincter weakness.

  Content: Evidence establishing causation for proposed environmental risks is generally weak except for tobacco and aristolochic acid. Tobacco exposure increases relative UTUC risk 2.5 to 7.0 fold. A population study including 229,251 relatives of UC cases and 1,197,552 relatives of matched controls found familial aggregation independent of smoking-related behaviour, but not for UTUC, which represented more than 9% of its cohort; the authors inferred that familial aggregation of UC may concern the lower tract specifically. Aristolochic acid from aristolochia plants can irreversibly injure renal proximal tubules, producing chronic tubulointerstitial disease, and its mutagenicity can lead to UTUC. Exposure can occur through agricultural contamination, as described for Balkan endemic nephropathy, or through aristolochiabased herbal remedies. Following bioactivation, persistent aristolactam-deoxyadenosine DNA adducts provide exposure markers and produce a characteristic spectrum dominated by A>T transversions on the non-transcribed DNA strand. Aristolochic acid has also been linked with BC, renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Less than 10% of exposed people are estimated to develop UTUC. Two retrospective series found aristolochic acid-associated UTUC more frequent in females, whose prognosis nevertheless exceeded that of affected males. Arsenic in drinking water together with aristolochia-based remedies appears to produce an additive carcinogenic effect; links between drinking-water arsenic and UTUC in Taiwan and Chile remain tentative. Alcohol may also be associated with UTUC: a case-control study of 1,569 cases and 506,797 controls found significantly greater risk among ever-drinkers than never-drinkers (OR: 1.23; 95% CI: 1.08–1.40, p = 0.001), identified a risk threshold of > 15 g of alcohol/day relative to never-drinkers, and observed a dose–response relationship.

  Description: A bacterial infection of the urinary tract in babies, children and young people under 16. Its diagnosis can be difficult, particularly in children younger than 3 years, because symptoms may be nonspecific and urine collection and interpretation can be challenging.
  Epidemiology: The guideline describes UTI as a common bacterial infection in babies and children but provides no incidence figure.
  Clinical presentation: Features that increase the likelihood of UTI include dysuria, increased urinary frequency, new bedwetting, malodorous, dark or cloudy urine, visible haematuria, reduced fluid intake, fever, shivering, abdominal pain, loin or suprapubic tenderness, capillary refill longer than 3 seconds, and a history of confirmed UTI. Absence of dysuria, nappy rash, breathing difficulties, abnormal chest or ear findings, and fever with a known alternative cause decrease its likelihood but do not necessarily exclude it. The list is not exhaustive; isolated findings should be interpreted with clinical judgement, and multiple findings probably increase the likelihood of UTI.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: acute upper UTI
      Distinguishing features: In babies and children, bacteriuria with fever of 38°C or higher, or bacteriuria with fever lower than 38°C plus loin pain or tenderness, supports this diagnosis.
    - Name: lower UTI (cystitis)
      Distinguishing features: Bacteriuria without systemic symptoms or signs supports this diagnosis in babies and children.
    - Name: atypical UTI
      Distinguishing features: Features include serious illness, poor urine flow, an abdominal or bladder mass, raised creatinine, septicaemia, failure to respond to suitable antibiotics within 48 hours, or infection with non-E. coli organisms.
    - Name: recurrent UTI
      Distinguishing features: Defined by Two or more episodes of UTI with acute upper UTI; One episode of UTI with acute upper UTI plus 1 or more episodes of UTI with lower UTI; or Three or more episodes of UTI with lower UTI.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Urine collection
      Purpose: Obtain a specimen for testing before antibiotics are given to children and young people.
      When indicated: Test when symptoms or signs increase the likelihood of UTI; consider testing an unwell patient if UTI remains suspected despite the absence of listed features. Do not routinely test those aged 3 months and over whose findings suggest another infection, but consider testing if they remain unwell and the diagnosis is uncertain. Collect without delay, ideally obtaining a sample returned within 24 hours if collection at the consultation is not possible.
      Interpretation: Clean catch is preferred where possible. If it is not feasible, use another non-invasive method such as a urine collection pad; if non-invasive collection is impractical or impossible, use a catheter specimen or suprapubic aspiration (SPA). Confirm urine in the bladder by ultrasound before SPA. Do not use cotton wool balls, gauze or sanitary towels for collection.
    - Test: Urine dipstick testing for leukocyte esterase and nitrite
      Purpose: Guide the diagnosis, need for culture and antibiotic decisions.
      When indicated: Use in babies and children between 3 months and 3 years with suspected UTI, and follow the age-specific strategy for children 3 years or older.
      Interpretation: Between 3 months and 3 years, either positive result calls for culture and antibiotics; when both are negative, do not give antibiotics or send microscopy and culture unless a culture criterion applies. At 3 years or older, two positive results support treating UTI, with culture for high or intermediate risk of serious illness or previous UTI. Positive nitrite with negative leukocyte esterase calls for culture and, if the specimen is fresh, antibiotics. Positive leukocyte esterase with negative nitrite calls for microscopy and culture; give antibiotics only if there is good clinical evidence of UTI. Two negative results support seeking another cause rather than treating or culturing for UTI.
    - Test: Urine microscopy
      Purpose: Assess pyuria and bacteriuria.
      When indicated: Obtain urgently, with culture, for suspected UTI in babies under 3 months; obtain with culture for children 3 years or older whose dipstick is positive for leukocyte esterase and negative for nitrite.
      Interpretation: Bacteriuria supports UTI whether or not pyuria is present. Pyuria without bacteriuria supports starting antibiotics if UTI symptoms or signs are present. If both are absent, assume UTI is absent. Clinical findings should guide decisions when a negative urine result conflicts with the presentation because false negatives can occur.
    - Test: Urine culture
      Purpose: Investigate suspected UTI and inform subsequent management.
      When indicated: Send for suspected acute upper UTI, high to intermediate risk of serious illness, age under 3 months, positive leukocyte esterase or nitrite, recurrent UTI, symptoms and signs inconsistent with dipstick findings, or failure to respond within 24 to 48 hours when no specimen has yet been sent. Additional indications depend on the age-specific dipstick strategy.
      Interpretation: If culture cannot occur within 4 hours of collection, refrigerate the specimen immediately or preserve it with boric acid, following the manufacturer's instructions for specimen volume.
    - Test: History and examination
      Purpose: Identify factors associated with UTI or serious underlying pathology.
      When indicated: After UTI is confirmed.
      Interpretation: Record poor urine flow, suspected or confirmed previous UTI, recurrent unexplained fever, an antenatally identified renal abnormality, family history of vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) or renal disease, constipation, dysfunctional voiding, enlarged bladder, abdominal mass, signs of a spinal lesion, poor growth and high blood pressure.
    - Test: Urinary tract ultrasound
      Purpose: Detect structural abnormalities, including obstruction.
      When indicated: During an atypical acute infection and otherwise according to age, response to treatment and recurrence. In toilet-trained children, perform it with a full bladder and estimate bladder volume before and after urination.
    - Test: Dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) scintigraphy scan
      Purpose: Detect renal parenchymal defects.
      When indicated: Perform 4 to 6 months after the acute infection when indicated by the age-specific imaging schedules. If another UTI occurs while awaiting the scan, review its timing and consider an earlier scan.
    - Test: Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG)
      Purpose: Investigate VUR in selected circumstances rather than routinely.
      When indicated: Use according to the age-specific imaging schedules. Between 6 months and under 3 years, consider it if ultrasound shows dilatation, urine flow is poor, infection involves non-E. coli, or there is a family history of VUR.
    - Test: Power doppler ultrasound
      Purpose: Confirm or exclude acute upper UTI when localisation is clinically important.
      When indicated: Use only in rare instances when confirmation or exclusion matters clinically.
    - Test: C-reactive protein
      Purpose: Assessment of UTI localisation.
      Interpretation: Do not use this test alone to distinguish acute upper UTI from lower UTI in babies and children.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Do not routinely arrange follow-up for babies and children who have not undergone imaging, or outpatient follow-up when investigation results are normal. Do not routinely retest urine when the patient is asymptomatic after UTI.
    Recommended tests:
      - For renal parenchymal defects, assess height, weight, blood pressure and proteinuria.
      - Arrange paediatric specialist assessment for recurrent UTI or abnormal imaging.
      - Arrange monitoring by a paediatric nephrologist for bilateral renal abnormalities, impaired kidney function, raised blood pressure or proteinuria.
    Long term effects:
      - UTI and VUR in young children are associated with congenital and acquired renal damage.
      - Progressive renal scarring is documented in children with high grade VUR and recurrent UTI.
      - Renal scarring has been associated with severe hypertension, proteinuria, complications in pregnancy and established renal failure; the frequency and magnitude of these risks in unilateral and bilateral renal damage remain unclear.
    Survivorship notes: Do not offer long-term follow-up solely for minor, unilateral renal parenchymal defects unless recurrent UTI, family history or lifestyle risk factors for hypertension are present. Agree how imaging results will be communicated and provide parents or carers with written results of all investigations.

Document sections:
  Heading: 4.8.4.3 Management of ureteric fistulae
  Content: Higher-risk operations require surgeons able to protect ureteric blood supply and promptly recognise injury. An intraoperative injury should be repaired immediately using debridement, adequate vascularity, a tension-free anastomosis and internal stenting. After relevant abdominal or pelvic surgery, unexpectedly slow recovery, fluid leakage or pelvicalyceal dilatation should raise suspicion of delayed upper-tract injury. No operative approach has proved superior; consensus favours established tissue-repair principles and experienced teams. Options include internal or external drainage, nephrostomy and stenting, and repair early (< 2 weeks) or later (> 3 months) when needed. Functional and anatomical imaging after repair should detect ureteric stricture or declining renal function. Early postoperative UVF, chiefly following hysterectomy, is the most frequent upper-tract fistula presentation in urological practice. In an RCT of 3,141 women undergoing open or laparoscopic gynaecological surgery, prophylactic ureteric stents did not alter the low injury risk (1%). Selected endoscopic approaches include retrograde or antegrade stenting with nephrostomy, or ureteroscopic realignment, but long-term success is unknown. Distal antegrade ureteric occlusion plus nephrostomy often palliates terminal malignant-fistula leakage. Failure or secondary stricture after endoluminal treatment usually calls for abdominal repair, potentially including end-to-end anastomosis, reimplantation with psoas hitch or Boari flap, or bowel replacement. Nephrectomy is a last resort, particularly with poor function on the affected side and a normal opposite kidney.

Document sections:
  Heading: 4.1. Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis
  Content: Early FG manifestations may include localized pain, swelling, erythema, and warmth. Progression can produce fever, chills, generalized weakness, and eventually septic shock. Isolated penile swelling despite normal-appearing skin has also been documented. Clinicians should consider FG with swelling, fever, leukocytosis, or pain disproportionate to examination findings, particularly in older people; genital bruising, crepitus, and bullae are additional reported signs. Diagnosis primarily depends on clinical assessment because treatment is urgent, and suspicion warrants prompt surgical consultation. Laboratory abnormalities include leukocytosis, raised serum creatinine, and metabolic acidosis. Blood cultures help establish the polymicrobial cause and guide antibiotics. CT can delineate perineal anatomy and assess possible retroperitoneal extension. Among FG severity and outcome scores, Fournier Gangrene Severity Index (FGSI) and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) are described as the most reliable predictors of in-hospital mortality. The authors cite a decline in mortality to 7.3% in the last 20 years alongside improvements in care.
